synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
On the night of her father’s birthday, in front of two hundred guests, Aurelia Song’s mother raises a glass and announces that her daughter’s jewellery boutique is losing four million a year and will close in January. Aurelia walks out onto the balcony in gold silk, shaking, doing sums in her head. A stranger at the far end gives her his coat.

Six weeks later, the stranger walks into her boutique and asks to rent it. His name is Chen Si. He runs the Syndicate. He wants her shop for his business. She sets a price instead: a seat at his table.

Then she proposes. Eleven pages, in red ink, with terms. Clause nine is about the bedroom. Clause ten is a single word.

Between them stand a mother who loves only winners, a vice-minister who framed his father, a poisoned glass of wine on New Year’s Eve, a traitor at the table, and a woman who has never once in her life been loved without having to win.

The Woman Who Sets the Price is a sharp, glamorous, power-couple romance about a queen who refuses to be a title, and a man who never once asks her to win.

The main story is told across four volumes and is complete. Side stories at the end can be read any time. Aurelia and Chen Si first appear in Every Flower in the Shop and Proof by Induction, but this book stands on its own.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This book has some dark moments:

• A parent who humiliates her daughter in public, and emotional coercion within a family

• Organised crime, with threats and violence mostly off the page, and a car attack (A Snake in the Syndicate)

• A poisoning, intensive care and a long recovery (Volume Three)

• A panic attack and its aftermath, and therapy (The Word Is Milan)

• Memories of a parent’s wrongful arrest and death in custody, and of a riot and a stabbing in a juvenile detention centre (The Sewer, Nineteen Years Ago)

• Consensual power-play love scenes between a married couple, with a contract, orders, blindfolds, silk ties and a safe word. They are sensual but not explicit

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Aurelia Song was the rival in Every Flower in the Shop: gold, sunglasses, a slap in the rain, a running score. I wanted to know who she was at two in the morning, when nobody was watching her walk. This is her book.

The crime is kept at the level of a story; nothing here is a how-to. The jewellery is as real as I could make it: piercing saws, gravers, box links soldered one at a time, rouge on the wheel for the last pass.

Thank you for reading. Second is just the first of the ones who kept going.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
AURELIA — Aurelia’s jewellery boutique on Harbour Road.
The Syndicate — The organisation Chen Si runs. Thirty years old, and older than him.
The terms — Aurelia’s price for laundering money through her shop: a share, real pieces, the books, no lies, a seat at the table.
The marriage agreement — Eleven clauses, renewable after ten years, when the Wife may rewrite every one. At the renewal, he adds a twelfth and a thirteenth.
Clause twelve — The Wife is not the Husband’s queen.
The word — The safe word written into the agreement. It is “Milan.”
Numero Uno — The necklace she named at two in the morning, after a phone call with her mother.
The Jade Hall — A restaurant on Temple Street with a round table for twelve. It has belonged to the Syndicate for thirty years.
The house on the Peak — Her parents’ house, where the party for her father’s fifty-seventh birthday was held.
The Song Group — Her father’s company.
The Pearl — The restaurant booked for New Year’s Eve, same as always.
Tesoro — Her father’s name for her, from before Vienna.

chapters.title: The Balcony Where He Lent Her His Coat
chapters.desc: Her mother closes her shop in the middle of a birthday toast. Out on the balcony, a stranger lends her his coat and doesn’t try to make it better.
chapters.epigraph: “The world is obsessed with your shine. I’m more interested in what you do in the dark.”
chapters.content:
Aurelia Song knew the toast would be bad. She’d known since Tuesday.

On Tuesday her mother walked into the boutique on Harbour Road without calling. White coat. Dark glasses. She stood in the middle of the shop floor and said nothing at all. She looked at the rings on their velvet. She looked at the necklace in the window. She looked through the workshop door at Enzo, her goldsmith, until Enzo found something urgent to polish. Then Vittoria Song took off her glasses.

“How much did you lose last quarter?”

Italian. Always Italian, for the knives.

“Mamma, the second half is—”

“How much.”

Aurelia told her. You didn’t lie to Vittoria Song. It was like lying to the weather. Her mother put her glasses back on and left. The bell over the door rang behind her, very cheerful. Enzo stopped polishing.

“Cara. Was that… good?”

“No. That was a weather report.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The party was for her father’s fifty-seventh birthday, at the house on the Peak, and two hundred people came. Two hundred people always came when Song Weiren invited them. Bankers. Developers. A deputy minister.

Aurelia wore gold. Bias-cut silk that poured when she walked. Her own earrings. Her mother’s red lipstick.

She was twenty-two. She had been first at everything she’d ever been allowed to compete in, except once, and she was not about to let her mother see her scared.

So she smiled through the champagne. She smiled through the lobster. She smiled at the deputy minister, a soft pink man with wet eyes, who tapped her necklace with one finger.

“Your father’s work?”

“Mine.”

“Ha! Wonderful. Yours!”

He laughed like she’d told a joke. She let him. She was saving it. Then her mother stood and tapped a glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria Song gave toasts the way nurses gave injections. Fast, exact, and somewhere you’d feel for days. She did her husband first. Two languages. The Song Group, the new department store over the border, Harbour Bridge Two, if the right people say yes. The deputy minister smiled into his wine. The room laughed in the right places. Then she turned down the long table.

“And of course, our girls.”

Aurelia’s fingers went tight on the stem of her glass. Here it was.

“Serafina can’t be with us. She is, I believe, under a car somewhere in the industrial district.” A pretty little pause. “We wish her well with that.”

A ripple of nervous laughter. Everyone knew. Serafina had walked out of her own engagement dinner two years ago, at nineteen, and out of the house, and nobody said her name in it any more.

“And Aurelia has a little shop.”

Two hundred heads turned. Aurelia smiled. She’d been smiling through things since she was four, in the front rows of Milan, with her mother’s hand on the back of her neck.

“Jewellery. On Harbour Road. She designs it all herself. Isn’t that charming?” The smile from two covers of Italian Vogue. “It lost four million last year. Weiren and I have agreed to close it in January. We’re so proud of her for trying.”

The glass went up.

“In this family we’ve always said that second place is just the first of the losers. But children have to learn that for themselves.”

She drank. The room hesitated. Then it drank with her. ** She didn’t run. No crying either. Nobody at breakfast was getting the Song girl burst into tears at her father’s party*.

“Excuse me,” she said to the developer on her left, very pleasant.

And she walked. Chin up. Runway pace, drilled into her at eleven. Past the ice swan. Past the quartet. Out through the glass doors, which she closed without a sound. Then she grabbed the stone balustrade with both hands, because her knees had quit.

The whole city lay under her, black and silver. October wind off the water. No sleeves. She didn’t feel it. Four million. Fine. She’d known that. She’d sat up with the accounts every night for a month.

In January. That one she hadn’t known. Cry? Absolutely not. A cold little clerk in the back of her head had already started on the numbers. Second half was better. The necklace in the window has had three enquiries. One serious buyer. One. If I could just—

She was so busy not crying that it took her a while to notice she wasn’t alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

A man stood at the far end of the balcony, in the shadow where the music-room light didn’t reach. Grey suit. Long camel coat. A cup of coffee he obviously hadn’t touched. He was looking at the harbour, not at her. Two hundred people had stared at her all night. This one didn’t even turn his head.

“Sorry,” she said. Her voice came out perfectly level. A miracle. “I didn’t know anyone was out here.”

“I came out before the lobster.” Quiet voice. Educated. An accent she couldn’t place. “I don’t like lobster. Or toasts. I hoped to miss both.”

“You missed a very good toast.”

“I heard it. The doors are glass.”

She shut her eyes. Of course they were. She waited for the kind, useless thing. She didn’t mean it. You look lovely. People always said it.

He said nothing. He let her stand at her end with her hands on the stone. It was the first silence in that house all evening that didn’t feel like an exam.

Then he put the cup down, took off his coat and walked it over to her. He stopped an arm’s length away and held it out. He didn’t try to put it on her.

“I’m not cold.”

“You’re shaking.”

“I’m angry.”

“Yes. I can see.” He didn’t lower the coat. “You can be angry in a coat.”

She looked at him properly then. Twenty-four, maybe twenty-five. Not tall. Slight, and very still, with a calm, handsome face and dark eyes that were looking straight into hers. Was that pity? No. She’d had pity all night. This was something worse. He looked interested. She took the coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was warm from him. Cedar, rain, something bitter like the coffee he wasn’t drinking. It came down to her knees and swallowed her shoulders, and she pulled it shut with both fists and was so grateful she could have screamed.

“Thank you,” she said, through her teeth.

“You’re welcome.”

He went back to his end and picked up his cup.

“Aren’t you going to tell me she didn’t mean it?”

“She meant it.”

The laugh came out of her like a bark. Short. Shocked.

“Aren’t you going to tell me the shop will be fine?”

“I haven’t seen the accounts.” He tipped his head. “I’ve seen the window. The necklace with the broken chain that isn’t broken.”

Her whole body went still inside his coat. That necklace. A heavy collar of yellow gold that looked snapped and mended, the links wrenched apart and soldered back with bright little seams of white gold, so the break was the best part. She’d drawn it at two in the morning on cold coffee. Three enquiries in four months. All three had asked if she could make it without the break.

“You’ve seen it.”

“I walk down Harbour Road every morning. I’ve looked at it every morning for six weeks.” A pause. “I thought whoever made it must know something about breaking.”

What was she supposed to say to that?

“Your mother’s obsessed with your shine,” he said. “The whole room is. The dress, the earrings, how you walked out. Everyone in there is thinking how well you did it.” He looked down at his cup. “I’m more interested in what you do in the dark. At two in the morning, when nobody’s watching you walk.”

She had nothing. Not one word.

“Who are you?”

Most of his smile happened in his eyes.

“Someone who doesn’t like lobster.”

The wind came up and the coat fell open at her throat. He looked at it. Then he walked the length of the balcony again, set his cup by her hand, and took the two lapels of his own coat and drew them together under her chin. He turned the collar up. One side. Then the other. His knuckles touched her throat, right where her pulse was going like a drum. He felt it. She knew he felt it. He didn’t move his hands. He looked at her mouth. Her mother’s red. She’d bitten half of it off during the toast.

“I’d like to kiss you,” he said. The way you’d tell someone the time. “I’m not going to. You came out here to be angry, not to be kissed by a stranger in front of a glass door.” His thumb shifted on the lapel, a centimetre from her jaw, and stopped. “I wanted you to know I’d thought about it.”

She should have been offended. She’d been offended by much less tonight.

“And if I said yes?”

He let go of the coat one finger at a time, like each one was being taken off him.

“Then I’d wait until your hands were steady.” A beat. “And I wouldn’t ask.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The doors banged open behind her. Quartet. Laughter. One of her father’s assistants, red in the face.

“Miss Song! Your mother’s asking for… the cake, they’re bringing the—”

He saw the coat. He saw the man a step from her. He went grey.

“Mr. Chen. Sorry, I’m so sorry, I didn’t… the minister was looking for you, sir.”

The man shifted half a step, so he stood between her and the door. Not much. Enough.

“Tell the minister I’ll be in shortly.”

The assistant fled. Mr. Chen. Everybody knew that name, and everybody said it lower. Her father had said it once at dinner and changed the subject. Her mother had said it once on the phone, in Italian, in a voice that on anyone else Aurelia would have called scared.

“Chen Si,” she said.

He gave one small nod. She looked down at the camel cashmere. The coat of a man her father wouldn’t do business with. A man the newspapers never named, because the newspapers weren’t stupid. Take it off, Aurelia. Hand it back. Go in. Eat the cake. Smile. She pulled it tighter.

“I’m keeping this. Until I go in.”

“Keep it as long as you like.”

He picked up his cup and went to the doors. There he stopped and looked back at her, and he looked too long. Not at the dress. At her face, her bitten mouth, her fists holding his coat shut.

“The necklace. Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break.”

He went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car down the Peak, Qian Yu sat with the laptop open on his knees and waited. Six years working for Chen Si. You learned when to wait.

“Harbour Road. Number eighteen.”

“The boutique, sir? The one in the toast?”

“Last year’s accounts. This year’s. Who supplies her gold. Who her landlord is. What she pays the old man at the bench.”

Qian typed. Then stopped.

“Those are private accounts, sir.”

“So were the minister’s.”

Qian typed faster. Chen Si watched the city go by. Six weeks he’d walked past that window. Six weeks he’d thought about a stranger who understood breaking. Tonight the stranger had a face. A gold dress. A pulse he could still feel on his knuckles if he closed his hand. He closed his hand.

“Draft a letter. A commercial arrangement concerning the premises.”

Qian looked up. “What kind of arrangement?”

“An insulting one.”

“Sir?”

“She’ll hate it.” Chen Si watched the harbour lights slide by. “I’d like to see what she does when she hates something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t go back in for the cake. She went down the side stairs and out of the garden gate and called a car. At midnight she let herself into the boutique in a gold dress and a man’s coat, turned on one lamp, sat at her bench in the back, and drew. She drew until the windows went grey.

At home she hung the coat on the back of her bedroom door. It hung there a week. Ridiculous. On the third night she put it on over her pyjamas. Turned the collar up, one side, then the other. Lay on top of the covers in the dark and thought about I’d like to kiss you said like the time. About knuckles on her throat. She didn’t sleep much. Was that his fault? Completely.

On the eighth day a letter came to the shop. Thick cream paper. No letterhead. A client would like to discuss a commercial arrangement concerning the premises at 18 Harbour Road. Two initials. C.S. Enzo read it over her shoulder and put a hand on his heart.

“Madonna. Is that… is that him?”

Aurelia folded the letter in half. She went home, took the coat off the back of the door, and laid it over her arm.

“Mind the shop,” she said. “Back after lunch. If I’m not, call my sister.”

chapters.title: The Man Who Wanted to Rent Her Shop
chapters.desc: He comes to her shop offering to wash his money through it. She hands him back his own letter, covered in red ink.
chapters.epigraph: “You want my shop. I want a seat at your table. Those are the terms.”
chapters.content:
The letter gave Tuesday at eleven, and Aurelia spent the whole morning getting ready not to impress him.

Black dress. Long sleeves. One ring. No gold at her throat at all, which felt like going out without skin. She had decided at six that morning that she was not going to dazzle Chen Si. She was going to make him look at the work.

The coat hung on the back of a chair by the counter. Dry-cleaned. On a hanger. A note pinned to the collar in her writing. Thank you. A.

Enzo leaned out of the workshop door with his magnifying glasses on his forehead.

“You polished the cases twice.”

“They were dirty.”

“They were not dirty, cara. They were terrified.”

The bell rang. One minute early. Of course.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in alone. Grey again, a different grey. Two coffees from the café across the road, lids on. He stopped just inside the door and looked round her shop like a buyer from one of the big houses in Milan. Not at the jewellery. At the room. The cases, the lights, the angle of the windows, the workshop door, the safe.

Then at her.

“Miss Song.”

“Mr. Chen.” She came round the counter and didn’t offer her hand. “Your coat.”

He looked at it, and at the little note.

“You had it cleaned.”

“It smelled of my father’s house.”

The corner of his mouth moved. He set one coffee on her counter, on a folded napkin, and slid it towards her.

“Oat milk. No sugar. Extra hot.”

She stared at the cup.

“How do you know that?”

“You buy it every morning before you open. The girl at the café writes your name on it with a heart.” He took the coat off the chair and folded it over his arm. “I asked her to stop doing the heart.”

“You what?”

“It seemed familiar of her.”

Was that a joke? His face said no. Her stomach said something else entirely, and she told it to shut up.

“Your letter mentioned a commercial arrangement. I assume you didn’t walk past my window for six weeks because you wanted a ring.”

“No. I thought about buying the necklace.” He looked at the window, where it lay on its black velvet throat. “Then I thought you’d sell it to me, and I’d never see it in the window again. I like walking past it.”

What did you say to that? Nothing. She said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her what he wanted at the counter, in a low, even voice, like he was reading out train times.

He wanted to use the shop.

Not buy it. Use it. He had associates abroad who needed to move value from one place to another, quietly, without banks. Gold was gold everywhere. Stones were small. A real boutique with a real designer and real customers was the best place in the world for money to change clothes.

“That’s the shape of it. I won’t bore you with the rest.” He turned his coffee cup a quarter turn and didn’t drink it. “You’d be paid a fee. A generous one. Enough to cover last year’s four million, and next year’s. Your mother wouldn’t close you in January.”

“And I’d do what?”

“Sign certain invoices. Not ask about certain customers.”

Aurelia looked at him across her own counter.

“You want to wash your money through my shop.”

“Yes.”

“And pay me to look the other way.”

“Yes.”

“After six weeks of staring at my necklace. That’s what you came to say.”

“I find it’s best to be clear.”

She let him wait. Then she smiled.

It wasn’t her mother’s smile. She had last used this one at sixteen, in a school library, reading a boy’s private notebook out loud, and the whole school had taken a step back.

“No.”

He didn’t look surprised.

“May I ask why?”

“You can ask.” She walked round the end of the counter and ran one finger along the case of emeralds. “You thought I was a socialite with a hobby. Rich girl. Little shop. Humiliated at Daddy’s party.”

“That isn’t—”

“So grateful to be rescued she’d sign anything!” She glanced back over her shoulder. “That’s what you thought on the balcony, isn’t it? She’s desperate.”

“I thought you were angry. I still think so.”

“I’m furious. I’m not desperate. And I’m not for hire.”

She went into the workshop. Enzo was bent over his bench, pretending so hard to set a stone that his ears had gone red. She took a sheet of paper off her own bench and came back and laid it in front of Chen Si.

His own letter. Thick cream paper. No letterhead. Two initials.

She’d written all over it in red ink.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it without picking it up. Slowly. Every word. At the top, in red capitals: COUNTER-OFFER.

“One,” he read aloud. “No fee.”

“I don’t want your money. I want a share.”

“Twenty per cent of every piece that passes through for my associates. Into an account in your name that I don’t touch.” He looked up. “Twenty.”

“Keep reading.”

“Two. Every piece is a real piece. Designed by you, made in your workshop.” His eyebrows went up a millimetre. “If I am going to be a front, I am going to be the best front in Asia.”

“I’m not putting my name on paste.”

“Three. You see the books. All of them.”

“I don’t sign what I haven’t read.”

“Four. You’re not to be lied to. Ever.”

“Ever.”

“Five. A seat at my table. Not as your laundress. As your partner.” He stopped. His eyebrows stayed up. “Six.”

She folded her arms.

He read it to himself first. Then out loud, flatly. “You will never again stand on a balcony and decide I am desperate.”

Was the most dangerous man in the city trying not to laugh? He was. His mouth had gone very straight. His eyes hadn’t.

“Number six…”

“Is not negotiable.”

“I gathered.” He picked up the page at last. “Twenty per cent.”

“The going rate for a fee is five. I asked. Discreetly. A man who used to buy watches for my father.” She tapped the case. “You were going to offer me eight, because I’m young and you think I don’t know.”

“Am I.”

“I want twenty. Without me you’ve got a window and no designer. And customs in Milan know my mother’s name. Nobody looks twice at a crate with mine on it.”

“Who told you I’d offer eight?”

“Nobody. I guessed.” She smiled. “You just told me.”

There was a pause in the boutique on Harbour Road. A tram went by outside.

Then Chen Si laughed.

It came out short and low and startled, like he’d forgotten the noise was in him. He put his hand over his mouth and turned his face away. When he turned back his eyes were bright.

“I’ve negotiated with ministers.”

“Congratulations.”

“With men holding guns. With my own brother, and he doesn’t speak.” He set the page down. “Nobody has ever got my number out of me in four minutes.”

“Then you’ve been negotiating with idiots.”

“So it seems.”

She’d put both hands flat on the glass, because they wanted to do something stupid and she wouldn’t let them. He looked at them. Red ink ran down the side of her right forefinger, where she’d pressed too hard on number six.

He reached across the glass and took that hand. Didn’t ask. Turned it palm up to look at the ink, like it was his.

“There’s nothing in your six points about this.”

Take it back, Aurelia. Number four. Number five. Not for hire.

She left it there. Her fingers curled towards his. Traitors.

He bent his head over her hand, across her own counter, and kissed the inside of her wrist just below the ink. Slowly. He stayed long enough to feel her pulse jump under his mouth, and when he lifted his head his eyes had gone dark and he didn’t bother pretending they hadn’t.

“Thank you,” he said, and let her go.

She put the hand behind her back like he’d burned it. Her face was on fire. She had read a boy’s notebook to a whole school without going pink, and here she was, in her own shop, scarlet over a wrist.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say yes.

He put the coat on. He picked up his coffee, still full. He folded her counter-offer in half and slid it into his inside pocket, on the left, and went to the door.

“Number five,” he said, with his back to her. “The table. You understand what table it is?”

“I understand what the newspapers don’t print about you.” She lifted her chin. “I was first in my year at school two years running. I can read.”

“Two years.” He turned round. “What happened the third?”

The cold went straight down her spine.

“Someone else came first.” Flat. Perfectly flat. “She didn’t even try.”

He looked at her face. What did he see? She didn’t want to know.

“I’ll think about it. All six.”

“How long?”

“A week.”

“You have three days. After that I’ll find someone else to laugh at my terms.”

He opened the door. The bell. Traffic, a tram, the chestnut man on the corner shouting prices.

“Nobody else will laugh at them, Miss Song.”

“Why not?”

“They won’t realise you mean it.”

He went out.

Through the window she watched him stop at the necklace. He looked at it the way he said he did every morning. Then he looked up through the glass at her, behind the counter, arms folded, one ring.

He lifted the coffee cup an inch. Like a toast.

Then he walked on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Enzo was at his bench with his tweezers in the air and no stone in them at all.

“Well?”

Aurelia sat down on her own stool, hard.

“He laughed.”

The tweezers went down. Enzo Bellini. Sixty-three, formerly of Valenza, the best bench jeweller she’d ever met. He’d followed her here from Milan when nobody else would. He took his magnifiers off his forehead and looked at her over the top of them.

“Chen Si laughed.”

“Yes.”

“Cara. Seven years I have lived in this city. I have heard many things about that man. Never once that he laughs.”

“Well. He does. Badly! Like a car that won’t start.”

Enzo picked his tweezers back up.

“So either you are going to be very rich, or we are both going to be at the bottom of the harbour.”

“Which?”

He set the stone. It went in first time. His hands were steadier than his voice.

“I think you should start designing something with a great deal of gold in it. Just in case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Qian Yu put the folder on the desk on the thirty-ninth floor and stepped back from it, like it might go off.

“Everything, sir. As asked.”

Chen Si opened it. Her accounts, this year and last. Her landlord. Her supplier in Valenza. Enzo’s salary, which was too generous by a third. A Milan school report from when she was nine, in Italian, with eccellente in every box. Her rankings here. First. First.

Third year: second. Above her, a name he knew. Lin Elowen.

He’d known that before he asked her. He’d wanted to see her face when he did. He had seen it.

Behind the rankings, clipped in order, every review AURELIA had ever had. A fashion column from last spring. Two lines in a trade paper. A blog by a girl who’d bought earrings and cried about them. He read the blog twice. Then he took it out of the folder and put it in the drawer he kept locked.

Qian watched him do it and very wisely said nothing.

“The girl at the café, sir. She asked me this morning if she’s in trouble.”

“Why would she be in trouble?”

“The heart.”

“No.” Chen Si turned a page. “Tip her. She spells the name right.”

Chen Si unfolded the red ink and smoothed it flat on the desk.

“Sir.” Qian cleared his throat. “If I may. Twenty per cent is…”

“Yes.”

“The men won’t like it.”

“No.”

“Mr. Sun won’t like it.”

Chen Si uncapped his pen.

“Then Mr. Sun can come and tell her so.” He wrote one word under the first point. “I’d like to watch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The courier came on the evening of the third day. Flat envelope. Inside was her own counter-offer, her red ink on his cream paper.

Under every point, in a small exact black hand, one word.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

And under number six:

Agreed. With pleasure.

At the bottom he’d added a seventh point of his own.

7. Dinner. Thursday. To discuss the books. You choose the restaurant. I’d like to see what you choose. C.S.

Enzo read it over her shoulder and made a noise like a kettle.

“Thursday! What will you wear? Not black. You looked like a widow.”

“I looked serious.”

“You looked like you were burying him.”

She picked up her red pen. Under number seven she wrote:

Agreed. Not lobster.

She sent it back by the same courier. Then she sat at her bench and drew nothing for an hour, which was a first.

Her phone buzzed.

Unknown number: Not lobster. Noted.

She stared at it.

Aurelia: how do you have this number

Unknown number: You gave it to the café. For the loyalty card.

Aurelia: that is DEEPLY illegal

Unknown number: Yes.

Aurelia: …

Unknown number: You’re on your ninth stamp. The tenth is free.

She saved the number under Do Not Answer.

Then she lay awake until two, answering it in her head.

chapters.title: Aurelia Negotiates a Don Into a Corner
chapters.desc: She takes him to a basement with no menu and finds a thief in his books before the fish goes cold. Under a streetlamp, he stops waiting.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t drink things people give me. I drink things I take.”
chapters.content:
She chose a basement.

Old town. Under a shop that sold funeral paper. Down a flight of stone steps so narrow you went sideways in heels. Eleven tables, no menu, white tiles like a hospital, plastic chairs. A cook called Old Fan, who had been there forty years and decided what you ate by looking at your face.

The chilli oil was the best in the province. That wasn’t an opinion.

She’d been coming since she was sixteen. Since the week after the library, when she walked out of school at lunch with her face still burning, got lost in the old town on purpose, and went down the first steps that looked like nowhere her mother would ever set foot.

She had never brought anyone.

Black trousers. Cream silk shirt. Flat shoes, because of the steps. Gold, because he wasn’t seeing her without it twice.

Old Fan looked up from his wok.

“Ah. Princess.”

Then he saw the man coming sideways down the steps behind her, grey suit, leather folder under one arm, a coffee he wasn’t drinking. Old Fan put his ladle down. Wiped his hands. Bowed from the waist.

“Mr. Chen.”

“Uncle Fan.” Chen Si bowed back.

Aurelia looked from one to the other.

“You know each other?”

“His brother drove my father. Twenty years ago.” Chen Si looked round the white room. The card players in the corner. The calendar from 2009. “You chose this.”

“You said you wanted to see what I’d choose.”

“I thought it would be the Peninsula. The roof at the Harbour Hotel. Somewhere with a view.” He set the folder on the table by the wall. “I didn’t think it would be somewhere I used to come with my mother.”

Oh. Oh no.

“I didn’t know.”

“I know you didn’t.” He pulled out a plastic chair for her. “That’s why I like it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Fan brought food without asking. Smashed cucumber with garlic. Pork belly in chilli oil so red it was nearly black. A whole fish in a clay pot, still bubbling. Rice. A big green bottle of beer for her, no glass. Tea for him.

Chen Si looked at the bottle.

“You drink from the bottle.”

“Here I do.” She did. “My mother would die. Open the folder.”

He opened it.

The books. Not all of them, he said straight away. “Not yet. You’ll see why.” But a lot. Ledgers for four companies. A shipping firm. A property developer. A chain of pawnshops. An importer of Italian furniture. Bank statements in three languages. Columns of figures in a small exact hand she recognised from the bottom of her counter-offer.

“You keep these yourself?”

“Some.” He picked up his tea and didn’t drink it. “I don’t trust accountants. I trust one, a little. He’s seventy and very frightened of me. I check his work.”

She pulled the first ledger across the table, past the fish.

“May I?”

“That’s what they’re for.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she tried to explain it to Enzo and couldn’t.

It was like the first time she’d put a loupe to a stone. The room went away. The wok, the card players, the fish. Him, even. There was just the page and the pattern under the numbers, swimming up into focus like the silk inside a sapphire.

She read for forty minutes without saying a word.

He didn’t interrupt her once. When Old Fan came to take the fish, Chen Si shook his head and Old Fan went away. When she reached out for the beer without looking, he moved it ten centimetres so her hand landed on it.

Somewhere in the second ledger she noticed her bowl had filled up. Fish. White, clean, every bone gone. A neat little pile of bones sat on the side of his plate. His chopsticks were already back on their rest.

When had he done that? She hadn’t seen him do it.

She ate it anyway. Without looking up. Like it was normal.

It was not normal.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Here.”

She turned the ledger round and put her finger on a line.

“The furniture company. Milan to here. Walnut dining tables. Twelve in March. Declared at eight thousand euros each, sold to a hotel on the east side for ninety.”

“Something like that.”

“I’m not asking how. I can see how.” She flipped two pages. “But June. Eighteen tables. Same prices. Except when the money comes back, only sixty goes where the rest of your money goes.” Another page. “Thirty thousand a table doesn’t.”

He didn’t move.

“That’s over half a million. It goes to a different account, at a different bank. Again in August. Again in September.”

The card players had stopped arguing. Old Fan’s ladle had stopped scraping.

“Someone’s taking a slice of your slice. Someone who knows the hotel, and the furniture, and your accountant’s handwriting. It only looks wrong if you read the whole year at once.” She sat back. “And you don’t. You check his work month by month. That’s why you missed it.”

Chen Si looked at the line under her finger. Kept looking.

“How long have you been reading?”

“Forty-one minutes.”

“He’s had those books for two years.”

“He’s seventy and frightened of you. Frightened people don’t go looking for things they don’t want to find.” She picked up the bottle. “I’m not frightened of you.”

“No.” Something moved in his face. “You really aren’t, are you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t ask who she thought it was.

She noticed that. He closed the folder and laid his hand flat on it and looked at the tiles. Thinking three moves out. Four. When he looked back at her his face was perfectly calm.

“Thank you. That changes things.”

“I hoped it would.” She put her elbows on the table. Her mother would have died about that too. “So here’s what else changes.”

“Go on.”

“You agreed to six points. Seven, with dinner. But you agreed because you thought I’d make a pretty front with a nasty temper. You didn’t think I’d find half a million in forty-one minutes.” She smiled. “So the price has gone up.”

“Has it.”

“Twenty-five per cent.”

He just looked at her.

“And the furniture company. I want it. Not the man running it. I don’t care what you do with him. The route. Milan’s my city. I speak the language. I know the customs men by their first names. I know which ports my mother’s friends use and which they don’t.”

“And?”

“And you’ve got a man who can’t tell walnut from veneer running Italian furniture for you, and someone’s robbing you through his paperwork.” She picked up her chopsticks. “Give it to me and nobody robs you again. I’ll read every line, every month.”

“That’s your counter-offer.”

“Twenty-five and the Milan route. Take it or leave it.” She pointed her chopsticks at the clay pot. “The fish is getting cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat back in his plastic chair.

He looked at her so long that she wondered, for one second, if she’d gone too far. Was this where the mild man in the grey suit turned into the thing the papers didn’t name?

He reached across the table, past the fish, and picked up her beer.

He drank from it. One long swallow, straight from the bottle. Put it back exactly where it had been.

“Done.”

She stared at him.

“You don’t drink. You hold coffee and never touch it. You’ve been holding that tea for an hour.”

“I don’t drink things people give me.” He looked at the bottle. “I drink things I take.”

That went right through her, and it had nothing at all to do with business.

She looked at the bottle, at the place his mouth had been. Then at him. He was watching her with that interested look, only darker now. He didn’t look away.

“Twenty-five,” he said. “And Milan. And the seat. And you read every line. And you come to the next meeting, Thursday. With the men who run the routes.”

“Fine.”

“They’ll hate you. They’ll try to frighten you. I won’t stop them.”

“Why not?”

“I want to watch you do to them what you just did to me.”

She couldn’t help it. She grinned.

“You’ve been negotiated into a corner, Mr. Chen.”

“Yes.” He picked up his chopsticks, finally, and took a piece of the cold fish. “I walked in. I wanted to see what it looked like.”

“And?”

He chewed. Swallowed.

“Fan’s fish is better than I remembered.”

Old Fan, who had been listening from the wok the entire time, banged his ladle on the edge.

“Better? BETTER? Forty years the same fish!”

“I was twelve, Uncle.”

“So you had no taste. Now you have taste.” Old Fan jabbed the ladle at Aurelia. “Because of her. Princess never brings anyone. Never! Six years!”

“Uncle Fan…”

“He picked the bones out of your fish. I saw! My wife never did that for me in thirty years!”

“Your wife’s been dead for ten,” said one of the card players.

“And before that, NEVER.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he walked her up the stone steps. Sideways, him first, so if she slipped in the dark she’d land on him.

She didn’t slip.

At the top the old town smelled of incense and frying garlic. Two doors down a woman was screaming about the price of a fish. They stood under a streetlamp outside the funeral-paper shop, him with the folder under his arm, her with her hands in her trouser pockets.

He stepped close enough that she had to tip her head back. He took one of her hands out of her pocket. Not a handshake. He held it, and his thumb went once across her knuckles, and stayed.

He looked down at it. Her hand. Perfectly steady. She’d never held still so well in her life.

“I said I’d wait until your hands were steady.” His thumb stopped. “I’ve been waiting since the balcony.”

“You took my beer without asking.”

She’d meant it as a joke. It came out much lower.

“Yes,” he said.

And took her mouth the same way.

His free hand came up along her jaw and tipped her face and he kissed her like he’d stood outside a shop window for six weeks waiting to. Not careful. Not mild. Not anything she’d guessed. He opened her mouth with his and she tasted chilli and beer and something underneath that was only him, and her other hand came out of her pocket and grabbed the front of his jacket in a fist. The folder hit the pavement. Nobody picked it up.

When he lifted his head she was breathing like she’d run up the steps.

So was he. The most dangerous man in the city, under a streetlamp in the old town, his forehead almost on hers, breathing like she’d hit him.

“I don’t want to go yet,” he said against her temple. “I’m telling you so you know. I’m going anyway.”

“Why?”

“Because if I stay, I won’t let you go home.” He kissed the corner of her mouth, quick, like initialling a page. “And you haven’t read the rest of the books.”

✦ ✦ ✦

A long black car waited at the corner. A very large man stood beside it with his hands at his sides.

“Your driver?”

“My brother. He insists on Thursdays.”

The very large man looked at her. He didn’t blink. Did he blink ever?

“He doesn’t look like your brother.”

“We’re not related. A different kind of brother.” Chen Si bent and picked up the folder. “Zhendong. Miss Song.”

The very large man considered her. It took ages.

“Hm.”

That was all. That was the entire speech.

“He likes you.”

“How can you possibly tell?”

“He didn’t check you for a weapon.”

The bark came out of her before she could stop it, and Chen Si looked at her laughing under the streetlamp like he was writing it down somewhere.

“Goodnight, Miss Song.”

“Goodnight, Mr. Chen.”

He let go of her hand last. He went towards the car. Halfway there he turned round.

“Aurelia.”

He’d never said it before. It stopped her dead.

“The thirty thousand a table. You know whose account it is.”

“No, I don’t.”

“You do. You saw the bank. You saw where the branch is.” He was quiet a moment. “You didn’t say, because you weren’t sure if I knew. You didn’t want to watch my face find out. In case it was someone I loved.”

She said nothing. What was there to say? He was right.

“It isn’t. I don’t love many people. Tell me Thursday.”

He got in. The very large man looked at her once more over the roof of the car, and got in too.

The car slid away down the narrow street. She stood under the lamp with the taste of him still in her mouth and her hand still curled like it had his jacket in it.

I am in so much trouble.

And the cold little clerk who’d done the sums on her father’s balcony said, very clearly:

Good.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, Zhao drove with one hand and said nothing for three streets.

Chen Si looked at the folder on his knee. There was grit on the leather from the pavement. He didn’t brush it off.

“Short list.” Zhao didn’t take his eyes off the road.

“Shorter than you’d think.”

He took out his phone and typed one line to Qian. Which of ours banks in the east district. Quietly. Touch nothing.

Zhao glanced at him in the mirror. At his mouth.

“Hm.”

“Don’t.”

Another street. The harbour came up in the windscreen, black and gold.

“Song’s daughter.”

“Yes.”

“She drank from the bottle.”

“Yes.”

Zhao turned onto the harbour road. His face did nothing at all.

“She’ll eat you.”

Chen Si looked out at the water.

“I know.”

He sounded pleased about it. Zhao nearly missed the turn.

chapters.title: Aurelia Song Does Not Do Second Place
chapters.desc: The men who run his routes take away her chairs, so she sits in his. Then she kisses him in it and wins every hand of mahjong in the building.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one of a room full of men who want you gone: sit down first.”
chapters.content:
The meeting room on the thirty-ninth floor had one long black table and one enormous window, and the window looked straight across the harbour at her father’s office.

Song Group Tower. Forty storeys of gold glass, with SONG across the top in letters three metres high. You could see it from every chair at the table.

Had Chen Si picked this room on purpose? Obviously he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were five of them, and they were already sitting down.

All on one side, backs to the window. Good suits that didn’t fit. A man with a shaved head and a gold watch the size of a saucer. A thin man in tinted glasses. A heavy man eating sunflower seeds out of his jacket pocket and spitting the shells into a coffee cup. A small neat man in a cardigan who looked like he marked homework for a living.

And at the end, a tall grey-haired man with a kind, tired, handsome face, who stood up when she came in. Nobody else did.

“Miss Song. I’m Sun Wei. I’ve heard a great deal about you.”

“From who?”

He had a lovely smile. Warm. Fatherly. “From Chen Si. He doesn’t usually talk about anyone.”

“Then you’ve heard more than most.”

Chen Si wasn’t there. On purpose. They’ll hate you. They’ll try to frighten you. I won’t stop them. He wasn’t there because he wanted to see what happened when he wasn’t.

At the head of the table, one empty chair. His. Five full chairs along the window. And on the other side, facing the window, nothing. No chairs at all. Somebody had carried them out.

The sunflower man spat a shell into his cup.

“You can stand. Won’t take long.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at the empty side of the table. Then at the empty chair at the head of it.

Then she walked the whole length of the room in her heels. Dark green suit, gold buttons, made overnight by a tailor who owed her mother a favour. Past all five of them. She pulled out the chair at the head of the table and sat down in it.

Crossed her legs. Put her bag on the table. Folded her hands on top. You could have heard a sunflower seed drop.

“Rule one of a room full of men who want you gone.” She was very pleasant about it. “Sit down first. My mother taught me. Most of what she taught me was about walking. That one was about chairs.”

The shaved head laughed. Not nicely.

“That’s the boss’s chair, little girl.”

“And he isn’t here, and I am, and somebody took all the others away. So I assumed this one was mine.” She smiled at the sunflower man. “Unless you’d like to give me yours?”

The sunflower man stopped chewing.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the room next door, Chen Si sat in front of Qian’s laptop with his coffee and watched her do it.

The camera in the corner of the ceiling gave him the whole table. Five men. One woman. His chair.

Qian stood behind him and made a noise like a man swallowing a fishbone.

“Sir. She’s in your chair.”

“I can see.”

“Nobody’s ever… sir, should I go in and…”

“No.”

On the screen she tipped her head at something the shaved head said. She looked bored. She looked like she owned the building. Only he could see her left thumb, under the table, pressing so hard into her ring that the skin had gone white.

He watched that thumb. Ten seconds, she’d lasted, with five men laughing at her, before she sat down in the one place in the building nobody sat. He’d been sure she’d stand. He’d been wrong. He couldn’t remember the last time he’d enjoyed being wrong. Then he stood up and buttoned his jacket.

“Bring a chair. An ordinary one.”

“Where do I put it?”

“Next to her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Miss Song.” Sun Wei had sat back down. He looked amused. He also looked like he was doing sums. “Nobody means you disrespect. We were told Chen Si was bringing a… consultant. A designer. For the Milan route.” He spread his hands. “These gentlemen have run the routes twenty years. Some of them since before he was born. They’re not used to advice from a young lady with a shop.”

“A shop that lost four million.” The tinted glasses. “We read the papers too.”

“Then you read that my mother’s closing it in January.”

“We did.”

“She isn’t. I’m keeping it open. With my share of the Milan route.” She turned her head. “Which used to be yours, I think? The furniture.”

The tinted glasses went white.

The door opened. Chen Si came in with a coffee. Qian came in behind him, carrying an office chair on wheels like it was a bomb.

Chen Si stopped. He looked at the five men. At the bare side of the table. At his own chair, with Aurelia Song in it, legs crossed, hands folded on her bag, smiling.

Nobody breathed. His face did nothing at all.

Qian put the office chair at the corner of the table, at her right hand. Chen Si sat in it. He set his coffee down and looked along the row.

“I see you’ve met my partner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting lasted two hours. She would remember almost none of the numbers and all of the rest.

The sunflower man tried to talk over her three times. Chen Si didn’t stop him. She didn’t stop either, until the third time. Then she just stopped talking and looked at him. He kept going for a bit. His voice ran down like a cheap clock. Everyone at the table was looking at him.

“Are you finished?” she asked kindly, and went on.

The tinted glasses spent ten minutes explaining why the customs office in Milan was impossible. She took out her phone, rang a number and talked very fast in Italian for two minutes.

“Dottor Rossi says the November shipment will be cleared on the fourteenth.” She put the phone face down. “He sends his love to my mother.”

The tinted glasses took his glasses off. Put them back on. Didn’t speak again all afternoon.

The cardigan said nothing for an hour and a half. Then, right at the end, he leaned forward.

“A stone with no papers. How would you value it?”

She told him. Properly. With a diagram on the back of her agenda, a loupe from her bag and a bit of swearing about Thai heat treatment. He listened with his head on one side like a sparrow.

Then he sat back and said to Chen Si, “She’s right. I’ve been doing it wrong for nine years.”

And Sun Wei, at the far end by the window, smiling his warm, tired smile, said almost nothing, and watched her the whole time.

And Chen Si, at her right hand, in an office chair on wheels, said nothing at all. No help. No interruptions. He sat back with his cold coffee and watched her take his table apart. There was something on his face she didn’t dare look at straight. Every time she did, her sentence fell off a cliff. Was he enjoying this? He was. The bastard was having the time of his life.

✦ ✦ ✦

When it was over the five men filed out.

The sunflower man didn’t look at her. The tinted glasses didn’t look at her. The cardigan stopped by her chair, gave a little bow, and said, “Miss Song.” So that was one.

Sun Wei came last. He stopped in the doorway.

“Remarkable. Truly. Twenty years, and I haven’t seen anything like it.” He smiled at Chen Si. “You’ve found yourself a treasure, Si.”

“Yes. I have.”

The door shut.

Aurelia let out the breath she’d been holding for two hours and put both hands flat on the table, because they’d started to shake. Great. Now they shook.

“Well?”

He didn’t answer. She turned her head. He was sitting in the office chair with her father’s tower glittering behind him across the water, looking at her.

“You sat in my chair.”

“They took the others away.”

“I know. I told them to.”

She stared at him.

“You told them to?”

“I wanted to see what you’d do. Most people stand. Some leave. One man sat on the floor.” He tilted his head. “Nobody’s sat in my chair.”

“Are you angry?”

“No. I’m something else. I haven’t decided what.”

He leaned over and put his hand on top of hers on the black table, right over the shaking, and pressed it flat. He held it there until it stopped. No asking. His eyes never left her face.

“That’s a lie. I know exactly what.”

Oh.

“Since Thursday I’ve thought about very little else.” His hand stayed on hers. “I’d like to do it again. Here. You can say no. Five men just spent two hours telling you what to do. I’m not going to be the sixth.”

She didn’t say no.

She leaned forward in his chair and took his tie in her free hand, the way she’d pick up a chain to check the clasp, and pulled him the last few inches herself.

Under the streetlamp, he’d taken it. This time she did. First, and without anybody’s permission, the same way she’d sat down at his table. He made a low noise against her mouth and let her. His hand clamped tight over hers on the glass. He didn’t try to take over. When she let go of his tie he stayed exactly where she’d left him, an inch away, eyes gone black.

“There.” Not steady. Not even close. “Now I’ve done that in your chair too.”

“I’m never getting through a meeting in this room again.”

She needed to say something that wasn’t about his mouth. Anything.

“Sun Wei.”

He didn’t move.

“The account. It’s his, isn’t it? The branch is in the district his wife’s family comes from.”

“Yes.”

“You knew.”

“Since Thursday night. Since you didn’t say it.” He picked up his coffee and didn’t drink it. “I’ve known him since I was eighteen. He gave me my first work in this city. He taught me how the routes run. He calls me Si.” He put the cup down. “Nobody else does.”

“And you’re going to do what?”

“Nothing. Yet.”

“Why not?”

“A man who steals half a million is a thief. A man who steals it and smiles at you across a table and calls your partner a treasure is something else.” His voice didn’t change at all. “I want to know who he’s stealing for.”

“You’re playing chess.”

“Always. So are you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Thursday, and she didn’t want to go home and he didn’t offer, so he took her downstairs to a mahjong parlour.

Ground floor, behind a door with no sign. Fourteen tables. Smoke. Old women in cardigans. Tiles clattering like rain on a tin roof. The woman who ran it was eighty, had one gold tooth, and called Chen Si little boy.

She put them in the corner with two of her friends, also eighty, who looked at Aurelia’s green suit and gold buttons and cackled.

“She’s pretty! Can she play?”

“I don’t know.” He looked at Aurelia. “Can you?”

She sat down. She took her rings off, one by one.

He held out his hand under the table, palm up. She hesitated. Then she dropped them into it, one at a time. He closed his fingers round them and kept his fist on his knee.

“My father’s mother taught me, in Milan, in a kitchen full of cigarette smoke. She said a woman only needs two things in this world. Read a contract. Count tiles.” She began to shuffle. “I’ve never lost.”

“NEVER?” The gold tooth flashed.

Aurelia kept shuffling. The old women looked at each other. Chen Si sat back with his coffee and her rings and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t lose.

Three hours. Three of the best players in the old town, two of whom had been playing since before her mother was born. Not one round. She played fast and hard and without mercy. She counted every tile. In the second hour the gold tooth tried something very old and very clever, and Aurelia looked at her across the table.

“Nonna. I saw that.”

Sweet enough to strip paint. The old woman threw her head back and slapped the table and howled.

At last the old women gave up.

“A monster!” The gold tooth was thrilled. “Little boy, where did you find a monster like this?”

“On a balcony.”

He opened his fist. Her rings lay warm in his palm. He put them back on her fingers one by one, under the table, in the right order. Every one. Like he’d been counting too.

“You didn’t play.” Her voice came out odd. “You sat there three hours and watched. Why?”

He slid the last ring onto her finger and didn’t let go of the hand.

“You play like you think if you lose once, you’ll disappear.” His thumb pressed the ring flat. “I wanted to see if that was true.”

Her hand went still in his. She took it back. She stood. She picked up her bag.

“Goodnight, Mr. Chen.”

Her voice wobbled. She hated it.

“Goodnight, Aurelia.”

She walked out with her chin up. Heels clicking. Heart going like a hammer. She didn’t look back. Did she need to? She could feel him watching her all the way to the door.

Behind her, the gold tooth said loudly to the whole room, “Little boy is in love!”

Fourteen tables of grandmothers laughed at him. He let them.

chapters.title: The First Ledger She Ever Read
chapters.desc: Her first crate gets through customs at dawn, and she loves every minute. That night at her counter he looks at her mouth, and leaves.
chapters.epigraph: “It isn’t that I like breaking rules. I like knowing exactly which ones I’m breaking, and what they cost.”
chapters.content:
Chen Si: You don’t need to be there.

Aurelia: i know

Chen Si: Qian will be there. The men will be there. Nobody needs to see your face at a customs shed at four in the morning.

Aurelia: i know

Chen Si: Then why are you still awake?

She looked round. She was on the floor of her flat at midnight in silk pyjamas, with every invoice and customs form laid out round her in a circle, a pot of cold coffee, and a pencil behind her ear. Was it that obvious? Apparently it was that obvious.

Aurelia: because its mine. the first one. i drew every piece in that crate. i want to see it land

Nothing for a full minute. She watched the dots appear and vanish twice.

Chen Si: Wear flat shoes. The docks are wet.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came in on the fourteenth of November, exactly when Dottor Rossi had said it would. And it was a real crate. She had insisted on that at the second meeting, and the tinted glasses had argued for twenty minutes and lost.

Six walnut dining tables from a workshop in Cantù that had been making furniture since 1890. Proper joints. Proper wax. A hotel on the east side would put them in its restaurant and real people would eat real soup off them. And in the base of each table, under a panel only one man in Cantù had the screwdriver for, a flat grey velvet case. In each case, a necklace.

Hers. Drawn at her bench. Made by Enzo. Stamped with her name. Invoiced at a price that had nothing to do with the gold in it, sold on paper to a buyer who’d sell it on paper to someone in Singapore. The gap between the numbers was the whole point.

That was the shape of it, Chen Si would say. She didn’t need the details. She’d built the details.

✦ ✦ ✦

Flat shoes. Black trousers. Black coat. A black cashmere hat pulled down over her hair. No gold at all, not even the ring.

She stood in the shadow of a stack of containers at the edge of the customs yard at the Iron Docks, in the cold, in the stink of diesel and rust, and watched a crane lift a forty-foot box off a ship from Genoa. It swung through the dark under the floodlights. It came down on the concrete as gently as someone putting down a cup.

Was it stupid to find that beautiful? It was beautiful. She didn’t care if it was stupid.

“There.”

She jumped. She never heard him coming. He was in the camel coat with his hands in his pockets, a little way off in the shadow, watching the crane. No coffee for once.

“You said you wouldn’t come.”

“I said you didn’t need to. I didn’t say anything about me.”

The customs men opened the container. Crates came out one by one on a forklift. A man in a peaked cap with a clipboard walked down the line checking numbers.

He stopped at the crate from Cantù. She stopped breathing.

AURELIA — Song & Associates — Furniture — Cantù. He read the label. He read his clipboard. He read the label again. He took a crowbar off his belt and levered up one corner of the lid.

Straw. Tissue. The curved walnut leg of a table, gleaming. He put the lid down, ticked his clipboard and walked on.

Her breath came out white and hung in the air. Her hands, in her pockets, were shaking so hard she could hear the lining.

“Well?”

She turned and looked at him. She was twenty-two and she’d just watched a crate of her own necklaces walk through customs inside a dining table. She knew exactly what that made her. So did he.

Was she scared? Guilty? Not one bit.

“I want to do it again.”

He looked at her a long while without answering. So she grabbed his lapels with both cold fists, went up on her toes in her flat shoes and kissed him. Hard. Quick. Her nose was freezing. His mouth wasn’t. He made a sound of pure surprise against her lips, and by the time his hands came out of his pockets she’d already let go.

“For luck,” she said. “The next one.”

He looked at her with the crane light sliding over his face. Then he took her cold hand out of her coat pocket and put it, with his own, into the pocket of the camel coat. He laced his fingers through hers inside the wool. And kept it there while the crane swung the next container through the dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

Breakfast was a stall at the edge of the docks where the crane drivers ate. Rice porridge with century egg. Fried dough sticks. Hot soy milk in plastic bowls. Plastic stools in the cold, coats on.

She ate everything. Two days of nerves and no food. She ate like a docker. He watched her eat. He didn’t touch his own.

“You liked it.”

She looked up with a dough stick in her hand.

“Not the porridge. The crate.” He turned his bowl a quarter turn. “You liked it.”

She thought about lying. About the money, saving the shop, her mother. Then she didn’t.

“I liked it.” She put the dough stick down. “I liked the paperwork. I liked Dottor Rossi on the phone.”

“And?”

“I liked the tinted glasses losing.” She couldn’t stop now. “I liked standing there watching the man with the clipboard and knowing exactly what was in that crate. Knowing what happens if he looks properly. And knowing he wouldn’t, because I made sure!” She stopped. “Is that terrible?”

“Yes.”

The laugh came out of her so loud the crane drivers looked over.

“I like it too.” He picked up his soy milk in both hands and didn’t drink it. “That’s why I’m good at it. Most people in my line do it because they have to. Born into it. Or greedy.”

“Some of them like hurting people.”

“Some.” He looked at the milk. “I do it because the whole city’s a machine, and nearly nobody knows how it works. I do. Every bribe. Every judge.” He set the bowl down. “I like knowing.”

“You like knowing which rules you’re breaking.”

He looked up.

“And what they cost. Exactly what they cost.”

For once he looked startled. Properly startled. Like she’d read something off the inside of his skull.

“Yes. That’s it.”

At the next table, three crane drivers nudged each other. One of them said something about the boss and never, and got hit with a dough stick.

Her bowl was empty. He pushed his full one across the table without a word and took hers.

“You haven’t touched it.”

“No.”

“You’re not hungry?”

“I’m watching you eat.” He took a dough stick off her plate. “It’s better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Qian found him in the car afterwards, while Aurelia was asleep in the back of a different car on her way home.

“Sir. One of the forklift men.”

Chen Si didn’t look up from his phone.

“He took a photograph. At the shed. Of her.” Qian held out his own phone. A grainy picture. A woman in a black hat with her face turned up towards a crane. “He’s offered it to a paper. The Song girl at the docks at dawn.”

Chen Si looked at the photo. She looked happy in it. That was the annoying part. It was a good photograph.

“Which paper?”

Qian told him.

“Buy the paper’s copy. Buy his phone. Then his name comes off the dock rolls.”

“All the docks, sir?”

“All of them.”

“He has a mortgage, sir.”

“Then he’ll want work quickly.” Chen Si sent the photograph from Qian’s phone to his own. Deleted it from Qian’s. “There’s a quarry in the north that’s hiring.”

Qian wrote it down. His hand didn’t shake. He’d worked for Chen Si for six years. It used to shake. Chen Si opened his messages.

Chen Si: Home?

Aurelia: bed. dont talk to me

Chen Si: Did you eat?

Aurelia: you WATCHED me eat

Chen Si: That was four hours ago.

Aurelia: …i hate you

Chen Si: There’s congee coming up in ten minutes. The doorman has it.

Aurelia: how do you know which doorman

He didn’t answer that. He put the phone away and went to see about the quarry. On the lock screen, saved, was a grainy woman in a black hat looking at a crane like it was the best thing she’d ever seen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten she opened the shop on no sleep, congee in her and the dock still in her hair. The first customer was a banker’s wife in a cream suit who’d been in twice before. She went straight to the window.

“The collar. The broken one.”

“Yes?”

“Could you make it without the break? My husband thinks it looks damaged.”

Fourth time. Fourth! Aurelia smiled her very best smile, the one from the head of the black table.

“I could. But then it would be a chain. You can buy a chain anywhere.” She came round the counter. “Your husband’s the one at the Pacific bank?”

“Yes…”

“Then you’ll want the emeralds. He gave his secretary rubies last Christmas. Emeralds are better than rubies.” She unlocked the case. “Much better. And twice the price.”

The banker’s wife went pink, then white, then bought the emeralds. Enzo watched her go from the workshop door.

“Cara. How do you know about the secretary?”

“Everyone knows about the secretary.” Aurelia locked the case. “I just say it out loud.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That week he gave her the second ledger. Not furniture. Something bigger. A shipping company that ran containers between this city and four ports in Southeast Asia, eleven years old, profitable on paper. In real life it was the spine of something she didn’t have a name for yet. Four leather volumes and a hard drive. He brought it to the boutique after closing. One lamp on.

“It’ll take you a month.”

“A week.” She was already opening the first volume. “Why are you giving it to me?”

He stood at the counter with the broken necklace dark in the window behind him.

“I’ve run it six years. I’ve never once had anybody to talk to about it who knew what I was saying.”

She looked up. He wasn’t smiling. He looked tired, and very plain about it. That one had cost him.

“Zhendong knows.”

“Zhendong knows the parts with guns in. He doesn’t like paper.” The corner of his mouth went. “He says paper’s for people who are scared of their own hands.”

“And you?”

“I’m not scared of my hands. I’m just better at paper.”

She shut the ledger and put her hand flat on top of it.

“Then sit down. Talk to me.”

He sat on the stool on the customer side, where women sat to try on rings. She sat on her side. They talked about the shipping company until three in the morning.

“You’re paying the agent in Manila twice.”

“Once. And his cousin once.”

“Why does his cousin get paid?”

“He has a boat.”

“Everyone has a boat!”

“Not on that river.”

She flipped back four pages, furious. “Fine. Keep the cousin. Cut the agent.”

“The agent is the cousin’s father.”

“Oh my GOD.”

“They don’t speak. That’s why I pay them both.”

“That’s the stupidest thing I’ve ever…” She stopped. She read the column again. “No. That’s clever. I hate it.”

“Noted.”

By two they were finishing each other’s sentences and arguing about the rest. By three they were laughing so hard she had to put her head down on the ledger.

Had anything ever felt this close? The boy in the garden in Milan at eighteen? Please. Two people at a counter in the dark, talking ports and bribes and a machine nobody else could see. She’d been kissed by men who knew less about her.

At three he looked at his watch and stood up.

“I should go. You have customers at ten.”

“I do.”

He didn’t go.

He reached across the counter, slow, the same way he’d held out his coat on the balcony. Two fingers under her chin. He tipped her face up to the lamp and just looked. At her eyes. At her mouth. At a grey smudge of pencil on her cheekbone she hadn’t known about since midnight.

He wiped it away with his thumb. His thumb stayed. It went once along her lower lip. His eyes went dark. She felt his hand go rigid against her jaw, like he was holding something back by force. He was looking at her mouth. He was counting something. She could see him counting.

“Not tonight,” he said, and his voice wasn’t mild at all. “Next time, I don’t want to stop at three because you have customers at ten.”

He took his hand back.

“That’s not fair.”

“No.”

“You can’t just… you look at me like that, and then you leave?”

“Yes.” He put his coat on. He turned the collar up, one side, then the other, and watched her recognise it. “Think about it.”

“About what?”

“Goodnight.”

The bell. His car at the corner. Gone. She sat at her counter with her hand on the ledger and her face burning where his thumb had been. She’d kissed him at the docks for luck. She’d been sure, absolutely sure, he’d kiss her back properly the next chance he got. She’d wanted him to.

And he’d looked at her mouth on purpose, told her so in that voice, and walked out.

“Oh, you bastard.”

There was nobody to hear it. She laughed anyway, with her forehead on four volumes of his shipping company.

chapters.title: He Never Asks Her to Win
chapters.desc: She loses a game of chess on purpose to see what he’ll do. He lays down his own king.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t care if you win, Aurelia. I don’t care if you lose. You could lose every game you ever play me and I’d just want another one.”
chapters.content:
By December, Chen Si was driving her mad, and he hadn’t done a single thing.

That was the problem. Everybody wanted her to win. That was the rule of her whole life. Her mother wanted it because a daughter who lost was a bad reflection. Her father wanted it because a daughter who won could be shown to ministers. Boys wanted it so they could be seen with her, and then, once they had been, they wanted to beat her. She could spot that one coming from across a ballroom.

Chen Si watched her win and said nothing.

He’d sat in an office chair while she took his meeting apart. He’d sat in the smoke for three hours while she flattened three grandmothers. He’d sat at her counter until three in the morning while she won an argument about container fees, and when she won it, he didn’t look pleased. Or annoyed. He just looked at her.

What did he want?

She didn’t know. She always knew. It was unbearable.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a chess set in his office on the thirty-ninth floor. Heavy old pieces in black and white jade. Qian said he played against himself in the evenings, when he was thinking.

“Who wins?” she’d asked.

Qian had looked at the ceiling for help. “He does, Miss Song. Both sides. It’s very upsetting to watch.”

On the second Friday of December she walked in without knocking, in a red dress, sat down on the other side of the board and said, “Teach me.”

He looked up from his laptop.

“You don’t play?”

“I know how the pieces move. My father taught me at six. He stopped when I beat him at eight.” She picked up a jade knight and turned it over in her fingers. “I want to play you.”

He closed the laptop.

“All right. But I don’t go easy.”

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At first she played properly. She was good. Not as good as him, she could tell that inside ten moves, but fast and nasty and not scared of anything. For an hour she made him work. He sat forward with his elbows on his knees and his coffee going cold. Twice she surprised him. Once she nearly had his queen.

Then she reached a position with three moves that kept her alive and one that killed her.

She took a breath. She picked the one that killed her.

Rook. To a square where he’d take it. She sat back and watched his face.

He looked at the board. He didn’t take the rook. He looked up.

“Why did you do that?”

“Do what?”

“You had the bishop.” He touched it. “Bishop to c4. Pins my knight. I give you the exchange. You saw it. I watched you see it.” He sat back. “Then you put your rook where I could take it.”

“Maybe I didn’t see it.”

“You found half a million in my books in forty-one minutes. You saw a bishop.” His voice was mild. “You lost on purpose.”

She lifted her chin.

“So?”

“So I want to know why.”

She didn’t answer.

He waited. He was very, very good at waiting. She was starting to think it was the most dangerous thing about him.

“I wanted to see what you’d do. When I lost.” It came out harder than she meant. “Everyone does something. My mother goes cold. My father changes the subject. Boys used to smile, like they’d been waiting all day.” Chin higher. “So. Go on. Do it.”

He reached across the board. He took her rook and set it to one side.

Then he picked up his own king and laid it down on its side.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stared at it. Black jade, lying flat. The oldest sign in the game. I resign.

“What are you doing?”

“Resigning.”

“You were winning!”

“Yes. I was.” He sat back. “But you stopped playing. So I don’t want to play any more. What’s the point of beating someone who isn’t playing?”

“That’s… that’s not how chess works.”

“It’s how I work.”

He looked at the fallen king.

“I don’t care if you win, Aurelia. I don’t care if you lose. You could lose every game you ever play me and I’d just want another one.” He looked up. “I care that you’re so scared of losing.”

She sat very still in her red dress.

“I watched you play mahjong for three hours. Those old women were laughing. Smoking. Having a lovely time.” His voice stayed level. “You didn’t enjoy one minute. You played like you were defusing a bomb.”

“I won—”

“You walked out of your father’s dining room like it was on fire. You sat in my chair because if you’d stood, you’d have lost. And if you’d lost…”

“Don’t.”

“You’d have stopped existing.” He turned the fallen king in his fingers. “That isn’t ambition. That’s fear. Somebody taught it to you. I’d like to know who.” Mildly. “So I can find them.”

Was that a joke? It was not a joke. She’d seen his face when he said find.

“My mother. Obviously. You heard her. Second place is just the first of the losers.”

“I heard her.”

“She says it every time. Every exam. Every recital. Every time I came home with a number.” She was talking too fast and she couldn’t stop. “When I was eleven I came second in a piano competition in Vienna. Second out of a hundred and forty.”

He didn’t move.

“She didn’t speak to me for nine days. Not one word. Not at breakfast. Not when I said goodnight. Nine days.” Her hands were in fists in her lap. “On the tenth she came into my room and opened the curtains and said Second place is just the first of the losers, I hope you’ve learned that, and went downstairs. And that was it. That was all. It was over.”

She stopped.

She had never told anyone that. Not even Serafina, who’d found her crying in a bathroom after Vienna and had been too little to ask why. She’d just told it to the most dangerous man in the city across a chessboard, because he laid down a king.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything right away.

He stood the king up again in the middle of the board, alone, where no king would ever stand in a real game.

“When I was fifteen my father was arrested.” Very level. “He was a deputy governor. They said corruption. He hadn’t done it. The men who arrested him had.”

“Chen Si…”

“They took him from the house at six in the morning in his pyjamas. My mother and I stood in the hall.” He touched the king’s crown. “He died in custody four months later. Before the trial. They said it was his heart.”

She couldn’t speak.

“The rest is long. Another night. Tonight’s yours.” He looked at her. “I wanted you to know I’m not saying any of this from somewhere safe.”

He leaned over the board.

“You don’t have to win anything for me to see you. Not a game. Not a meeting. I saw you on that balcony before you’d done one thing except stand there shaking.” A pause. “You don’t have to earn it.”

“That’s…”

“You can lose to me on purpose and I’ll still see you. I’ll just be very annoyed. I was three moves from mate.”

She laughed. It came out wet and cracked down the middle.

“You were not three moves from mate.”

“Four. I was being generous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then she cried.

Not much. Not long. She hadn’t cried since she was eleven and she’d forgotten how. She put her face in her hands across his jade chessboard, in her red dress, and her shoulders shook, and no noise came out at all. Two minutes. Maybe three.

He didn’t touch her. No coming round the board, no handkerchief. He sat on his side, with the king standing alone between them, and let her. Just like he’d let her stand at the balustrade.

When it stopped she wiped her face with the backs of her hands. That destroyed her eye make-up completely.

Then he came round the board.

He crouched in front of her chair and took her face in both hands. He cleaned the black from under her eyes with his thumbs, one side and then the other, slowly, like nothing else in the city needed doing. His hands weren’t quite steady either. Then he leaned up and kissed her eyelids. Left. Right. She felt her lashes against his mouth.

“Don’t be nice. Not when I look like this.”

“Like what?”

“Like a panda that’s been in a fight!”

“You look like a woman who just lost a game of chess.” His thumbs stayed on her cheekbones. “And like the only thing I want to look at. Both.”

That got a real laugh out of her.

His thumbs stopped moving.

“I’m going to kiss you.” It wasn’t a question. “You just cried in front of me. Hate me for it in the morning.”

“I’ll hate you more if you don’t.”

So he did. Gently this time. Her face still in his hands and the salt still on her mouth, careful in a way that undid her worse than any streetlamp. When he pulled back she had both hands in his hair and couldn’t remember putting them there.

“Play me again.”

“Properly?”

“Properly. No losing on purpose.” She started setting the pieces up. Her fingers kept fumbling the pawns. “And if I lose, I lose, and you don’t say anything, and I won’t… I won’t disappear.”

He watched her line up the pawns.

“And if you win?”

She put the last one down and looked up at him with her ruined make-up.

“Then you owe me something. I’ll decide what later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight Qian put his head round the door with a folder.

“Sir, the Singapore…”

He saw the board. He saw Miss Song in red with her mascara somewhere around her chin. He saw his boss on the floor beside her chair, cross-legged, in his shirtsleeves, frowning at a pawn.

“…can wait.”

Qian shut the door very gently.

Aurelia didn’t even look up.

“Does he always do that?”

“Only when he’s scared.” Chen Si moved a knight. “He’s scared most of the time. He keeps antacids in his desk.”

“Why?”

“Me, mostly.” He tapped the board. “Your move.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost.

Properly, this time. Two hours. A slow, patient endgame she didn’t see coming until four moves out. When she finally saw it she sat back and said a word in Italian that would have made her grandmother faint.

He waited.

She looked at her king. Trapped. Nowhere to go.

She waited for it. The cold. The drop. Nine days of nothing at breakfast.

It didn’t come.

What came instead was something she hadn’t felt since she was tiny, before Milan, before runways and rankings. A fierce, furious, delighted interest. In the endgame. In how he’d done it. In how she’d beat it next time.

She reached out and laid her own king down.

“Again.”

He smiled then. All the way. It took over his whole face and made him look his age, which was only twenty-four, which she kept forgetting. Tired, and very glad.

“Tomorrow. It’s two in the morning. You’ll fall asleep on my rook.”

She stood up and reached for her coat. He got there first. He held it for her, and when her arms were in he came round the front and did up one button, the top one, under her chin. Just one.

“The rest is your job.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Yes.”

At the door she stopped and looked back. Him behind the jade board in the lamplight. The city in the window. Cold coffee.

“You never asked me to win. Not once. Not at anything.” Her voice came out small and she let it. “Why not?”

He took his time.

“I’d rather have you happy than first.”

She left before he could see her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sat with the king standing alone in the middle of the board until her lift reached the ground. He knew when it did. The night guard texted. Miss Song in lobby. Make-up bad. Smiling.

Then he rang Qian, who was still outside the door, and who answered before it rang.

“Vienna. A junior piano competition, the year she was eleven. I want the results.”

“The… results, sir?”

“Who came first.”

A pause. Qian’s pen.

“And sir? If I find them?”

“Nothing. I want to know their name.” He picked up the black king and turned it over. “And her mother’s diary. Where she has lunch. Who she has it with.”

“Sir.” Very carefully. “Mrs. Song is…”

“Aurelia’s mother.” He put the king down. “Yes. I’m not going to touch her.”

“Then why…”

“I’d like to know where she is.”

Qian didn’t ask again. He’d learned that around year two.

Chen Si stayed where he was. Then he did what he never did. He took a piece off the board, the black queen, the one she’d nearly taken off him, and put it in his jacket pocket. The set was a hundred years old. It could manage with one queen missing.

He’d give it back when she noticed.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the lift, alone, going down thirty-nine floors, she looked at herself in the mirror. Panda. Total disaster. She grinned at it anyway, then leaned her head back and shut her eyes.

I’m going to marry that man.

And then, because she was Aurelia Song and had never once wanted anything without immediately starting to plan how to get it:

And I’m writing the contract myself.

chapters.title: Dinner on the Forty-Fourth Floor
chapters.desc: He cooks her dinner and tells her how his parents died. Then she tells him to kneel, and he does.
chapters.epigraph: “Take off your watch. I don’t want you counting.”
chapters.content:
The lift camera showed her fixing her lipstick twice between the lobby and the forty-fourth floor.

Chen Si watched it on his phone, propped against the rice cooker, with a cleaver in his other hand. Once at the twentieth floor. Once at the fortieth. Then she glared at herself in the mirror and said something. He couldn’t hear it. From the shape, it was rude, and it was in Italian.
