She was eleven minutes early. She’d never been early to anything in her life. Qian had checked.

He put the phone face down and went back to the spring onions.

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened the door himself. Dark blue jumper, sleeves shoved up, a tea towel over one shoulder.

“You’re early. The fish isn’t ready.”

And he went back to the kitchen.

Aurelia stood in the doorway in a black dress, her mother’s red lipstick and a coat she’d spent forty minutes choosing, and looked at the room.

Huge. Nearly empty. Glass on three sides, the whole harbour spread out underneath in the dark. Pale wood floors. One long sofa. One long table. Books along the only wall that wasn’t window, hundreds of them. And by the glass, on a low table, the jade chess set from his office.

No art. No photographs. Like nobody had ever lived anywhere else.

She went to find the kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was steaming a whole grouper over a wok, with ginger and spring onion. Cutting more onion with a cleaver, fast, the way cooks did in the old town. She’d never seen anyone do it in a penthouse.

She leaned on the doorframe.

“Who taught you?”

“My mother.” He didn’t look up. “She said a boy should feed himself. My father thought it was ridiculous. They fought about it for years.” He swept the onion into a bowl. “She won.”

He heated oil until it smoked and poured it over the fish. It hissed and spat. The whole kitchen filled with the smell. She was so hungry she felt dizzy.

“Sit. Please.”

She sat.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the end of the long table by the glass. The fish. Greens with garlic. Rice. A clear dark soup that had been going all afternoon, dried scallop and pork.

He ladled her a bowl and blew on it before he handed it over. Didn’t think about it. Just did it, like she was six.

She stared at the bowl.

“It’s hot,” he said.

“I’m aware soup is hot.”

“Then why are you looking at it like that?”

Because nobody had blown on her soup since her grandmother. She didn’t say that. She drank the soup.

There was a white wine from Friuli, which he’d clearly picked because it came from the north of Italy. He opened it. Poured two glasses. Didn’t touch his.

“You still don’t drink things people give you.”

“Nobody gave me this. I bought it.” He looked at his glass. “I don’t drink much. I don’t like not knowing exactly what I’m doing.”

“You drank my beer.”

“I took your beer. That’s different.”

He picked up the glass and drank.

She felt it all the way down her spine and looked very hard at her fish.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her afterwards. On the long sofa with the lights off, so they could see the harbour, the Friuli on the floor between them.

He’d said he would. The rest is long. Another night. She’d waited six weeks without asking. For Aurelia Song that was basically a medical event.

“My father was Chen Mingyuan. Deputy governor.” He looked at the water. “Not a saint. A good man. He refused to sign off a land deal on the east side that would have made three other men very rich.”

“Who?”

“One of them was a councillor called Fu Jianguo.”

She knew that name. Everybody knew that name. Vice-minister now.

“Six months later my father was arrested for bribes he never took. The evidence was perfect. Fu made sure.” Flat. Calm. “I told you. Six in the morning. He went down the stairs in his pyjamas and looked back at me from the door. Look after your mother. I’ll be home soon.”

She didn’t move.

“He died in a cell four months later. They said his heart. It wasn’t his heart.”

“And your mother?”

“The next winter. They said her heart too. That one was true. It broke.” His voice stayed level. That was the worst part. “She stopped eating. She sat in his chair in the study every night and watched the door.”

“Chen Si…”

“I was sixteen. Everything was frozen. The house, the accounts. Fu’s people saw to it.” Something almost like a smile. “So I unfroze some of it. One account. I was good with computers and very angry. I moved her money somewhere they couldn’t see, so she could keep the flat and the heating and the doctor on Tuesdays.”

“That’s…”

“Clever. Illegal. They caught me in eleven days.” The smile went. “They took me in November. She died in December. Nobody was with her. They didn’t let me out for the funeral. A guard told me at breakfast. Between the rice and the tea. Then he asked me to pass the salt.”

Aurelia’s throat had closed up completely.

“Block C,” she managed.

His head turned.

“Zhendong told you?”

“Zhendong has said four words to me. One of them was hm.” She looked at him. “You told me. You said they caught me, and your hand went to your arm.”

He looked down. His right hand was on his left forearm, over the blue wool. He hadn’t known.

He took it away.

“Juvenile detention. That’s where I met him. There was a riot that first winter, and we left. Through the drains.” He stopped. “The rest is his as much as mine. One day I’ll tell you about the drains. Not tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a metre and a half of pale grey sofa between them. Her shoes were off and her feet tucked under her. He had one arm along the back. She’d never been so aware of a metre and a half of anything.

“Fu Jianguo was at my father’s party.” She sat up. “That’s why you were there.”

“Yes.”

“What are you going to do to him?”

He looked at the harbour.

“I’ve been building something since I got out. The routes. The judges. The men on the thirty-ninth floor. All of it’s for one thing.”

“Fu.”

“One day I take everything he has. His job. His money. His sons’ names. Legally, if I can. The way he did it to my father.” His voice didn’t rise at all. “I stand in his hall at six in the morning and watch them walk him down the stairs.”

His face was perfectly calm. That scared her more than any of the words.

“And then?”

He thought about it.

“I don’t know. I’ve never thought about then. There wasn’t any. There was only that.”

She held his eyes.

“There is now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Who moved first? They’d argue about it for years. At dinners. In front of people who were scared of both of them. She said him. He said her. Zhao Zhendong, asked to settle it at a New Year dinner three years later, said “Hm,” and wouldn’t say another word.

What she knew was that there was a metre and a half of sofa, and then there wasn’t. His hand was in her hair. Her fists were in his jumper. He was kissing her.

Not like the streetlamp. Not like the chessboard. Every other time, he’d stopped. Right at the edge, like there was a clause somewhere nobody had written down.

She’d imagined what it would be like when he didn’t stop. She’d pictured him like he played chess. Patient. Three moves ahead.

He wasn’t.

He kissed her like he’d been holding his breath since October. Hard and deep and not careful at all, one hand cradling the back of her skull, and she made a noise she’d never made in her life and dragged him closer by the jumper and heard him make one back, low in his chest.

She pulled back first. One inch. Breathing like she’d sprinted.

“You walked out. At the counter. You looked at my mouth for ten seconds and walked out!”

“Eleven.” Against her mouth. His voice had gone rough. “I wanted you to think about it every time you saw me.”

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Her jaw. Unhurried. Fully aware of how well it had worked. Not sorry at all.

She took his face in both hands and held it an inch away and looked at him in the harbour light. At his eyes, gone black. His mouth.

And something rose up in her. The same thing that had sat down in his chair. Cold and bright and absolutely delighted.

“No.”

He stopped dead.

“You made me wait three months. Streetlamp, then home. Counter, then walked out.” She let go of his face and sat back. Not far. Just enough. “So now you can wait for me.”

He didn’t look offended. He looked more interested than she’d ever seen him.

“What do you want?”

She stood up. Barefoot on his floor, in her black dress, the harbour behind her in the glass. He looked up at her from the sofa.

“Kneel.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing in the room moved.

She’d never said it to anyone. She’d never thought she would. It came out from the same deep sure place as the counter-offer. A place she’d never been allowed to use.

Would he laugh? Stand up? Look at her like the boys at school had when she won, working out how to make her pay?

He got up off the sofa and knelt.

No hurry. No embarrassment. Like he’d been waiting years for someone to ask. The most dangerous man in the city, on his knees on his own floor at her bare feet, looking up. Waiting.

She forgot to breathe.

“Take off your watch.” Not steady. “I don’t want you counting.”

He unbuckled it and held it up to her. Warm from his wrist. Heavy. She put it on the window ledge behind her without looking.

“What else?”

His voice had changed. Low and rough and calm. It went straight through her.

“Your jumper.”

He took it off slowly, on purpose, over his head, and dropped it beside him. Then he knelt there bare to the waist in the harbour light, and waited.

He was lean and pale, broader across the shoulders than the suits let on. And on the inside of his left forearm, from wrist nearly to elbow, a long shiny burn scar, the skin pulled tight. Across the palm of the same hand, one thin white line.

She went down on her knees in front of him. She didn’t decide to. Her legs did it. Knees touching his. She took his left arm and turned it over and put her fingertips on the scar at the wrist.

He flinched. She’d never seen him flinch at anything.

“Block C?”

“The riot. The mattresses burned. There was a drain grate in the floor, too hot to touch.” His eyes didn’t leave her face. “I didn’t have time to wait for it to cool.”

“And this?” Her thumb on the white line in his palm.

“That one I did on purpose. Zhendong has the same.”

She traced the whole scar with her fingertips, wrist to elbow and back down to his palm. Then she lifted his hand and kissed the line. He knelt absolutely still with his other hand on his thigh. His chest was going faster and faster. His jaw was locked. He wasn’t allowed to move until she said. He knew it. It was costing him a fortune.

Had she ever felt anything like this? Never. Not once.

He didn’t move his hands. He moved his head, a few centimetres, until his mouth was on the inside of her wrist where she held his arm, right at the edge of what she’d allowed.

“Let me,” he said against her pulse. “Please. You can say no.” His eyes came up. “But tell me first if you want it too.”

“Chen Si.”

“Yes.”

“You can touch me now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was slow.

She’d never be able to explain it to anyone. Not even Elowen, years later, drunk on the floor of a flower shop. He’d been told he could touch her, and he did, and he was so slow about it that she thought she might actually die.

One hand on her face. Then the other. He kissed her gently, which was worse than hard. He found the zip at the back of her dress and took it down so slowly she felt every tooth come apart, his knuckles trailing down her spine the whole way. By the bottom she was shaking.

“You’re punishing me.”

“No.” He eased the dress off her shoulders and kissed where it had been. “You told me to kneel. To wait. To take my watch off so I wouldn’t count.”

“I didn’t mean…”

“So I’m not counting.” His mouth went along her collarbone. “I’m in no hurry. I have no idea what time it is.” He lifted his head. His eyes were black and completely merciless. “You set the terms. I’m just following them. Very carefully.”

Half a laugh came out of her and half something she’d never heard herself make.

“I hate you.”

“I know,” he said, and laid her back on his pale wooden floor in the light off the harbour, and took his time.

He took so much time that somewhere in it she forgot who’d been giving orders.

He learned her like he’d learned the city. Patiently. Thoroughly. Missing nothing. Every place that made her breath catch, he found, and went back to, and went back to again, watching her face the whole time like she was a puzzle worth more than the city. When she reached for him he caught both her wrists and held them on the floor above her head with one hand, and looked at her.

“Tell me if you want me to let go.”

She didn’t want him to let go.

She found that out flat on his floor with her wrists in his hand and the whole harbour glittering behind his shoulder, and it frightened her more than anything she’d ever learned about herself. Aurelia Song, who sat in other people’s chairs and never lost, wanted this one man to hold her down and not let go.

“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t let go.”

He shuddered all over.

“Say it again.”

“Don’t let go…”

He didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later she lay on his chest on the long grey sofa, under a blanket he’d got from somewhere, wearing his blue jumper and nothing else. She’d stolen it off the floor. He’d watched her do it and said nothing, which meant he was keeping it in his head for later. The harbour had gone dark except for one ship crawling out to sea.

“I thought I was in charge.”

“You were. Then you told me you didn’t want to be, for a while.” His hand went up and down her back over the wool. “You can tell me to kneel. You can tell me not to let go. Both in one night.” Lower. “I like both. Very much.”

She lifted her head.

“Nobody’s ever let me be both.”

“I know. I could tell.”

She looked past him at the chess set by the window, in the last of the light.

“You’re missing a queen.”

“Am I?”

“The black one. The one I nearly had.”

He reached down to the floor without looking, into the pocket of his trousers. He held it up between two fingers. Black jade. Warm.

“You’ve been carrying it?”

“Six weeks.”

“Why?”

“You nearly took it.” He put it in her palm and closed her fingers round it. “I wanted to see how long before you noticed.”

“Six weeks! You psychopath.”

“Yes.”

He pulled her back down by the nape of her neck and kissed her again, slow and thorough, like the first time had only been an opening offer.

“You’re staying.” Not a question. “I’ll make you breakfast. Then I’ll take you back to bed and you can give me orders again.”

“What time is it?”

He glanced at the window ledge, where his watch lay face down exactly where she’d put it. Still ticking.

“No idea.”

chapters.title: A Proposal With Terms and Conditions
chapters.desc: She proposes with eleven pages of red ink. He signs every one, and writes something in the margin she can’t argue with.
chapters.epigraph: “Clause 9. In private, the Wife sets the terms, unless and until she says otherwise. Clause 10. The word is ‘Milan’.”
chapters.content:
“I need a sheet of his paper. The cream kind. No letterhead.”

Qian looked at Aurelia across his desk on the thirty-ninth floor. Then he opened a drawer, took out one sheet and handed it over. He didn’t ask a single question. That told her everything she needed to know about Qian.

“If this is what I think it is, Miss Song…”

“What do you think it is?”

He took the antacids out of his drawer, shook two into his hand and looked at them.

“I think I’d like to be told what time to cancel his diary from.”

“Tuesday. All of it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter went on Monday. A client would like to discuss a commercial arrangement concerning the gentleman on the 44th floor. Two initials.

He came on Tuesday at eleven, a minute early, with a coffee. He stopped inside the door. He looked at her behind the counter. She’d worn white on purpose. She watched him see the white and understand something, and then she watched him look down at the counter in front of her. Eleven stapled pages. Her handwriting. Red ink. He put the coffee down.

“Aurelia.”

“Read it. All of it. Then we’ll talk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d written it on the floor of her flat over four nights. Silk pyjamas. Cold coffee. The whole time it had felt like falling off something very high and not wanting to land. She’d consulted two lawyers and a priest without telling any of them why. She’d read eleven marriage contracts from the archives of three old Milanese families, including her own grandparents’, which had a clause about a racehorse.

He read the first line standing up. AGREEMENT OF MARRIAGE between AURELIA SONG (the Wife) and CHEN SI (the Husband). Whereas the Husband has repeatedly failed to ask the Wife to win anything. Whereas the Wife finds this intolerable and wishes it to continue forever. The parties agree as follows.

He looked up at intolerable. She looked back at him with no expression at all. It took everything she had. He read on.

1. The Wife keeps her name, her boutique, her designs and every gram of gold she has ever cut. The Husband keeps his companies, his routes, his brother and his chess set. What is acquired together is held together.

2. The Wife sits at the table. All tables. Including the ones the Husband would prefer she did not know about.

3. Neither party will lie to the other. About anything. If something cannot be told, it will be said: I cannot tell you this yet. And it will be told later.

4. The Husband will not at any time try to keep the Wife somewhere safe. If he does, the Wife will leave him, and take with her the Milan route, the furniture company, the man in the cardigan who runs the pawnshops, and approximately half of the Husband’s people, who like her better.

He stopped at four. Read it again. Put his hand flat on the counter and looked down at it. His shoulders moved once. Was he laughing? He was trying very hard not to.

“Half.”

“I counted.” She folded her arms. “The sunflower man hates me. The tinted glasses are scared of me. Everyone else likes me better. Qian likes me better.”

“Qian’s liked you better since you sat in my chair.” He turned the page. “He told me so. Boss, if you don’t marry that woman, I’m going to go and work for her.”

She didn’t let her face move. It was extremely difficult.

✦ ✦ ✦

5. On the subject of Fu Jianguo, the Wife accepts the Husband’s prior claim and will not interfere. But when it is done, she will be standing in the hall beside him at six in the morning. Then they will go and have breakfast.

He read that one twice. He didn’t say anything about it. He lifted one hand and pressed two fingers against his eyes, just for a second, and turned the page.

6. The Husband attends the opening of every collection the Wife makes, in the front row, and does not look at his phone.

7. The Wife attends the Husband’s brother’s birthday every year and eats whatever he cooks, including fish with the heads on.

“He’ll make you eat the eyes.”

“I’ll eat the eyes.”

“He’ll watch you do it.”

“Then I’ll eat them slowly.”

8. Neither party will ever, under any circumstances, say: second place is just the first of the losers.

He looked up.

“Agreed.”

He hadn’t even turned the page yet. *** Page nine.

9. In private, the Wife sets the terms. She may tell the Husband to kneel, to wait, to take off his watch, not to move, to move, to beg, or anything else she likes. He will do it slowly, exactly as he did on the forty-fourth floor. Unless and until she says otherwise. When she says otherwise, he sets the terms, completely, until she says otherwise again. Both parties acknowledge that the Wife will say otherwise frequently. This is not a contradiction.

He read it twice. Did he know what that look did to her? Obviously he knew. When he finally lifted his head his face was perfectly calm and his eyes had gone black.

“Frequently.”

“I’ve been considering the evidence.” Her own voice was not as steady as she’d planned. “Six weeks of it. It seemed best to be honest. Clause three.”

He nodded. Very slowly. And turned the page.

10. The word is Milan. If either party says it, at any time, in any room, everything stops. At once. No questions. No sulking. No consequences. Then the parties lie down together, and the one who said it is held for as long as they want to be held. The word is Milan because it is the city where the Wife learned to be afraid. She would like it to mean something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t turn page ten. Outside on Harbour Road a tram went by. The chestnut man was shouting. Somebody leaned on a horn. Inside, under the one lamp, the most dangerous man in the city stood looking at a page of a marriage contract and didn’t move.

“Aurelia.”

“Yes.”

“Have you had one before? A word?”

“No.” Chin up. “I never needed one. With anyone else I was always…” She stopped. Clause three. She made herself say it. “With anyone else I always won. You don’t need a word if you always win.” She looked at him. “With you I don’t want to. Not always. And that scares me. So I wanted a word.”

He looked at her across the counter.

“It’s a very good word.”

“I know. It took me ages.”

“I’ll keep it. Safer than anything I own.”

Then he turned to the last page.

11. This agreement will be renewed after ten years, on the anniversary of its signing, at which point the Wife reserves the right to rewrite every clause. Signed: A. Song. Underneath, a space.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took a fountain pen out of his inside pocket. Heavy. Black. He uncapped it. And stopped.

“One amendment.”

Her eyebrows went up. “One?”

He turned back to page one. Up in the margin, in his small exact black hand, he wrote. Then he turned the contract round so she could read it.

The Husband would like it noted that he has been in love with the Wife since a balcony in October, when she was shaking in a gold dress and doing sums in her head. That he walked down Harbour Road for six weeks before that to look at a necklace. That nobody has ever asked him to marry them, and that he did not know, until this morning, that he had been waiting for someone to.

She read it twice. Then a third time, because the words had gone swimmy.

“That isn’t an amendment.” Her voice had gone very strange. “That isn’t a clause. It doesn’t do anything.”

“No. It’s just true.”

He signed every page. All eleven. Bottom right-hand corner, black beside her red. It took forever, because he did it the way he did everything that mattered, without hurrying. Somewhere around page six she noticed she’d stopped breathing and had to start again on purpose.

He capped the pen. He slid the contract back across the counter.

“Is that a yes?”

He looked at her.

“I’ve read clause nine four times. Of course it’s a yes.”

The bark came out of her. Then she was laughing properly, helplessly, hand over her mouth, at her own counter, in white. He came round the end of the counter to her side. The first time he’d ever come round to her side. He took her face in his hands and kissed her, hard, and her lipstick went everywhere.

When he pulled back there was red at the corner of her mouth. He wiped it off with his thumb. Then he put his thumb in his mouth. She forgot what language she spoke.

“Clause nine,” he said, an inch away. “Does it start now?”

“It starts when I close the shop.”

She reached past him and turned the sign on the door to CLOSED.

✦ ✦ ✦

Enzo wasn’t there. She’d given him the day off. She’d told him she’d need the bench, and he’d looked at her over his magnifiers with his old brown face perfectly still and said, “Cara, I don’t want to know,” and gone home.

The workshop was small and bright. Metal and polish and gas from the torch. Two benches, his and hers, each with a leather skin slung under it to catch the gold dust. Tools on every wall. And on her bench, on a square of black velvet, the broken necklace from the window.

He saw it and stopped.

“You took it out of the window.”

“This morning.” She picked it up. Heavy. Yellow gold, wrenched apart and mended with bright white seams. “It isn’t for sale any more.”

“Why not?”

She turned round.

“Take off your coat. And your tie.”

He looked at her in the bright little room with that black, absorbed attention. Then he folded his coat over Enzo’s stool. Then he pulled his tie loose and drew it out from under his collar inch by inch, watching her the whole time, and held it out. Grey silk. Warm from his neck.

“Sit down. On my stool.”

He sat.

She stood between his knees. She put the broken necklace round his neck, over his white shirt, and fastened it at the back with her fingers on his nape. He shut his eyes.

“That’s why. It isn’t for sale. It’s yours.”

“It’s heavy.”

“Nearly four hundred grams.” She ran a finger along the links, along the bright seams. “Every time you feel it, I want you to know I know about breaking. And I don’t want the break taken out. Not mine. Not yours.”

He opened his eyes. She held his tie up between them.

“Give me your hands.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He held them out, wrists together, without a word. She wound his tie round them twice and knotted it loose. He could have pulled free in a second. They both knew it.

“If you pull free, I stop.”

“I won’t pull free.”

“I know.” She lifted his tied hands and put them behind his head, elbows up, chest open, four hundred grams of her gold lying across his white shirt. “Keep them there.”

He kept them there.

She undid his shirt one button at a time. No hurry. She’d learned that from him, on his floor, and she used it now with interest, kissing the skin under each button as it came open. By the bottom button his breathing had gone loud in the bright quiet room and the gold was rising and falling on his bare chest.

Then she took his bound wrists and kissed the burn scar. All the way up, from the knot of silk to the inside of his elbow. He made a noise like she’d punched him. His hands tightened in the silk behind his head. They didn’t move.

“You’re very good at doing what you’re told.”

“Only by you.” Gravel. “Nobody else was ever worth it.” He tipped his head back against his tied hands and looked at her. “Counter-offer.”

“Now?”

“You keep every term. I keep my hands exactly here. In return, you let me kiss you once. Wherever you choose.” A breath. “Do you want that? Say no and I’ll keep still.”

She let him suffer for it. Then she leaned in and put her mouth on his, quick, and pulled back before he could follow.

“Accepted. Once.”

She looked at him. On her stool, in her workshop. Shirt open. Hands tied with his own tie behind his head. Her necklace on his chest. Looking at her like there was nothing else in the city.

And because clause nine allowed for it, and because she wanted to, and because she had never once in her life been able to say it to anyone:

“Chen Si. Otherwise.”

He went still.

Then he moved. One pull and the silk came off his wrists like it had never been tied. He stood and caught her by the waist and turned her and lifted her onto the edge of her own bench, onto Enzo’s polishing cloths, in among the files and the pliers and the little pots of borax. He stood between her knees and took her face in his hands.

“Otherwise.” Very low. An inch from her mouth. “You’re sure.”

“Clause three. I’m sure.”

He smiled. The black, merciless, delighted smile from the forty-fourth floor.

“Then hold on to the bench. And don’t let go until I tell you.”

She held on to the bench. *** He didn’t let her let go for what felt like hours.

The bench, hard under her palms. A file, cold, somewhere against her hip. His voice, low and steady and merciless, telling her exactly what he was going to do before he did it. Then doing it. Until she shook.

Not yet, against her throat. Not yet, against her shoulder. Not yet, into her hair, while her pulse went wild. Every time she thought she couldn’t stand it, he said it again. Until not yet was the most unbearable thing anyone had ever said to her, and she’d have done anything at all to hear him say the other thing.

She begged. Aurelia Song, who had never begged for anything, on her own workbench among her own tools, with four hundred grams of her own gold swinging against her skin every time he moved. In Italian. Then in Chinese. Then in no language at all.

“Please. Please, I can’t…”

“You can.”

And when he finally said it, now, Aurelia, now, rough against her ear, she let go of the bench and held on to him instead. It was the balcony in October. The whole city glittering below her in the dark. That one second of thinking she might fall.

She fell. He caught her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they sat on the workshop floor with their backs against her bench, in among the dropped tools, his coat round both of them. He hadn’t taken the necklace off. He kept touching it. Running his fingers along the mended links.

“I’m going to have to explain this to Enzo.”

“Explain what?”

She looked at her bench. The scattered files. The knocked-over borax. The polishing cloths on the floor. The faint but unmistakable print of a man’s hand on the leather skin underneath, where he’d braced himself.

“Everything.”

He laughed. Properly. Head back against her bench. She leaned on his shoulder. The contract was still out on the counter in the shop. Eleven pages. Red and black. Signed.

“I didn’t say Milan.”

He waited.

“I nearly did. Once. At the end.” She hesitated. “Not because I wanted you to stop. Because I didn’t think I could bear it if you didn’t.”

His fingers stopped on the necklace. He turned his head.

“I know. I felt it.” His mouth against her hair. “That’s why I said now.”

She put her face in his neck, inside the coat, with the gold between them. He held her for as long as she wanted to be held. Clause ten, though nobody had said the word.

From the shop, very faintly, came the sound of someone rattling the locked door, and then Enzo’s voice through the glass.

“Cara! I forgot my glasses! I am not coming in! Push them through the letterbox!”

chapters.title: The Song Parents Are Not Told
chapters.desc: She marries him in Milan with eleven guests and the sister she hasn’t spoken to in two years, and lets her mother find out from Vogue.
chapters.epigraph: “Shouldn’t we tell your parents?” “We will. They read Italian Vogue.”
chapters.content:
She married him in Milan on Thursday the sixteenth of May, at four in the afternoon, and did not tell her parents.

It wasn’t an accident. It wasn’t a whim either. She’d decided it on the workshop floor the day of the proposal, wrapped in his coat.

“They didn’t tell me they were closing my shop.” She’d had her head on his shoulder. “They told two hundred people. Between the lobster and the cake.”

“Yes.”

“So I want them to find out the way I did. In public. From someone else.”

He’d been quiet for a bit.

“That’s cruel.”

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Clause three. Yes.”

“Then I approve.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Enzo picked up on the first ring. He always did. It was late, and he’d been waiting by the phone with a glass of grappa, the way he’d waited every night since March.

“Allora. Again. From the balcony.”

Chen Si stood at the window on the forty-fourth floor with the harbour under him and a sheet of paper in his hand.

“Ti ho vista per la prima volta su un balcone. Tremavo…”

“NO!” A thump. Enzo had hit something. Probably the table. “Tremavi! YOU were not shaking. SHE was shaking. If you say tremavo in front of her she will laugh until she dies and I will have to make a coffin out of gold.”

“Tremavi.”

“Better. Now the sums.”

“E facevi i conti.”

“Good. Again from the start. And slower, per l’amor di Dio, you sound like a man reading a bus timetable.”

He did it again. Slower. Enzo grunted.

“Eight weeks, and you are almost not terrible.”

“Thank you.”

“It was not a compliment.” The grappa glass clinked. “Does she know?”

“No.”

“Good. Don’t tell her. I want to see her face.”

Chen Si put the phone down, and then picked it up again and rang someone else. A man in Milan who owed him for a thing in a port two years ago. These days he worked at a magazine.

“A photographer. One. On the sixteenth of May. Palazzo on the Naviglio Grande.”

“For which pages?”

“The ones Vittoria Song reads last.”

A long silence from Milan.

“You understand who her mother is?”

“Yes.” He looked at the harbour. “That’s why.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose Milan because it was where she’d learned to be afraid.

She didn’t tell anyone that except him. Everyone else got the other reasons, all true. The light was better. The lawyers there were the only ones she trusted with this. An Italian citizen with a Chinese surname. A man with a very complicated history. Fast, and no fuss. And the city was full of the best goldsmiths on earth, and she wanted one at her wedding.

The night before, in a hotel suite over the canal, she lay awake beside him in the dark and told him the rest.

“My mother took me to the shows from when I was four. Front row. A little dress she picked. I wasn’t allowed to move. Not for the whole show.”

“How long?”

“Two hours. If I moved, she knew.” She touched the back of her own neck. “She’d put her hand here. And squeeze. Just a little. Just so I knew.”

He didn’t say anything.

“I didn’t move at a fashion show from four until I was fifteen. Then we came to your city and I thought, I am never sitting still again.”

He put his hand on the back of her neck, right where she’d touched it. And left it there. Warm. Not squeezing.

She felt her shoulders come down for the first time in days.

“I want it to be where I got married. To you. That’s all. I want it to mean that instead.”

“It will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The palazzo was on the Naviglio Grande, the long canal in the south of the city where the antique dealers set out their stalls. It belonged to a family of goldsmiths who’d been making jewellery in Milan since 1832 and had known her grandmother. A courtyard full of wisteria in full flower, so heavy it hung down off the balconies in purple ropes. A fountain. A long room upstairs with the windows open on the water, and the bells of San Cristoforo across the bridge.

Upstairs, an hour before, Enzo did up the clasp at the nape of her neck. His fingers were the steadiest in Milan. Today they kept missing.

“Cara, stand still.”

“I am standing still!”

“You are vibrating. Like a fridge.”

“I’m not…”

“There.” The clasp clicked. He stepped back and looked at the chain down her spine, the break in the middle. His chin went. “Madonna. Your grandmother would have killed for this.”

“She’d have asked me to take out the break.”

“Yes.” He blew his nose, enormously. “And you would have told her no, and she would have been so proud she’d have cried for a week. Go. Go! Before I ruin my suit.”

Eleven guests.

Enzo, who’d flown with her, wore a suit for the first time in nine years and started crying the moment he saw her.

Qian had never been out of Asia. He’d read an entire guide to Milan on the plane and taken notes. He’d also, she found out later, taken four antacids.

Mr. Lu, the small neat man in the cardigan who ran the pawnshops, had asked to come. He’d brought his wife, a tiny smiling woman with no Italian and no English. She held Aurelia’s hands in both of hers and didn’t let go for a full minute.

The old goldsmith who owned the palazzo, ninety-one. His son. His grandson.

Dottor Rossi from the customs office, with flowers and a wink.

A registrar from the commune, in a sash.

Zhao Zhendong.

And right at the back, in the doorway, at the last possible minute: Serafina Song. Leather jacket. Boots with oil on them. Hair dripping from the rain, a motorcycle helmet under one arm.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia saw her sister and stopped walking.

She’d posted the invitation to a garage in the industrial district where Serafina sometimes slept. Would it get there? Would Serafina even open it? They hadn’t spoken properly in two years. Not since the night Serafina walked out of her own engagement dinner. Aurelia had stood at the top of the stairs and watched her go. She’d said nothing. Their mother was standing at the bottom.

Serafina was twenty-one. Taller than Aurelia, and thinner, with hair she’d clearly cut herself with kitchen scissors, and a burn scar on the back of one hand. She stood in the doorway of the long room dripping rainwater onto the old goldsmith’s marble floor and looked at her sister.

At the dress.

Aurelia had designed it in a week. Ivory silk. Plain. Close to the body, long sleeves, high neck. No lace, no beads, nothing to look at at all. Until she turned round.

The back was open from the nape of her neck to the base of her spine. Down the middle of it ran a single chain of yellow gold. Fastened at the nape. Falling in one long line to the small of her back. Wrenched apart in the middle. Mended, with a seam of white.

Serafina looked at it. And kept looking.

“You look like a gilded bird,” she said, in Italian, and her voice wasn’t quite steady.

It was what Serafina had called her since they were tiny. Gilded bird. It had never once been a compliment.

Aurelia lifted her chin.

“Yes. But I let myself out of the cage.” She turned so Serafina could see the back. The broken chain. “Look. I did it myself.”

Serafina looked.

Then she dropped her helmet on the marble. Qian jumped. She crossed the room in three long strides in her oily boots and grabbed her sister and held on.

“You idiot,” she said into Aurelia’s hair. “You absolute idiot. Two years!”

“I know.”

“You could’ve called!”

“You didn’t call me!”

“So could you!”

“I don’t have a phone! It’s in a river!”

Over Serafina’s shoulder, at the far end of the room by the registrar, Aurelia saw Chen Si in dark grey. He didn’t come over. He just watched, like he was learning it by heart.

Beside him stood Zhao. Best man. He’d flown eleven hours and said one word since landing, which was “No,” to Dottor Rossi at the door. He looked at the two sisters wrapped round each other in the middle of the room. Then he looked out of the window at the canal for a while.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si stood by the registrar’s table and checked his inside pocket.

Zhao watched him do it.

“Rings.”

Zhao held up his huge hand. Two gold bands sat in his palm. Plain. Heavy. Enzo had made hers the night before, in a borrowed workshop, out of a pair of her grandmother’s earrings she’d melted down herself.

Chen Si looked at them. Then he checked his inside pocket again.

“Hm.”

“I know.”

“Fourth time.” Qian didn’t look up from his guidebook.

“I know, Qian.”

Zhao closed his hand over the rings. He reached out with the other and straightened Chen Si’s collar, one side and then the other. He’d never done that. Not in nine years. Not even at the riot.

“She came.”

“Who?”

Zhao tilted his head at the middle of the room, where the sister in the leather jacket still had both arms round the bride.

Chen Si looked. He didn’t say anything. His hand went to his pocket again and stopped halfway.

Qian turned a page of his guidebook.

“Five.”

Zhao looked at Qian. Qian looked at the ceiling. It was a very nice ceiling. Somebody had painted fat little angels all over it a very long time ago, and Qian counted every single one of them until the registrar cleared his throat.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were married at four.

The registrar read the articles of the civil code aloud in Italian. Then again in English, for Qian, who nodded very seriously and wrote it all down. Article 143. With marriage, husband and wife acquire the same rights and assume the same duties.

At the same rights, Chen Si glanced sideways at her.

Clause nine. He was thinking about clause nine. In front of a registrar. She had to look at the floor.

“Do you wish to say anything?”

She hadn’t planned to. She’d written eleven pages. Surely that was plenty?

But Chen Si said, “Yes,” in his mild voice. He turned to her in the wisteria light. Across the water the bells of San Cristoforo started up. And he spoke in careful, slightly accented Italian she had no idea he knew.

“Ti ho vista per la prima volta su un balcone. Tremavi, e facevi i conti. Da allora non ho più voluto guardare nient’altro.”

I first saw you on a balcony. You were shaking, and doing sums. I haven’t wanted to look at anything else since.

The old goldsmith said “Ah,” under his breath and put his hand on his heart.

Enzo sobbed out loud. Then, through it, much too loudly: “Tremavi! He got it right!”

Aurelia stared at the man in front of her. The man who’d walked past her window for six weeks. Who’d laid down his king. Who’d knelt on his own floor because she told him to.

“When did you learn Italian?” Chinese, under her breath.

“March. Every night.” Also Chinese. “On the phone, with Enzo. He’s very harsh.”

She laughed, and found out she was crying, and didn’t care in the slightest.

She turned to the registrar.

“Sì. Lo voglio. Yes. I do. Write it down.”

Chen Si didn’t wait for anyone to tell him he could. He took her face in both hands in front of eleven guests and a man in a sash and kissed her. Not a photograph kiss. A long one, deep, no hurry, like the room was empty and he had all afternoon. Somewhere a camera clicked. When he let her go her lipstick was on his mouth, Enzo was sobbing again and the registrar had completely lost his place.

“Mine,” he said, very low, in Chinese, for her alone. “Now write that down.”

Qian, who was close enough to hear, wrote it down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Six days later, on a terrace above Lake Como, Vittoria Song sat at breakfast. A pot of coffee. The June issue of Italian Vogue.

She turned the pages slowly. She always read the society pages last, the way some people saved the best bite.

Page two hundred and eleven. MATRIMONI.

A long room with the windows open onto a canal. Wisteria. A woman in ivory silk, seen from behind, walking away, her back bare except for one broken chain of gold down her spine. Beside her, holding her hand, a slight dark man in grey, looking at her and not at the camera.

The designer Aurelia Song, 22, daughter of the property magnate Song Weiren and the former model Vittoria Conti, has married the businessman Chen Si. A private ceremony at the Palazzo Ferraris on the Naviglio Grande, 16 May. The bride wore her own design. The couple will live in Asia, where Ms. Song’s label, AURELIA, opens a second boutique in the autumn. The bride’s parents were not present.

Vittoria Song looked at the photograph for a full minute.

Then she closed the magazine and laid it face down on the table. She poured another cup of coffee. She drank it. Her hand on the cup didn’t shake at all.

It was the maid, clearing the breakfast things, who noticed the cup.

A crack. Right down the side, rim to base. One thin, perfect line.

Nobody knew how it had happened.

chapters.title: Blood Brothers at the Reception
chapters.desc: Zhao makes a nine-word speech and Serafina offers her a getaway car. On the wedding night, the bride blindfolds her husband with her veil.
chapters.epigraph: “He is my brother. You’re his. So you’re mine.” — the complete best man’s speech of Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
The old goldsmith’s son had married a woman from Puglia, and the woman from Puglia believed that if there wasn’t too much food, there wasn’t enough.

So there were eleven guests and food for forty.

The table was in the courtyard under the wisteria. White cloth. Candles in glass. Aurelia sat at the head of it in ivory, with the broken chain cold down her spine and her husband beside her.

Her husband.

She kept thinking it. Was that allowed? Could you just have one, like that, with a sash and a signature? She kept turning to check, like he might have changed since four o’clock. He hadn’t. Dark grey suit. A glass of Franciacorta he’d poured himself and was actually drinking. He was listening to the old goldsmith tell an extremely long story about her grandmother in 1961, and every so often, under the table, without looking at her, he put his hand on her knee. Left it there. Took it away.

Every single time, she lost the story.

“Stop it,” she said, without moving her lips.

“Stop what?”

“You know what.”

His hand came back. His thumb drew one slow line above her knee through the silk.

“Signora Chen.”

“Don’t.”

“I’ve been practising.”

“Practise in your head!”

The old goldsmith beamed at them both and went on about 1961.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao Zhendong gave the best man’s speech.

Nobody had asked him to. Chen Si had warned her the week before. His brother didn’t do speeches. His brother had once been asked to say a few words at the opening of a warehouse, had stood in front of two hundred people for forty seconds in total silence, then said, “Open,” and walked off.

So when Zhao stood up at the end of the meal, enormous in his black suit, with his glass in his hand, the whole table went dead quiet. Qian put down his fork. Enzo stopped crying. Mr. Lu’s tiny wife looked up at him in terror.

Zhao looked down the table at Chen Si. Then at Aurelia. Flat. For much longer than was polite.

“He is my brother. You’re his. So you’re mine.”

He drank, and sat down.

Nobody said anything.

Then the old goldsmith, who was ninety-one, began to clap with tremendous dignity, and then everybody was clapping, and Enzo was crying again.

Aurelia turned to Chen Si. His hand on the white tablecloth had closed into a fist.

“That’s nine words,” she whispered.

“I know.” His voice had gone. “It’s the most I’ve heard him say at once. In nine years.”

She looked down the table. Zhao was eating a piece of cake with his fork, very carefully, looking at nobody.

She lifted her glass to him.

He looked at the glass. At her. Then he raised his own one inch.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina found her by the fountain when the candles had burned down to stubs and the grandson had put music on. Qian was dancing with Mr. Lu’s wife. Badly. Happily. Mr. Lu was filming it.

Serafina had a beer. She’d taken her leather jacket off. Under it was a black vest. Her arms were thin and strong, nicked all over with little burns and cuts. Engine arms.

“So. Chen Si.” She drank. “You know what he is.”

“Better than anyone.”

Serafina looked across the courtyard. The slight man in grey stood by the wall with his brother, not dancing, watching Aurelia over the rim of his glass.

“There are men in the industrial district who build cars for people who need to get away from things. Fast. Quiet.” Serafina’s eyes didn’t leave him. “Some of those people are getting away from him.”

“Sera…”

“I’ve heard things. He doesn’t shout. He doesn’t hit. He just… takes everything. Slowly. Until there’s nothing left.” She turned back. “I want you to know I know. And if you ever need to get away from him…”

“I won’t.”

“If you EVER do.” Very low. Very fierce. It was the voice Serafina had used at ten, when she found Aurelia crying in a bathroom after Vienna. “You call me. Day or night. Any city. I’ll have a car outside in an hour, and nobody will ever find you. Not him. Not his giant. Not God. Understand?”

Aurelia looked at her little sister by the fountain in the wisteria light.

“I understand. Thank you.”

She took the bottle out of Serafina’s hand and drank from it, the way she drank in the old town.

“And Sera. He’s never once asked me to win.”

Serafina stared at her.

“What?”

“Not once. Not at anything. He laid down his king.” She handed the bottle back. “He saw Mamma at the party. He knows exactly what she is. And he’s the only person who’s ever looked at me and not wanted me to be first.”

Serafina picked at the label with her thumbnail.

“So if you ever need to get away from her, you call him. He’ll have a car outside in ten minutes.”

Serafina didn’t say anything. She peeled the label off the bottle in one piece and folded it in half.

“You’re in love with him.” Like it was a diagnosis. “You. Aurelia.”

“Yes.”

Serafina looked across the courtyard again. Chen Si had seen them looking. He gave Serafina one small nod. A greeting. Or a promise. Hard to tell with him.

“What are you going to tell people? About today?”

“Three hundred guests. A choir. Fireworks over the canal.”

“Liar.”

“It’s my wedding.” Aurelia lifted her chin. “I’ll lie about it if I want.”

Serafina laughed for the first time all day. It came out of her exactly like Aurelia’s. A bark.

“God help him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d waited exactly as long as he was willing to. He crossed the courtyard, nodded politely to Serafina and held out his hand to his wife.

“Dance with me. I’ve shared you all day.”

He didn’t wait for an answer. He took her hand and pulled her out under the wisteria, among the candle stubs and Qian’s terrible dancing, and drew her in close. His palm went flat and warm on her bare back, right over the broken chain.

She kicked her heels off halfway through the first song. He bent, without letting go of her, scooped them up with one hand and kept dancing with them dangling off his fingers.

“You can’t dance holding my shoes.”

“I’m doing it.”

“It looks ridiculous.”

“Yes.”

Halfway through the second song he bent his head and kissed her. Slow. No hurry. In front of her sister and the grandson holding up his phone. He didn’t stop when the song stopped. When he let her breathe she caught Serafina’s face over his shoulder, beer in hand. It went from suspicious to something that looked very nearly like relief.

“Everyone’s looking,” she said into his jaw.

“Good.”

He kissed her again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The suite was right at the top of the palazzo, under the roof.

The old goldsmith had insisted. It had been his own wedding suite, in 1952. Clouds painted across the ceiling. An old walnut bed with carved posts and faded green silk curtains. Long windows open onto a little balcony over the canal. Down below, the bars along the towpath put their lights in the black water, and somebody was laughing, and somebody else was playing a guitar.

He’d carried her shoes all the way up the stairs. He put them side by side by the door. Neatly.

She went out onto the balcony in her ivory dress and looked at the water.

He came out behind her. She heard him. She always heard him now.

He put his arms round her from behind and pulled her back against him, hard, and put his mouth on the side of her neck just above the clasp of the chain. And stayed there. Breathing her in. Like he’d been waiting since four o’clock to do exactly this and couldn’t stand one more minute of it.

“A balcony.” Against her skin. “You’re not shaking.”

“No.” She watched the lights on the water. “I was. All day. I didn’t show it.”

“I know. Your left hand. You kept touching the ring.”

She looked down. Her right hand was on her left, turning the ring round and round. Plain yellow gold. Heavy. She hadn’t even known.

She turned round in his arms.

“Clause nine.”

His face didn’t change. All of him went still. A cat hearing a door.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went inside. He followed.

By the old walnut bed she reached up and took the veil out of her hair. Long and fine. Ivory silk tulle, no lace, no embroidery. It had fallen all day from the back of her head over the broken chain to the floor. She held it in both hands.

“Turn round.”

He turned round.

She folded the veil once, twice, three times into a long soft band. She put it over his eyes and knotted it loosely at the back of his head.

“Can you see?”

“No.”

“Good.” She put her hands on his shoulders and felt him breathe. “All day, everybody looked at me. A hundred photographs. You. You haven’t stopped looking at me since four o’clock.”

“No. I haven’t.”

“So now you don’t get to.” She put her mouth right by his ear. “Now you have to find me without looking.”

He shivered. All the way down.

She stepped back.

She took off her earrings, one, two, and dropped them in a dish on the dressing table, where they rang like little bells. His head turned towards the sound.

Then she reached behind her for the clasp at her nape. The broken chain held up the whole dress. She’d designed it like that. When the chain came undone, everything did.

She undid it.

The ivory silk slid off her shoulders and down and lay on the old goldsmith’s floor in a pale puddle. She stood under the painted clouds in nothing but the long gold chain, held in one hand, and looked at her blindfolded husband by the bed. Listening.

“Where am I?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her.

He took his time. He didn’t grope about blind, the way she’d expected. He stood still and listened with his head tilted, the way he listened to a room full of men before he spoke. One step towards her voice. Then another. She moved, barefoot, on the old wooden floor. He stopped. Listened again. Turned. Straight at her. Like he could hear her heart going.

“You’re cheating.”

“You’re breathing. I’ve been listening to you breathe for months. I’d know it anywhere.”

His fingertips found her shoulder, barely there. Stopped.

Then they went down her arm. Elbow. Wrist. Back up. Across her collarbone. She watched his face under the folded veil as he worked out that there was nothing at all between his hand and her skin.

“Aurelia.” His voice had almost gone. “You took off the dress.”

“I took off everything. Except this.” She laid the broken chain in his palm, still warm from her spine. “I wanted you to find out by touch.”

His hand closed round the gold. He was shaking. She could see it.

“Clause nine.” Barely. “What are the terms?”

She took the hand with the chain in it. She wound the chain once round his wrist, then once round her own, so they were joined by it. A long loose loop of gold.

“You don’t take off the blindfold. You don’t let go of the chain. You learn me with your hands and your mouth. All of me. Every centimetre.” She stepped in until she was against him, his suit on her bare skin. “And you don’t look. Not once. Not until I say.”

“And?”

“And you don’t hurry.”

“I never hurry.”

“I know. That’s why I married you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t hurry.

He learned her by touch, in the dark behind the veil, on the old walnut bed with the green curtains, with the gold looped between their wrists and a guitar somewhere on the towpath playing something slow.

He did it like he went through her ledgers. Every centimetre, exactly as instructed. Not one faster than he wanted. His hands first. Then his mouth, following his hands. Her palm, next to the chain. The crook of her elbow. Her shoulder. Then the long line of her spine where the broken chain had lain all day. Every vertebra, one at a time. Like he was counting them.

Was he counting them? He was counting them.

“You said you wouldn’t count!” It came out as a gasp.

“I said I wouldn’t count time.” Against the small of her back. “You never said anything about bones.”

She’d have laughed if she could have breathed.

Somewhere after the bones he stopped with his forehead on her shoulder and his fingers resting on the knot of the veil. Not pulling it. Just there.

“Let me see you. One look. Please.” Hoarse. “You can say no.”

“No.”

She felt him laugh against her skin. He took his hand off the knot and went back to work. He kept to the terms exactly, and she loved him so much for it she could have bitten him.

In the end what undid her was that he couldn’t see. Not her face. Not anything. So he listened. Every sound she made, every catch in her breath, every time she said his name. He heard it. He followed it. He went back to it and stayed. Until the sounds coming out of her were ones she’d never made in her life, and the chain was pulled tight between their wrists, because her hand had made a fist in the green silk.

“Look at me.” Her voice was wrecked. “Chen Si. Take it off. Look at me.”

He reached up with his free hand and pulled the veil away.

And looked.

She saw his face when he did. Candlelight. Painted clouds. Everything he’d felt about her since a balcony in October, all of it at once, and he wasn’t hiding a scrap of it.

Her mother had never looked at her like that. Two hundred people at a party hadn’t. The man from Vogue hadn’t.

“Found you,” said her husband.

Then he came up the bed to her, the chain still tight between their wrists, and kissed her on the mouth. The one place he hadn’t let himself go back to in an hour. She held his face in both hands and kissed him back like she’d been the one in the blindfold.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she lay across his chest with the chain still looped loosely round both their wrists. The veil was somewhere on the floor. The canal had gone quiet. Across the water, San Cristoforo struck two.

“Signora Chen,” he said, into her hair.

“I said don’t.”

“Aurelia Chen. Wife.” She could feel him smiling. “My queen.”

She lifted her head.

“You’ve never said that before.”

“I’ve thought it since you sat in my chair.”

“That was months ago.”

“Yes. I wanted to wait until it was true.”

She put her head back down on his chest. His heart was slow and steady under her ear. Forty minutes north, her mother was asleep and didn’t know a thing.

“In six days she opens the magazine.”

“Yes.”

“Do you think she’ll cry?”

“No.”

“Do you think she’ll break something?”

He thought about it, with his fingers going slowly up and down the chain on her wrist.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Aurelia Chen was asleep before he could say anything else. He didn’t try.

chapters.title: A Necklace on the Hit List
chapters.desc: She finishes the best necklace she’s ever made and drapes it over her husband’s shoulders while he stares at his list. He makes her count the stones out loud.
chapters.epigraph: “My King. You’ve been staring at that list for an hour. Everyone on it, put together, is worth less than this necklace.”
chapters.content:
“If you drop it, I’ll die. And then I’ll come back and kill you.”

“I have never dropped anything in my life, cara.”

“You dropped your glasses in the pickling acid on Monday!”

“That was the glasses’ fault.”

Enzo set the last claw with the tip of his pusher and sat back. He didn’t say anything. He took off his magnifiers. He wiped his eyes with the back of his wrist and pretended it was the polish.

Aurelia didn’t breathe.

On the black velvet between them lay a collar. High and stiff, the old Maharaja shape. It would sit at the bottom of a woman’s throat like a hand. Forty-one sapphires, all cornflower blue, all from one mine in Ratnapura, matched over three months until not one of them was a hair off the rest. Platinum. Claws so fine they vanished. The stones looked like they were floating.

Four months. Two broken saw blades. One fight with a dealer in Colombo that had lasted a whole night on the phone.

“Well?” Enzo blew his nose. “Say something. You are frightening me.”

“It’s the best thing I’ve ever made.”

“Yes.” He folded his handkerchief. “And the name? You still want to call it that horrible thing?”

“Numero Uno.”

“Madonna.” He put his glasses back on, the ones that had survived the acid. “Your mother will have a stroke.”

“That’s the idea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d named it at two in the morning in June, after a phone call. Her mother had rung from Lake Como to say she’d seen the magazine. She’d been calm. Pleasant. She’d said the photograph was flattering and the dress was brave. Then she’d asked whether the boutique was making money yet or whether her husband was paying for it.

She’d been working on it since April without a name. That night she hung up, went to the bench in her pyjamas and wrote it across the drawing in red ink. Underlined twice.

She took it home in its case that night on her lap in the car, both hands flat on the lid, like it might try to escape.

Home. She still wasn’t used to the word. Three months married and she still came out of the lift on the forty-fourth floor and felt the floor tilt a bit. Her shoes by his door. Her sketchbooks on his long table. Her toothbrush next to his, which was obscene somehow. The jade chess set by the window, still one queen short, because the black queen lived on her bedside table now and she wasn’t giving it back.

He was in the study. The light under the door said so.

She looked at the clock. Then she looked at it again. Ten. He’d gone in at nine.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard her in the corridor at the first step.

Bare feet. She walked differently barefoot. Lighter on the left. He knew that the way he knew the number of the lift and the weight of his own gun.

He didn’t look up. The list was under his hands. Nineteen names in his own small writing. A judge. Two men from planning. A banker. A security firm. A journalist who’d written something careful about the east side last spring. Lines between them. Dates. Amounts. And every line, if you followed it far enough, went up to the top of the page. To the space where he never wrote the name. He didn’t need to.

Fu.

His coffee was cold. He hadn’t drunk it. He never did.

The door opened.

“Five minutes.”

“You said that an hour ago.”

“I meant it an hour ago.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came round the desk. He kept his eyes on the paper. He could feel her standing behind his chair. Then he could smell her. Polish. Metal. The orange oil she used on her hands after the bench.

She was wearing his shirt. The white one from that morning. He knew without looking. He’d know that shirt on her in the dark.

Something cold and heavy came down across his shoulders.

He went still.

“My King.” Her mouth was right by his ear. Sweet as poison. “You’ve been staring at that list for an hour. Everyone on it, put together, is worth less than this necklace.” Her cheek came down against his. “Look at me instead.”

He put the pen down.

He lifted one hand and touched the first stone on his shoulder. Then the next. And the next. Reading them.

“Ratnapura.”

“How do you know that?”

“The colour. The silk inside.” He touched another. “You drew it for me. On a napkin at Old Fan’s. Sri Lanka on the left, Kashmir on the right.”

“That was months ago.”

“You did a little flower in the corner.” Another stone. “You’ve matched every one. That’s three months of work.”

“Three and a bit.”

“Forty-one.”

Of course he’d counted. She hadn’t even seen him count.

“When did you count them?”

“Just now.”

“You were reading them.”

“I can do both.”

“Show-off.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned the chair round. Slowly, so the collar didn’t slide. She was standing between his knees in his shirt, hair down, with his cold coffee in her hand.

“Are you drinking my coffee?”

“You never drink it.” She took another sip. Disgusting. Stone cold. “Somebody has to.”

“I might have.”

“Darling. You’ve never finished a coffee in your life. Qian thinks it’s a disease.”

She put the cup down on his list. Right on the judge. Then she reached into the shirt pocket and took out the black jade queen and set it on the empty space at the top of the page. Where the name wasn’t.

He looked at it.

He looked at it for long enough that she wondered if she’d gone too far. Was that cruel? It felt a bit cruel. She’d meant it to be.

“That’s where it lives now,” she said. “Until you’re done with him. Then it comes back to me.”

He didn’t answer. He reached up and tucked her hair behind her ear. Then he left his hand there, on her jaw.

“What’s it called?”

She lifted her chin.

“Numero Uno.”

His thumb stopped. He knew. Of course he knew. He’d been in bed beside her in June when the phone went.

“Put it on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t let her do it herself.

He stood up and lifted the collar off his own shoulders and turned her by the hips to face the window. The harbour was forty-four floors down and full of lights. The black glass gave them back. A slight dark man in a white shirt. A woman in a white shirt. A ring of blue fire in his hands.

He moved her hair over one shoulder. He put the collar round her throat. Cold. Heavy. It settled into the hollow at the base of her neck and stayed. He did up the clasp. His fingers stayed on it.

Then he undid the top button of his shirt. On her. Then the next one.

He watched her in the glass the whole time.

When the last button went he slid it off her shoulders. It hit the floor with a whisper.

She stood in his study in forty-one sapphires and nothing else, with the whole city looking up.

“Chen Si.” Her voice came out tiny. Mortifying. “The window…”

“Forty-fourth floor. Nobody can see in.” His mouth came down on her shoulder. “Only me.”

She looked at the woman in the glass. The blue at her throat. His hands on her waist.

“Clause nine.”

“Yes?”

She shut her eyes.

“Otherwise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She felt him smile. Against her skin. The bastard.

“Hands on the desk.”

She put them on the desk. Flat. One each side of the list. The queen sat between them on the empty space at the top.

“Don’t move them. Not until I say.”

“And if I do?”

“Then I stop. And we start again.” His hands went up her ribs. Slow. “And you count.”

“Count what?”

He touched the first stone. Left side of her throat.

“These. Out loud. One every time I touch one.” He didn’t sound sorry. He sounded like Christmas had come early. “Lose count and I go back to one.”

She opened her eyes. Found him in the glass.

“That’s evil.”

“You matched them all.” He touched the first stone again. “I want to hear how proud you are. One.”

“…One.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost count at nine.

He started again.

One, with his fingertip on the stone. Two, with his mouth open on her shoulder. Three, and his other hand went down her side. Four. She could see him in the glass. He wasn’t looking at the stones. He was looking at her face. By seven her voice had stopped being a voice. At nine he did something with his hand that wasn’t fair. What came out of her wasn’t a number in any language.

He took his hands away. All of them.

“One.”

“Dio!”

He laughed against the back of her neck.

“You know the word. You can stop me.”

“I’m NOT saying it.”

“I know you’re not.” His finger came back to the first stone. “One.”

“One,” through her teeth.

She got to fourteen the second time.

Twenty-two the third.

The fourth time she got to thirty-five. Palms flat on the wood. Whole body shaking. His mouth going down her spine one bone at a time. Her own face in front of her in the dark glass, wild and pink, and her voice saying numbers in a way she’d never be able to hear in a meeting again. Thirty-three. His hand. Thirty-four. His mouth. Thirty-five. And at thirty-six he did something she didn’t see coming and her hands left the desk and grabbed for him.

He stopped.

“Hands.”

She put them back. She was laughing. She was nearly crying. Both.

“I hate you.”

“I know.” He kissed the side of her neck, just above the platinum. “One.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fifth time she got to forty-one.

How? She’d never know. She’d stop asking eventually. Her palms were pressed so hard into the wood they’d leave prints in the polish, and the cleaner would find them in the morning and pretend she hadn’t.

Thirty-eight, with her eyes shut. Thirty-nine, barely. Forty, like falling off something.

He touched the last stone. Right side of her throat.

She opened her eyes and found him in the window.

“Forty-one.”

He went very still behind her.

“All of them.” His voice had gone rough and strange. “Number one.” His arms came round her. “Now you can let go.”

She let go of the desk.

He turned her round and lifted her onto it. Onto his list. Onto nineteen names and a cold coffee and the black queen, which went skidding off somewhere. She wrapped herself round him with forty-one stones at her throat and the city behind her, and quit counting anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later she lay on the rug in his study with her head on his chest. The collar was still on. She’d refused to take it off.

The list was under the desk somewhere. So was the queen. So was his shirt.

“I’m selling it.” She touched a stone. “Geneva. November. It’ll make three times what the stones cost. Maybe four. That’s the third boutique paid for.”

“And your mother gets the catalogue.”

“By courier. First class.”

“She’ll send it back.”

“She’ll keep it. She’ll keep it in the drawer with the knives.” She smiled at the ceiling. “Numero Uno. Aurelia Chen. Estimate on request.”

He laughed. She felt it go through him under her ear.

“You’ve ruined it, you know. For me. I’ll never look at it again without thinking about this.”

“Good.”

He lifted his head and looked at her. Just looked. Her face, the blue at her throat, her hair all over his chest. He held her face in both hands to do it. Like he was checking she was real. Like he’d checked the stones.

“What?” Her ears were getting hot. “What is it?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re doing the face.”

“I don’t have a face.”

“You have a face, and you’re doing it.”

He didn’t answer. He reached up and touched the first stone. Left side of her throat.

She went rigid.

“One.”

“NO.” She was laughing. She rolled on top of him, collar and all, and slapped her hand over his mouth. “No. Absolutely not. I’ll call Qian. I’ll call your brother.”

He laughed into her palm. Flat on his back on his own rug, the most dangerous man in the city, with an eight-hundred-thousand-dollar necklace swinging an inch from his nose.

“Two,” he said, muffled.

She took her hand away and kissed him to shut him up.

It didn’t work.

“Three.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at nine with the collar still on and a crease from his pillow down one cheek.

He’d gone, obviously. On her side of the bed, lined up with the edge of the table, sat the case for the collar, open and waiting. A glass of water. Two painkillers on a saucer. She always woke up with a headache after sleeping in jewellery. She’d mentioned it once. Once! In March!

And his coffee from this morning. Full. Stone cold. With a torn corner of cream paper under it.

Your turn.

She laughed out loud at nobody.

Chen Si: The cleaner found your hands on my desk.

Aurelia: WHAT

Chen Si: Ten fingers. In the polish. She asked if she should leave them.

Aurelia: tell me you said no

Chen Si: I said yes.

Aurelia: chen si

Chen Si: I’ve taken the list to work. The queen came too. It goes where the list goes.

Aurelia: that is MY queen

Chen Si: Then come and get it.

She was still staring at that when the next one came in. A different number.

Qian: Good morning, Mrs. Chen. Mr. Chen has moved the bank to Thursday. His diary for this morning now says Dental.

Aurelia: is that bad

Qian: The last time it said Dental he came back at four with lipstick on his collar.

Aurelia: it’s a very thorough dentist

Qian: I’ll buy more antacids.

chapters.title: Chen Si Lost an Argument (Once)
chapters.desc: A grey car follows her, and he wants two men behind her everywhere. She wins the argument with a cancelled shipment, three days at Zhao’s range and a page of red ink.
chapters.epigraph: “He lost. Good.” — Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
“Two of Zhendong’s men. A car behind you. Everywhere.”

“No.”

“You won’t see them.”

“No.”

“Aurelia…”

“Darling, I heard you the first time. I’m saying no to all three.”

That was the first night. There were eleven.

✦ ✦ ✦

It started with a newspaper.

The second boutique opened on a Wednesday in September, in the new mall on the east side. Two hundred people came. Enzo cried at the ribbon. On Thursday morning one of the papers put her on the front of its business section in gold, laughing, under the words THE QUEEN OF HARBOUR ROAD.

On Thursday afternoon a grey saloon followed her from the flat to the shop.

She saw it at the second set of lights. Three cars back. Still there at the fourth. When she parked on Harbour Road it pulled in across the street and sat there with its engine running for forty minutes. Then it drove off.

She told him that night at dinner. Clause three.

He put his chopsticks down.

He didn’t say anything for a bit. His face went very calm. Calm was the bad one. Had he always had that face? Probably. She’d just never been on the wrong side of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The eleven days were, everyone agreed afterwards, the worst in the history of the Syndicate.

Chen Si didn’t shout. He didn’t slam a single door. He just argued. Calmly. Constantly. Like a lawyer who’d been told the court would never close. At dinner. On the long grey sofa. In the car. In the shower, once, which she thought was low.

“Half the city knows your face now.”

“Then they can admire it.”

“They know which shop you’re in on which day.”

“It’s on the website, Si.”

“They know you’re married to me.”

“That was rather the point of the wedding.”

“Anyone who wants to hurt me has had a much easier way to do it since May.”

She didn’t have an answer to that one. She threw a cushion at him instead.

On the thirty-ninth floor, it was worse.

“Is he all right?” That was Mr. Lu, on day six, very gently, in the corridor.

“He’s married,” Qian said, and shook two more antacids into his hand.

Qian got through two boxes that week. At the Thursday meeting the man with the sunflower seeds made a joke about married life. Chen Si looked at him. Just looked. Without blinking. For a very long time. The man stopped laughing halfway through his own joke and didn’t make another one until Christmas.

On the fourth night, in the dark, he said the thing he hadn’t said before.

He was lying on his back. She thought he was asleep.

“Aurelia.”

“Mm.”

“Are you awake?”

“No.”

“My mother was on her own.”

She went still.

“When she died. In the flat. In his chair.” His voice was perfectly flat. “I was in Block C. Nobody was there.”

She found his hand under the sheet. It was cold.

“Two men, Aurelia. That’s all I want. Two men in a car.”

She held his cold hand for a long time.

“I won’t be followed. I won’t be watched. I won’t be kept somewhere safe.” She turned her head on the pillow. “Clause four, darling.”

He closed his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second day he’d found the man in the grey saloon.

It hadn’t been hard. A grey saloon is a grey saloon, but the city had cameras and Zhendong had people who watched the cameras. By noon the car was in a yard behind the Iron Docks. By two the man was standing in front of it.

He was forty or so. Sweating. He kept trying to explain.

“I just drive. They pay me to drive. I don’t…”

“Who paid you?”

“A man. Cash. I never saw him before.”

“What did he look like?”

“Old. Nice manners.” The man wiped his face. “He called me son.”

Chen Si looked at him for a while. Then he nodded to the crane driver.

The grey saloon went up on the magnet. Then it went into the crusher. It took about a minute. The noise was very loud and very ugly, and the man watched all of it with his mouth open, and when it was over his car was the size of a fridge.

“You’ll get a letter on Monday. Your licence has been withdrawn.” Chen Si took a bus pass out of his pocket and tucked it into the man’s shirt. “Number eleven stops at the end of the road.”

He walked back to his car. He checked his phone.

Chen Si: Where are you?

Aurelia: boutique. still angry

Chen Si: Good. Stay angry. Eat something.

Aurelia: is that an ORDER

Chen Si: It’s a request. With a very strong preference.

He read it twice in the back of the car. The saloon could stay out of it. So could the man with nice manners who called people son. Who called a stranger son? He knew one or two men who did. He filed that somewhere cold and kept it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not argue the way he did.

She’d been trained by Vittoria Conti. Vittoria Conti had once made a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman cry in a showroom in Milan without raising her voice above a purr. Aurelia didn’t lay things out like a case.

She just won.

On the fifth day she rang Dottor Rossi in Milan and explained, in fast, charming Italian, that there’d be a small delay. Then she rang the hotel on the east side and explained, in fast, charming Cantonese, that their walnut tables would be a month late. Then she sat in her boutique and painted her nails.

At four the man with the tinted glasses rang Chen Si in a panic.

At six Chen Si came home.

He stood in the kitchen doorway and looked at her. She was making her grandmother’s sauce in an apron that said KISS THE COOK. Qian had bought it for her as a joke and then gone pale when she wore it.

“You cancelled the shipment.”

“Postponed.” She stirred. “Until I’m allowed to go to the Iron Docks at four in the morning without a car full of your brother’s men behind me. It’s my route. Clause two. I sit at the table.” She held the spoon out. “Taste?”

“That’s blackmail.”

“That’s negotiation. You taught me. Thirty-ninth floor, my first week. Find what the other person can’t afford to lose.”

He looked at her for a long moment.

“I can’t afford to lose you.”

The spoon stopped.

“I know,” she said. “That’s why you’re going to lose this one.”

His eyes went down to the apron. Very slowly.

KISS THE COOK.

He crossed the kitchen in three steps. He took the spoon out of her hand. Licked it. Disgusting. Somehow not. He put it down. Then he took her jaw in his hand and kissed her. No warning. No question. Her back hit the counter. The sauce bubbled behind her and spat on her arm and she didn’t care at all.

When he lifted his head, she had both fists in his shirt.

“That doesn’t change anything.”

“I know.” He was breathing hard. “I’m still going to argue with you.”

“Then why…”

“I wanted to taste the sauce first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth day she went to see Zhao Zhendong. She didn’t tell anyone.

His office was in an old warehouse at the Iron Docks. Iron stairs. A sign on the door that just said ZHAO — IMPORT/EXPORT. She went up the stairs in heels. Every step rang like a bell. So much for surprise.

He opened the door himself. Black T-shirt. An oily rag in one hand. Behind him, on a cloth on the desk, a gun in pieces.

He looked at her. For quite a long time. She refused to look away.

“Hm.”

“I need you to teach me to shoot.”

“Why.”

“Because your brother wants two of your men following me everywhere I go. And I won’t have it. And he can’t sleep.” She hadn’t meant to say that part. It came out anyway. “He hasn’t slept properly in eight days. He lies there and looks at the ceiling and thinks about his mother.”

Zhao didn’t move.

“So I need to be able to look after myself. Properly. So when I say I don’t need two men, it’s true.” She lifted her chin. “And everyone says you’re the best. Even people who are terrified of you.”

“Especially them.”

He stood aside and let her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The range was in the hills behind a quarry. It didn’t exist, apparently. It belonged to a man who owed Zhao something and asked no questions.

Zhao didn’t talk. He showed. How to stand. Feet like this. How to hold it. How to breathe out before you squeeze. Squeeze, not pull. He moved her elbow with two fingers. He moved her chin with one. He took it apart in front of her. She took it apart after him. Put it back together. He watched her hands the whole time.

“Fast.”

It was the longest compliment he paid her in three days.

She was good. Not as good as him. Nobody was. But eight years of setting stones under a loupe will give you steady hands. On the second day she put six through the paper at fifteen metres in a group he could cover with his palm. He looked at the target. He looked at her.

“Hm.”

A different hm. She was almost sure of it.

On the third day, packing up, she asked.

“Is it true? About the drains?”

He stopped with the case half shut.

“He said there’s a story. He said it’s his and yours. He said he’d tell me one day.” She took off the ear defenders. “He hasn’t.”

Zhao looked out at the hills. The quarry dust was blowing.

“Three of them came for him. In the riot.”

“And you…”

“Got in the way.” He touched his own left side. Under the arm, down towards the hip. Quick. Like checking something was still there. “One had a piece of bed frame.”

She kept her mouth shut. If she opened it, something would come out.

“He held it shut with his shirt. An hour.” A pause. “Then he got the grate up. The fire was on top of it. It was hot. He held it up with his arm.”

“His arm…”

“Burned to the elbow. He didn’t notice till the snow.” Zhao shut the case. “He carried me. Half the way. Through the water. In the dark. I was bleeding. He was sixteen and he weighed fifty kilos.”

The wind blew grit across the bench.

“I would be dead.”

She stood there in the cold with her hands shaking for the first time in three days.

“He wants two men behind you because the last time somebody he loved was on her own, he was locked in a cell. And she died.” Zhao picked up the case. “He’ll never say that. He’ll argue about cars. He’ll argue about newspapers. He’ll never say it.”

“He said it. In the dark.”

Zhao stopped walking.

He turned and looked at her. Four seconds, maybe. Maybe five.

“Then he loves you.”

He walked on to the car. Over his shoulder, as an afterthought:

“More than I knew.”

✦ ✦ ✦
