She came home on the eleventh night with a small black gun in her gold clutch and a range certificate from a place that didn’t exist. She put both on the kitchen counter in front of him. Then a third thing. A sheet of his own cream paper, covered in red ink.

He looked at all three.

“Zhendong.”

“Three days. He says I’m fast.” She tapped the paper. “Terms. Read them.”

He read them standing up.

1. No men. No car. Nobody behind me.

2. I carry this. Everywhere.

3. I text you where I’m going. Every day.

4. If I ever see a grey saloon again, I call you before I do anything else. Including scream.

5. Serafina teaches me to drive properly. Evasive. In the industrial district. At night.

He looked up at five.

“Serafina.”

“She’s very good. Also slightly insane.”

He took the fountain pen out of his inside pocket. He uncapped it. He wrote one word under each line in his small black hand, the way he had on her counter-offer last November. A lifetime ago.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Under five he stopped. Then he wrote: Agreed. God help me.

Then he added a sixth.

6. The Husband keeps the Wife’s location on his phone. The Wife knows.

She looked at it. Then at him.

“How long have you had it?”

He capped the pen.

“Chen Si. How long?”

“Since the registrar.”

“Since the WEDDING?”

“Since about a minute after.”

She picked up the nearest thing, which was a tea towel, and hit him with it. He let her. She hit him again. He didn’t even put his hands up.

Then she took the pen out of his fingers and wrote under six, in red.

Agreed. And the Wife keeps his.

He read it. Something happened to his face. She didn’t know what to call it.

“I lose,” he said.

She didn’t move.

“I lose.” His eyes were wet. He didn’t do anything about it. “No men. No car. The gun. The texts. Serafina.” A breath. “The Milan shipment goes Thursday.”

“Obviously it goes Thursday.”

“I don’t lose arguments. Not since I was fifteen.”

“I know. Somebody should have it engraved on something.” She came round the counter. She took his face in her hands. “You won’t lose me, Si. Not like that. Not by putting me in a box.”

He pulled her in by the waist. Hard. Counter, gun, paper, all of it behind her. He put his face in her hair and held on.

“The man in the grey saloon,” he said into her temple. Very mild. “I found him on the second day. He won’t be driving behind anyone again.”

“What did you do?”

“I bought him a bus pass.”

She pulled back to look at him. He looked completely serious.

“If anyone ever touches you, I’ll take this city apart to find them.” Still mild. Still holding her. “I’m saying it so you know. It isn’t part of the argument.”

She didn’t answer that. She took hold of his collar instead, both sides, and pulled his mouth down to hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came to dinner on the Saturday.

He came every few weeks now. He ate a whole steamed fish with his hands, in silence, for two hours. Aurelia had stopped finding it alarming in about June. Now she found it restful. She’d told him so. He’d nodded, like that was reasonable.

After dinner the dishwasher broke.

It made a noise like a dying animal and stopped dead with water in it and a red light flashing. Chen Si looked at it with the polite blankness of a man who’d built an empire on paper and never once touched an appliance. Aurelia had grown up in a villa on Lake Como with eleven staff. Her face was exactly the same.

“Is it… is it supposed to do that?”

“I have no idea.”

“You own it!”

“I own the building. I’ve never met it.”

Zhao put down his fish.

He got up. He opened the dishwasher and looked in. Then he knelt on their kitchen floor in his good black suit, took a knife out of the block, and had the front panel off before either of them could say a word. He put his arm in up to the elbow.

He pulled out a piece of a broken wine glass. Then a clump of something unspeakable. Then something small and blue.

He held it up to the light.

They all looked at it.

“That’s from Numero Uno.” Aurelia’s voice came out high. “That’s the spare. I had a spare cut, just in case. I lost it in June!” She turned round. “How did it get in the dishwasher?”

Chen Si looked at the ceiling.

“Si.”

“I was looking at it.”

“In the kitchen?”

“You’d left it on the bench. I wanted to see it in daylight.” A pause. “I carried it round for a few days.”

“You carried…”

“It was in my shirt pocket. I may have washed a glass.”

Zhao put the panel back. He pressed a button. The dishwasher started up again, humming, perfectly happy. Then, underneath the hum, a thin high whine. Like a mosquito.

Zhao listened to it. He shrugged. He washed his hands at the sink and dropped the sapphire into Aurelia’s palm.

Then he looked at his brother. At his brother’s wife. At the gold clutch on the counter with a gun in it. At a sheet of cream paper stuck to the fridge with a magnet, red and black.

And he laughed.

Short. Low. Once. Like a door opening a long way off.

“He lost.” He sat back down and picked up his fish. “Good.”

chapters.title: The Song Family Is Coming to Dinner
chapters.desc: Her mother writes to invite herself to dinner. Chen Si cooks the fish, Aurelia leaves the dishwasher whining on purpose, and at the door her mother names the one man he can’t stand.
chapters.epigraph: “Your father and I would like to come to dinner. We would like to be proud of you.” — Vittoria Song, letter, 2 October
chapters.content:
“Enzo. Come here. Read this and tell me I’m wrong.”

“You are wrong.”

“You haven’t read it yet.”

“I don’t need to. It’s from your mother. You’re always wrong about your mother, cara. You always think she might mean it.”

He took it anyway. Cream envelope. Her mother’s initials on the flap in dark blue. V.C.S. It had come by hand on Wednesday morning, the second of October. Four months and ten days after page two hundred and eleven of Italian Vogue. Aurelia had counted.

Enzo read it over the top of his magnifiers.

Aurelia,

Your father and I have been in Shanghai and then in Milan for the summer. We have now returned. We would like to come to dinner, with your husband, at your home, on Saturday the twelfth. We would like to meet him properly. We would like to be proud of you.

Your mother.

He handed it back.

“We would like to be proud of you.” He said it like something gone off. He picked up his tweezers. “Forty years I’ve known that woman. She has never once wanted anything for free.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“She wants something.”

“Obviously she wants something, Si. I’m asking what.”

They were on the long grey sofa. She had her feet in his lap. He was holding them in one hand without seeming to notice, warming them, the way he always did when she came home from the shop with cold toes. With the other hand he held the letter up to the lamp.

He turned it. He looked at the watermark. He tilted it, so the light ran over the ink.

“She pressed hardest on proud.”

“Of course she did.”

“Shanghai, then Milan. That’s where your father’s banks are.” He laid the letter on the low table by the chessboard. “She’s spent the summer finding out about me.”

Aurelia’s feet went cold again in his hand.

“How much can she find out?”

“Quite a lot. If she’s good.” He looked at her. “Is she good?”

What could she even say to that? Her mother at twenty-six, walking into her grandfather’s office in Milan, a model with an economics degree nobody had known about, walking out three hours later with a contract. The buyer from Bergdorf Goodman. The coffee cup on Lake Como, cracked from rim to base. The maid had told Serafina. Serafina had told her, at the wedding, laughing so hard she’d choked.

“She’s the best I’ve ever met.” She wiggled her toes at him. “Except you.”

“Second.” He considered it. “I’ll take it.”

She laughed. She couldn’t help it. She’d been dreading that word since she was seven and now it was a joke on her own sofa.

“Then let her come,” he said. “Let’s see what she wants.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She spent ten days getting ready. She refused to call it that.

She told Enzo she was finishing the Geneva pieces. She told Qian she was redoing the window at the east-side shop. She told Chen Si, “I’m preparing,” in a voice that ended the subject.

She changed the menu four times. She wrote every version out in red ink and crossed every version out in red ink. She changed the wine twice. Italian? That would look like trying. French? That would look like trying not to. In the end she picked a white from Ningxia. It was very good. Her mother would never have heard of it. She’d have nothing to say.

“Who’s cooking?”

That was Chen Si, on day four, reading the fifth menu over her shoulder.

“A caterer. Obviously.”

“No.”

“No?”

“I’ll do the fish.”

She turned round on her stool and stared at him.

“You want to cook. For my mother.”

“I want her to eat something I made.” He took the menu out of her hand and drew a neat black line through the caterer’s number. “And then I want to watch her decide whether to say it’s good.”

Was that kind or evil? With him it was usually both.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flowers were the worst part.

The florist in the building did them badly. She sent them back. He did them badly again. On Thursday night, at midnight, she was sitting on the floor of the flat in her pyjamas with a bucket of white roses, doing them herself, and a thorn went straight into the side of her finger.

It barely bled.

She cried anyway. Hard. For about three minutes. Snot, the lot, sitting on the floor with a rose in her fist. For no reason she could have explained to anyone.

He found her there.

He didn’t say a word. He knelt on the floor beside the bucket. He took her hand and turned it to the light and looked at the cut. Tiny. Pathetic. He took the handkerchief out of his pocket and wound it round her finger anyway, twice, and held it there.

“She won’t look at the flowers.”

“She’ll look at everything.” Her voice was wrecked. “The flowers. The wine. My fork. My nails.”

“Aurelia…”

“Whether I’ve put on weight! Whether you have! Whether the flat’s too big or too empty or too yours!” She wiped her nose on her wrist, disgustingly.

“It isn’t too…”

“And she’ll find the one thing that’s wrong. And say it very nicely, right when it hurts most.” A huge sniff. “She always finds it.”

He was quiet for a bit, holding her finger.

“Then give her something to find.”

She looked up.

“What?”

“You’ve spent ten days making it perfect. So there’s nothing to find.” He picked a rose out of the bucket. “She’ll know you tried. That’s the thing she’ll find. So leave something wrong. On purpose. Pick it yourself.” He handed her the rose, stem first, thorns turned away from her. “Then when she finds it, it’s yours. Not hers.”

She stared at him with mascara down her face.

“You’re serious.”

“One thing. Your choice.”

She looked at the roses.

And then she started to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose the dishwasher.

Ever since Zhao had put his arm in it, it had whined. A thin high noise, like a mosquito, all the way through every cycle. Somebody was coming to replace it on Friday.

She rang them on Friday morning and cancelled.

On Saturday she put it on a quarter of an hour before her parents were due. She left the kitchen door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came at eight exactly.

Her father first. Song Weiren had turned fifty-eight the night before, at a dinner his elder daughter hadn’t been invited to. Silver hair. Navy suit. A pocket square her mother had definitely chosen. He looked older than he had on the balcony. He looked tired.

He shook Chen Si’s hand at the door and held on a beat too long. Aurelia saw his face and it took her a second to name the look.

Fear. Her father was frightened of her husband.

Good.

Then her mother.

Vittoria Song, born Conti, came into the flat in black silk, naturally, cut by the same house in Milan that had made her wedding dress. Small diamonds. Her own mother’s ring. Hair in a perfect low knot. She walked into the forty-fourth floor like it had been built for her to walk into.

She looked at the room. The glass. The harbour. The books. The jade chessboard, with the black queen back on its square for the evening. Aurelia had stolen it out of his jacket on Sunday. The white roses, done badly, by hand, and left.

Then she looked at her daughter.

Aurelia had stood in front of the mirror at six and taken off every piece of gold she owned. All of it. For the first time in her life. Dark green dress, plain, long sleeves. One ring. The wedding band, made from her grandmother’s earrings.

Her mother looked at the ring. For longer than anywhere else.

“Ciao, Mamma.”

“Ciao, tesoro.”

Two kisses. One each cheek. She didn’t actually touch her at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was perfect. That was the frightening part.

Her father talked shipping with Chen Si. Carefully. A man feeling for the edge of a cliff in the dark.

“And the port fees, Mr. Chen. Since the spring. Do you find… I mean, would you say…”

“Chen Si, please.”

“Chen Si. Yes. Of course. Sorry.”

Chen Si answered everything. Politely. Completely. In a voice so pleasant that her father’s hand shook a little on his glass.

Her mother talked to Aurelia about Milan.

“Bianca married a count. Did you hear? A real one.”

“I heard, Mamma.”

“Terrible teeth. Lovely house.”

Then the weather on the lake in August. For a long time. She didn’t mention the boutique. Or the wedding. Or the magazine.

She asked about the wine.

“Ningxia.”

Half a second.

“How interesting.” Her mother drank it.

The fish came. A whole grouper, steamed, ginger and spring onion. Chen Si carried it to the table himself in a tea towel and set it down and went back to his chair.

Her mother tasted it. Then tasted it again.

“This is very good. Who’s your cook?”

“My husband.”

Her mother put down her chopsticks. Just for a moment. Then she picked them up again.

“How unusual.”

“He says a boy should feed himself.” Aurelia smiled. “His mother taught him.”

Under the table, his knee found hers. Above the table, without looking, he put his hand on the back of her neck. Warm. Heavy. Not squeezing. Just resting there, right where another hand used to squeeze when she was four and wasn’t allowed to move.

Her mother saw it.

Aurelia watched her see it.

Nobody said anything about it at all. And the whole time, under everything, through the open kitchen door, the dishwasher whined.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten, over coffee, her mother put down her cup.

“That noise.”

Everybody stopped.

“In the kitchen.” Pleasant. Puzzled. “It’s been going all night. A little whistle. Is it the dishwasher?” She smiled at Chen Si. “You should have someone look at it. A flat like this. One little thing and it’s all you can hear.”

There it was.

Aurelia picked up her own cup.

“My brother-in-law fixed it. Zhao Zhendong. You might have heard of him.” A sip. “He took the front off with a kitchen knife, in his good suit, and put his arm in up to the elbow, and pulled out a sapphire. It’s whistled ever since.” She put the cup down. “I like it. I decided to keep it.”

Her mother looked at her.

For one second something went across that perfect face. Was it doubt? On her mother? Aurelia had no idea what to do with it.

Then it was gone.

“How charming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It came at the door. It always came at the door.

Coat on. Bag in hand. Car waiting. No time for an answer. That was how her mother did it. After Vienna, when Aurelia was eleven. Nine days of nothing. Then the curtains yanked open on the tenth morning, second place is just the first of the losers, and footsteps going downstairs. Gone.

Her father had already gone down. He’d shaken Chen Si’s hand again in the doorway and said, “Thank you for having us,” like a boy reading a card.

Her mother stood in the doorway in her black coat, pulling on her gloves.

“Thank you, tesoro. It was lovely. You’ve done very well.” Her eyes went past Aurelia. To the harbour. To Chen Si, standing by the sofa with his hands in his pockets. “Both of you.”

“Thank you, Mamma.”

“Oh. Your father would like lunch with your husband. Next week. Just the two of them.” The second glove. “About the bridge.”

Aurelia went cold all over.

“The bridge.”

“Harbour Bridge Two. His dream. Ten years.” The Vogue cover smile.

“Mamma…”

“A little difficulty at the ministry. One signature that won’t come. Your husband knows the right people. Everyone says so.”

She leaned in for the two kisses that didn’t touch.

“We’d be so proud, tesoro. Just this once. Family helps family.”

She turned to go. Then turned back, like she’d forgotten an umbrella.

“The minister’s name is Fu.” Lightly. “Fu Jianguo. Your husband will know him.”

The door shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d known since the fish.

Not the name. The shape of it. A woman who spent a summer in Shanghai and Milan didn’t come for the fish. She’d watched his hands the whole meal. She’d watched where he put them. She’d seen his hand on her daughter’s neck and filed it the way he filed things.

So when the name came, at the door, in that light voice, nothing happened to his face. Nothing at all. He’d had eleven years of practice.

Inside, something very old and very cold sat up and looked around.

He didn’t move from the sofa. He watched his wife instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia stood with her back flat against the door. Green dress. No gold.

“She knew.” It came out flat. “She found out. In Shanghai. In Milan. What that man did to your family.”

“Aurelia.”

“She ate your fish. She drank your wine.” She looked at him down the length of the room. “And at the door she asked you to go and beg Fu Jianguo for a favour. For her. For a bridge!”

He didn’t say anything.

“We would like to be proud of you.” She laughed. It wasn’t a laugh. “That was the price. It was always the price!”

In the kitchen the dishwasher finished. The whine stopped. The flat went dead quiet.

He took his hands out of his pockets.

He crossed the room. He put one hand flat on the door beside her head. The other went to her waist and pulled her off the wood and into him. Like her mother might still be on the other side, listening, and he wanted her to hear.

“She found the thing.”

“What thing?”

“You left the dishwasher for her. She didn’t want the dishwasher.” He looked at her face. “She found me. My father. Fu. The one thing in this flat you can’t fix.”

“Don’t…”

“She’s very good.”

Aurelia grabbed his face. Both hands. Hard.

“She is not better than you.” Fierce. Shaking. “She is not better than me. She doesn’t get to walk in here and put that man’s name in your mouth. Not in our home. Not EVER.”

She kissed him. Hard enough to hurt. Against the door her mother had just walked out of. Like she could take the name back out of his mouth with hers.

He let her. For about three seconds.

Then he kissed her back, slower, his hand still flat on the door, his other hand spread at the back of her head, until her shoulders came down and her fingers in his hair stopped being fists. Until the flat was theirs again.

“What are you going to do?” Against her hair.

She let go of his face.

She went to the hall table and picked up her phone and turned it over in her hand. Her finger was still wrapped in his handkerchief. She’d forgotten to take it off.

“My father is having lunch with my husband next week. About the bridge.” She looked up. “And I’m going to be at that lunch. And I’m choosing the restaurant.”

“Which restaurant?”

She smiled. It was a lot worse than her mother’s.

“Italian.”

chapters.title: What Her Father Wants
chapters.desc: Over risotto at Da Gianni, her father asks Chen Si to write to Fu Jianguo. Then he admits he’s already told Fu no.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s only a letter. A few lines. Your name at the bottom. It would mean so much.” — Song Weiren
chapters.content:
“Da Gianni.”

Qian looked up from the booking screen. Then he looked at Chen Si, standing behind her chair. Then back at her.

“The one on the sixty-first floor, Mrs. Chen?”

“Is there another?”

“No. No, there isn’t.” He typed. He stopped typing. “It’s just that they don’t really… take bookings. You have to be known.”

“Tell Carmine it’s Aurelia Song. The table by the window. Thursday, one o’clock.” She picked up her bag. “And tell him I’ll want the usual.”

Qian typed it. Then he reached into his drawer and took out the antacids. Just in case.

✦ ✦ ✦

Da Gianni sat on top of the Harbour Hotel like a crown somebody had forgotten to take off. A chef from Bologna. A sommelier from Piedmont. White cloths, silver, the whole harbour in the windows. Eleven waiters, every one of them Italian. And Carmine, the maître d’ from Naples, who’d been there since it opened and knew every important person in the city by name and by what they ate.

She’d eaten there every Saturday at sixteen. After piano. With her mother. At the table by the window.

Her mother had counted every grain of rice she put in her mouth.

Her father was already there when they came in. He stood up too fast and nearly knocked his glass over. He shook Chen Si’s hand. Then he kissed Aurelia on the forehead, carefully, the way he used to when she was very small, before Vienna and the rankings and all of it.

“Papà.”

“Tesoro.” He looked at her. Then at the man beside her. “I didn’t think you’d come. Your mother said it would be just the two of us.”

“Mamma says a lot of things.”

She sat down. Chen Si sat beside her and put his arm along the back of her chair. No touching. He didn’t need to. Her father looked at the arm and then very quickly at the menu.

Carmine arrived like weather.

“Signorina! No. Signora! Three years! Three years you don’t come to see Carmine!”

“Carmine, I…”

“And now you’re married, and nobody tells me, I have to read it in a magazine like a stranger…” He kissed her hand. He turned to Chen Si to do the same thing to him. Then he actually looked at Chen Si. His smile wobbled. It came back, but a size smaller. “Signore. Welcome. Welcome.”

“Thank you.”

“The usual, Signora Chen?”

“The usual, Carmine. Three. And a bottle of the Barolo. The 2010.”

Carmine went. Her father watched him go.

“You always had the risotto. Every Saturday.”

“I know, Papà.”

He looked at her for a moment like he wanted to say something else. Then he didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told them about the bridge over the antipasti.

He was good at it. He’d always been good at it. Her mother was the cold one, the one who found the crack. Her father was the warm one. The one who made you want to help.

“The ferry takes forty minutes. Forty! The bridge will take four. There’s a hospital on the far shore, did you know? Ambulances have to wait for the ferry. People… people die waiting for a boat.”

“I’ve seen the figures.”

That was Chen Si. Mild. Her father blinked at him.

“You have?”

“I read everything that comes through the ministry.”

“Ah.” Her father picked up his fork and put it down again. “Twenty thousand jobs. For six years. And my father… you know about my father, tesoro.”

“The suitcase.”

“The suitcase.” He smiled at Chen Si, a little embarrassed. “He came here in 1962 with nothing. Sold watches out of a suitcase on Harbour Road. Three doors down from her shop.”

“I know the spot.”

“Do you? Yes. Of course you do.” He swallowed. “He used to stand on the front and look at the far shore and say, one day somebody will build a bridge.”

His voice went. He waited for it to come back. “I promised him. In the hospital. Ten years ago.”

Nobody said anything. A waiter put down bread and fled.

“The money’s there. The engineers are there. The land is bought. Everything’s approved.” He turned his glass round on the cloth. “Except one signature.”

“From the ministry.”

“From the vice-minister for infrastructure.” Lower. “He’s had the file eleven months. He won’t sign. He won’t say why.”

“Have you asked to see him?”

“Six times! My people can’t get near him.” He looked up at Chen Si across the table. “Your people can. Everybody says so. If you want something from the ministry, there’s one man in this city.”

“What are you asking me for, Mr. Song?”

“Nothing improper! I’d never… I’m not asking for anything like that.”

He spread his hands.

“Just a letter. It’s only a letter. A few lines. Saying you know me. That you support the project. Your name at the bottom.” He tried a smile. It didn’t work. “It would mean so much. To me. To your mother.” He looked at Aurelia. “To the family.”

The table went quiet.

Over by the bar, Carmine was polishing one glass. He’d been polishing it for a while.

“The vice-minister for infrastructure is Fu Jianguo.”

“Yes.”

“You know who he is.”

“I know he’s… difficult.”

Chen Si didn’t move.

“You know what he did to my father.”

Her father went white.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d never watched it happen to him before. Her father realising he was standing in a room and didn’t know how big it was. How deep.

“I… Vittoria said… she said it was old history. Something between families. Years ago. A misunderstanding.” He looked at Aurelia. “She said you’d understand that business is business. Tesoro, I didn’t know. I didn’t know it was…”

“You didn’t ask.”

“I didn’t think…”

“You never do, Papà.” She said it gently. That was the worst part. It came out gently. “Mamma tells you what to think and you think it. She told you to close my shop. She told you to stand up at your own birthday and drink while she called me a loser.”

“That isn’t…”

“She told you to come here today and ask my husband to write to the man who had his father dragged down the stairs in his pyjamas. And left him in a cell to die.” She picked up her Barolo. “And you came. Because it was easier than asking her why.”

Her father stared at her.

“Aurelia. That’s not fair.”

“No. It isn’t.” She drank. “Nothing in our family ever was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The risotto came.

Saffron. Gold. A piece of bone marrow on top, the way her grandmother made it. Exactly the way it had come every Saturday at sixteen at this table by this window.

Nobody picked up a fork.

Chen Si hadn’t said a word since my father. He sat back with his arm still along her chair and his glass in his other hand. He hadn’t drunk from it. He was looking at her father with a face she knew now. The list face. Nineteen names and an empty space at the top. A hall at six in the morning.

She put her hand on his knee under the cloth.

He didn’t look at her. But after a moment his hand came down over hers and pressed it flat. Once. Then stayed.

“Mr. Song.”

Her father flinched like he’d been slapped.

“I want to understand something. Not the bridge. The bridge is a good bridge. I’ve seen the drawings. The hospital is real. The ambulances are real. Your father with his suitcase is real.” He put his glass down. “What I want to understand is why Fu won’t sign.”

“I told you, I don’t…”

“You do.”

“I…”

“A man doesn’t sit on a file for eleven months for nothing. Fu doesn’t do anything for nothing. I’ve been watching him a long time. He never says no.” A pause. “He says not yet. Then he waits until you’re desperate enough to give him what he really wants.”

Her father looked down at his risotto. A long time.

At the bar, Carmine finally put the glass down.

“What does he want from you, Mr. Song?”

“A share.” It came out of her father like a tooth. “For his son. Fu Kang. Fifteen per cent of the contract. Through a company in Macau with the son’s name nowhere on it.” He shut his eyes. “I said no. In March. I said no, because I’m not… I won’t…”

He couldn’t finish.

Aurelia sat very still.

“You said no?”

He opened his eyes.

“I’ve done a lot of things, tesoro. I’m not proud of all of them.” His voice cracked right down the middle. “But my father never paid a bribe in his life. I promised him a bridge. Not a bridge with Fu Jianguo’s son hidden inside it.”

He wiped his eyes with his napkin, roughly, like a boy.

“So I said no. He stopped taking my calls. Then your mother said there was another way. That your husband…” He looked across the table. “Is it true? Is Fu afraid of you?”

Chen Si looked at him.

“Not yet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her soft, tired father. Who did what her mother said. Who changed the subject at dinner. Who’d stood up at his own birthday and raised a glass while she was being sold off in front of two hundred people. She’d thought, most of her life, that he had no spine at all.

He’d said no to Fu Jianguo. In March. For a dead man with a suitcase.

Where had that been all her life?

She picked up her fork.

She ate the risotto. Every grain. Slowly. Not one left. Her father watched her do it from across the table where she’d sat every Saturday at sixteen being counted, and his eyes filled up, and he looked away at the harbour. At the far shore, where there wasn’t a bridge.

She held out her fork to Chen Si with the last mouthful on it.

He looked at the fork. He looked at her.

He leaned in and took it. Right there in front of her father and Carmine and a sommelier from Piedmont. A man who didn’t eat or drink anything anyone gave him. He took it off her fork without a word.

Her father saw. His mouth opened a little.

He shut it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si paid before her father could reach for his wallet. A tiny movement of two fingers to Carmine across the room. Nobody else even saw it. Carmine came and murmured that it was taken care of, and her father looked at his son-in-law like a man who couldn’t tell if he’d been given a present or a warning.

At the lift, her father stopped.

“I’m sorry. For asking.” To Chen Si. Then, to her: “I should have known. I should have asked. About a lot of things.”

“The letter.”

“Forget the letter. I won’t ask again. Not for that. Not to that man.”

“I’m not going to write a letter.”

“I know. I understand.”

“I’m going to think about it. The bridge. The son. The company in Macau.” He pressed the button. “I’m going to think about it very carefully. Then I’ll tell my wife what I think. And then she’ll decide.” He looked at Aurelia. “Not me. Her.”

Her father looked at him. Then at her.

The lift came. The doors opened. He stepped in and turned round, and looked at his elder daughter in the lobby of the sixty-first floor in green, no gold, next to the most dangerous man in the city. Who’d just told him she’d decide.

“Your mother always said you were the clever one. The clever one, the beautiful one. The one who’d be first.” He tried to smile. “She never said you’d be the brave one.”

The doors shut.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she didn’t say anything for ten minutes. He didn’t push.

He sat beside her in the back with her hand under his on the seat between them and watched the harbour go by. At some point he lifted her hand, turned it over and kissed the inside of her wrist. Right on the pulse. Still looking out of the window. Like he was thinking with it. Then he put it back under his.

“He said no,” she said. “My father. To Fu.”

“Yes.”

“And my mother found another way. She always finds another way.” She stared out of her own window. “She found you. She found your father.”

“Yes.”

“She praised your fish. And at the door she put that man’s name in your mouth so my father wouldn’t have to.” Flat. “She doesn’t care what it costs you. She just wants to stand on that bridge at the opening in black silk and be proud.”

He turned his head.

“What do you want?”

“Me?”

“You. Not your mother. Not your father. Not me.” He looked at her. “I meant it at the lift. If you want me to write the letter, I’ll write it.”

She stared at him.

“To Fu? The man who…”

“Yes.” Very even. “If you want your father’s bridge and that’s the price, I’ll pay it. For you.” A beat. “But I don’t think that’s what you want.”

Was it? She thought about it. Properly. Her father in the lift. I said no. A suitcase on Harbour Road. A man who’d never paid a bribe in his life.

And a son called Fu Kang, and a company in Macau.

She turned her hand over under his and laced her fingers through.

“I want my father’s bridge. Built. Properly. No bribe. No letter. No fifteen per cent for Fu Kang hiding in Macau.” She lifted her chin. “And I want Fu Jianguo to sign it anyway. Because he has to. Because he’s frightened not to.” She looked at him. “Not of you. Of me.”

He went very still.

Then, bit by bit, he started to smile.

“Clause five. You won’t interfere with my prior claim.”

“I won’t. I’m not going to touch Fu Jianguo.” She smiled back. “I’m going to touch his son.”

He had her jaw in his hand before she’d finished the word.

No warning. He pulled her across the seat by their laced fingers and kissed her. Hard. Deep. Not mild at all. His other hand spread at the back of her head, holding her there, like she might change her mind and he wasn’t going to allow it. She made a noise into his mouth she’d be embarrassed about later. Her bag slid off the seat. Somewhere in front of them, without a word, the driver put the partition up.

He pulled back an inch. He was breathing hard. For him, that was a riot.

“Do you know what it does to me? When you say things like that?”

“Yes.” She grabbed his tie and pulled him back. “Why do you think I say them?”

chapters.title: Aurelia Says No to Her Mother
chapters.desc: She tells her mother no in front of the maids. Then she and Mr. Lu work out how to get at Fu through his son.
chapters.epigraph: “No, Mamma. Not for the bridge. Not for you. Not ever.” — in Italian, so the maids understood too
chapters.content:
The man in the tinted glasses had been talking for six minutes. Chen Si had let him.

“…and the cousin is family, you understand, he’s my wife’s sister’s boy, he didn’t know the containers were…”

“He knew.”

“He’s twenty-three!”

“He’s twenty-three and he knew.” Chen Si turned a page in the file. He didn’t look up. “He moved forty thousand through the east-side containers in August. In his own name. That’s not stealing. That’s being stupid in front of me.”

The man in the tinted glasses opened his mouth.

On the table, Chen Si’s phone lit up.

Aurelia: Going to see my mother. Peak house. Gun in my bag. Back by twelve.

He picked it up. Read it. Read it again. Everyone along the window watched him do it and nobody breathed.

He typed one word.

Chen Si: Win.

Then he put the phone face down and looked up at last.

“Your cousin leaves on Wednesday. The ship’s called the Morning Star. It goes a long way south.” Mild. “If I see him in this city again, you’ll go and keep him company.”

The man in the tinted glasses sat down.

Qian, by the door, made a small note. Then a second note, which just said antacids.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the back of the car, Aurelia looked at Win. until the screen went dark.

She put the phone in her bag. The gun was in there. So was the black jade queen. She’d taken it off the bedside table that morning without really knowing why. A gun and a queen. Very subtle. Her grandmother would have laughed till she choked.

She got out of the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

The morning room was small and yellow, at the east end of the house, and every day from nine until ten her mother sat in it alone.

Italian papers. A pot of coffee. The day’s list. Nobody went in. Not her husband. Not her daughters. Once, a deputy minister had turned up at a quarter past nine and been made to wait in the hall for forty minutes on a hard chair.

And there were always three maids. Always polishing silver at the long sideboard. Two from the Philippines. And Signora Pina from Bergamo, who’d come with the family from Milan, who’d held Aurelia the day she was born.

Aurelia had worked out at about twelve why there were always three maids at nine o’clock. Witnesses.

Fine. Let them witness.

Vittoria Song looked up from the Corriere.

“Tesoro. What a surprise. You should have rung.”

“I didn’t want to.”

She didn’t sit down. She stood in the middle of the yellow room in a white suit and every piece of gold she owned. The earrings from the balcony. The cuffs from the Geneva pieces. The little collar she’d made in September out of the platinum left over from Numero Uno. Her wedding ring. All of it. Like armour. Like a dare.

“You sent Papà to ask my husband to write to Fu Jianguo.”

Her mother turned a page.

“Your father has a bridge to build.”

“You found out what Fu did to his family. In Shanghai, or Milan, or wherever. You knew.” Level. Perfectly level. “And you sent Papà anyway. And you didn’t tell him why. You let him walk into that restaurant and put that man’s name on the table without knowing what it meant.”

“Your father doesn’t need to know what things mean.” Her mother folded the paper. “He needs to know what to say. I gave him the right thing to say. He said it badly. He always does.”

“He said no to Fu.”

A pause. Very small.

“Fu wanted fifteen per cent for his son. Papà said no. Because Nonno never paid a bribe in his life.” She took a step forward. “Did you know that? Did he tell you?”

Her mother looked at her over the coffee.

“Of course he told me. I told him he was a fool.”

At the sideboard, Signora Pina stopped polishing.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Fifteen per cent is nothing, tesoro. Every bridge in the world has fifteen per cent of something hidden in it.” Her mother poured more coffee. “Your father is sentimental about his father. His father sold watches from a suitcase because he wasn’t clever enough to sell anything else.”

“Mamma…”

“I married your father because he wasn’t his father. I was wrong, apparently.” A sip.

At the sideboard, a spoon went down on the cloth.

“So I found another way. Your husband. One letter from Chen Si and the file signs itself. No fifteen per cent. Your father keeps his precious principles. Everyone wins.” The cup went down. “I thought you’d be grateful. I was helping.”

“You were using him.”

“I was using what I had. That’s all anyone does.” Pleasant. So pleasant. “That’s all you do. You married a man the whole city is afraid of. Don’t pretend that wasn’t because you wanted them to be afraid of you too.”

Nobody in the room moved. One of the girls from the Philippines had stopped with a spoon in each hand.

Aurelia had played this conversation in her head since she was eleven. Since nine days of silence and a curtain pulled open. In every version she was shaking. Or crying. Or screaming. And her mother sat there, cold and perfect, and won.

She looked down at her own hands.

Covered in gold. Dead steady. Steady as at two in the morning under a loupe, setting a stone. Steady as at fifteen metres behind a quarry with Zhao’s gun.

Huh.

She looked up. She said it in Italian. Milanese Italian, the kind her mother had spoken to her in since she was born, so that Signora Pina would understand every word and the other two would get enough.

“No, Mamma.”

Her mother went still.

“No. Non per il ponte. Non per te. Mai.” Not for the bridge. Not for you. Not ever. “My husband won’t write to Fu Jianguo. Not for Papà. Not for you. Not for anyone. You won’t ask him again. You won’t send Papà to ask him again.”

“Tesoro…”

“You won’t put that man’s name in my home again. At my table. Where my husband can hear it. As long as you live.”

The silver had stopped completely.

“And you will never again stand up at a dinner and tell two hundred people what I’m worth.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother put down her cup. Not a sound. Not a single click of china.

“And if I do?”

“Then I stop coming. To anything. Ever.” Aurelia picked up her bag. “You’ll find out about my life from magazines. My collections from auction catalogues.”

“Don’t be…”

“People at galas will ask about your daughter, the designer, the one married to Chen Si, and you’ll have to say you haven’t spoken to her in years.” She smiled. “And they’ll look at you the way everyone looked at me at Papà’s party.”

“You wouldn’t.”

“And Papà gets his bridge anyway. Without you. Without a letter. Without fifteen per cent.”

For the first time in her life, her mother’s face gave something away.

“How?”

“That is my business.”

She walked to the door.

At the door she stopped and looked back. Not at her mother. At the sideboard. At Signora Pina, who’d held her as a baby, standing there with a silver coffee pot in one hand and a cloth in the other and tears running straight down her old face.

“Grazie, Pina. For the silver.”

Then she went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell the driver to go. She just sat in the back of the car outside her mother’s house with her hands in her lap. They’d started to shake now. Now! Typical.

She got out her phone.

Chen Si: Win.

She typed with her thumbs going everywhere.

Aurelia: I didn’t win. I just said no.

It came back so fast he must have been holding the phone.

Chen Si: Same thing.

She put her head back on the seat and laughed without making any noise, until her ribs hurt and the driver started looking at her in the mirror.

“Harbour Road,” she said, wiping her eyes. “And when we get there, I need a list of every jeweller in Macau.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Fu Kang was thirty, handsome, idle and mad about watches.

She knew everything by Thursday. Qian had a file on him. Chen Si had a better one. Mr. Lu had the best one of all, because Fu Kang had pawned three watches in two years, when his allowance ran out. Three shops. Three names. Every one of those shops belonged to Mr. Lu.

“He likes Swiss.” Mr. Lu sat in the workshop behind the boutique with his cardigan buttoned to the chin and a cup of tea he hadn’t touched. “Independent makers. Small. The kind you wait four years for. He buys them through a dealer in Macau, Mrs. Chen. Always the same dealer. Always cash.”

“What kind of dealer?”

“An odd one.” He turned the cup a quarter turn on its saucer. “He was a bookkeeper until three years ago. Now he sells watches worth half a million each. From a shop with one customer.”

She went very still.

“And the shop belongs to a company.”

“Which belongs to a company. Which belongs to a company. Which is in Macau.” A small, neat smile. “I haven’t followed it all the way. I’m only a pawnbroker.”

“You’re not only anything, Mr. Lu.”

He bowed his head. His ears went pink. He was delighted.

“So if someone followed it. All the way.” She was thinking out loud now. She couldn’t stop. “And at the end there was fifteen per cent of everything. Not just Papà’s bridge. Every contract Fu has ever sat on for eleven months. All of it going through a watch shop with no customers…”

“Then someone would have a very interesting file.”

“And if Fu Kang were the kind of idiot who couldn’t resist a very rare watch…”

“Mrs. Chen.” Mr. Lu looked at her over his tea. “You don’t make watches.”

“No.” She smiled at him. “But I know a man in Geneva who does. He’s seventy-four. He makes four a year. The waiting list is nine years long.” She picked up her red pen. “He knew my grandmother.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told Chen Si that night in bed, in the dark, with her head on his chest.

All of it. Mr. Lu. The watch shop. The companies. The old man in Geneva.

He didn’t interrupt once. When she stopped, he was quiet for so long she thought he’d gone to sleep. Had he? He hadn’t. His hand was moving on her back.

“Not Fu Jianguo,” he said at last. “His son.”

“Clause five. The father’s yours.”

“Go on.”

“I sell his son a watch. The rarest one in the world. Through his own dealer.”

“And he pays…”

“The way he pays for everything. Through the companies.” She drew a line on his chest with one finger. Then another. “And I’m the seller. I’m at the other end of the money. So I see every company it goes through on the way to me. Every single one.”

“All the way back.”

“All the way back. To the account with his name on it.”

“And then?”

“Then I have lunch with Fu Kang. At Da Gianni. I show him the file.”

“Of course it’s Da Gianni.”

“I tell him that if his father’s signature is on Papà’s bridge by Christmas, the file stays in my safe for ever.” Her finger stopped. “And if it isn’t, it goes to the anti-corruption people. And three newspapers. And all his father’s enemies, and there are lots.”

“And he runs home.”

“And he runs home and tells his father what he’s been doing in his father’s name. And his father signs.” She lifted her head. “Because he’s frightened. Not of you. Of his own idiot son.”

He said nothing at all.

“Well?” She poked him. “Say something. You’re making me nervous.”

“That,” he said slowly, “is the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said to me in bed.”

She burst out laughing.

“I’m serious. I’ve watched Fu for nine years. I never once thought about the son.” His voice was strange. “The son’s an idiot. I thought he didn’t count.”

“Idiots always count. Mamma taught me that.” She put her head back down. “They’re the doors nobody locks.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He turned over in the dark and found her face with his hand.

“Aurelia.”

“Mm?”

“Clause nine.”

Her heart did something stupid.

“I’ve been thinking about you all day. Standing in her morning room. In all your gold.” His thumb went along her cheekbone. “Saying no. In front of witnesses.”

“All day?”

“I sent a man to the south on a ship this morning and I don’t remember what his face looked like.” His mouth found her jaw. “Tell me what you want.”

She lay there and thought about it. Then she reached over to the bedside table, where she’d dumped every piece of gold she’d worn that day in one heap.

She didn’t pick up any of it. She held out her wrists to him instead.

“Take it all off me. Then put the cuffs back on.” Her voice was not as steady as she’d hoped. “And then don’t let me take them off.”

He switched on the lamp.

He took her right hand first. He slid the wedding ring off and kissed the dent it left and put it back on, which didn’t count, he said, because that one stayed. Then the rest. One piece at a time. And as each one came off he said where it was from.

“Balcony.” The earrings. He lifted them out of her ears himself, very gently, one, two, and laid them in the dish.

“Geneva.” The cuffs. He clicked the little bolts open and set them on the sheet.

“Numero Uno’s leftovers. September. You cut the platinum on a Sunday because Enzo was at church.” The little collar, off her throat.

She stared at him.

“How do you know that?”

“You told me. You were cross about it.” He picked up the cuffs again. “You’re always telling me things. I keep all of them.”

He locked the cuffs back round her wrists. Two heavy bands of yellow gold, hinged. She heard the tiny bolts go home. One. Two. He lifted her hands up over her head and laid them on the pillow side by side, and held them there with one of his. Not hard. Just enough.

“Is this what you wanted?”

“Yes.” It came out tiny. “All day I was the one saying no. I want to be the one who can’t.”

He put his mouth by her ear.

“You can. You know the word.”

“I know. I won’t.”

And she didn’t. Not once. All night.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made her wait for everything.

He wouldn’t go near her mouth. For ages. She said his name. Then she said it again, not nicely. He laughed into her neck and went somewhere else entirely. She tried to bring her hands down and he caught the cuffs in one hand, and the bolts clicked against each other, loud in the quiet room.

“You told me not to let you.”

“I’ve changed my mind…”

“No, you haven’t.”

He was right. That was the worst bit.

He started talking to her in Italian. Low. Slow. Enzo’s Italian, the one he’d learned on the phone at midnight all spring and had clearly been saving. He told her exactly what he was going to do next, and got one verb wrong. On purpose. She was sure of it. She laughed so hard the cuffs rattled.

And while she was laughing, he did it.

The laugh broke in half. So did she, nearly. She arched off the bed with her wrists still pinned under his hand. His name came out of her in pieces. He kept hold. No hurry. No stopping.

“Look at you,” he said into her skin. Rough. Not mild. Not mild at all. “Saying no to her all morning. And look at you now.”

“Si…”

“Say it again.”

“Si…”

“Again.”

She said it again. And again. In the end she couldn’t tell any more whether she was saying his name or sì, yes, in Italian. Maybe both. Did it matter? He knew. He’d always known.

Near dawn he let go of her wrists at last and she didn’t move them. She lay there with her hands over her head in gold and looked at him in the grey light.

“Take them off now,” she whispered. “Please.”

He unlocked the bolts. One. Two. He rubbed her wrists with his thumbs, slowly, where the gold had been.

Then he leaned down to the floor, found her bag, took out the black jade queen and put it in her palm and closed her fingers round it.

“Yours,” he said. “You won it this morning.”

chapters.title: Her Mother’s Last Card
chapters.desc: Her mother sends a photograph of Serafina at a street race and names her price. Aurelia keeps it from Chen Si for one night and goes to the garage under the railway bridge.
chapters.epigraph: “You have something I want, tesoro. And I have your sister.”
chapters.content:
It came in an envelope, because everything from her mother did.

A courier brought it to the boutique on Wednesday, the thirtieth of October, and didn’t wait for a signature. No letter inside. Just a photograph. Eight by ten. Glossy. Taken at night with a long lens.

A wet road in the industrial district. The old paint works, with one floodlight on its wall. Two cars side by side at a line painted on the tarmac. A crowd in the dark on both sides. And between the cars, arm up, a white scarf in her fist, about to drop it, a tall thin girl in a leather jacket with hair she’d cut herself with kitchen scissors.

Serafina. Nineteen, maybe. The autumn she left.

On the back, in her mother’s handwriting:

The police have one of these. So does Li Zhenhua. Call me.

✦ ✦ ✦

Li Zhenhua was the man Serafina had nearly had for a father-in-law.

He owned the third-biggest construction company in the province. He’d wanted it joined to the Song Group. The easy way was his son and the younger Song girl. The engagement dinner was at the Harbour Hotel, three years ago. Two hundred guests. Serafina had stood up between the soup and the fish and said, in front of all of them, that she’d rather marry a carburettor.

Then she’d walked out.

Li Zhenhua had never forgiven it. Everyone knew. He’d told three people at three different parties that one day the Song girl would pay. He had a nephew in the city police. He had another nephew in the road traffic division. The traffic division badly wanted to catch somebody racing in the industrial district. So far it never had.

Until now, apparently.

Aurelia sat at her counter with the photograph in both hands while two trams went past.

Then she rang her mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tesoro. I knew you’d ring.”

“What do you want?”

“You know what I want.” The voice she used for buyers. Warm. Easy. “You have something I want, tesoro. And I have your sister.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

“A letter. One letter, from your husband to Fu. Before Christmas. That’s all.” A little pause. “And you come to the Christmas party at the Peak. With your husband. In gold. And you smile.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then on the second of January that photograph goes to Li Zhenhua’s nephew in the traffic division. With a name. An address. The dates of every race your sister has driven since she left.”

“You don’t have…”

“I have them all. I’ve had someone watching her for three years.” She might have been reading out a menu. “It’s three years in prison now. They changed the law in the spring. Li Zhenhua will make sure it’s the full three. And when she comes out, she’ll never be allowed to drive anything again.” Another little pause. “She’d hate that more than prison. Wouldn’t she?”

“She’s your daughter.”

“She was. She left. She chose a carburettor.” And then softer, the way she always went softer right before the worst thing. “You didn’t leave, tesoro. You stayed and fought me. I respect that. That’s why I’m giving you a choice. One letter. One party. One smile.”

“Mamma…”

“Or your sister in a cell for three years. You decide.”

The line went dead.

✦ ✦ ✦

She made it to the little bathroom behind the workshop before she was sick.

Twice. On her knees on the cold tiles in a cream silk blouse. Her whole body shook with it. When it stopped she stayed down there with her forehead on the edge of the sink and couldn’t get up.

A knock.

“Cara?”

“Go away, Enzo.”

The door opened anyway. He came in, looked at her, and didn’t say a word. He wet a towel at the tap and wrung it out and held it to the back of her neck. Then he held her hair while she was sick a third time, which was mostly nothing.

“Who?” he said, when she’d finished.

“Who do you think?”

He swore. In Venetian, which she’d never heard him use. It went on for some time.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell Chen Si.

It was the first thing she’d ever kept from him. Clause three. Neither party will lie to the other. About anything. She didn’t lie. She just didn’t say. She put the photograph in the workshop safe under the Geneva pieces. She went home. She cooked. After dinner she sat on the long grey sofa with her feet under her and talked about the Milan shipment. Monsieur Aubert. Fu Kang.

Not her sister. Not her mother. Not a wet road and a white scarf.

He watched her all evening.

Of course he did. Four mouthfuls, then pushing food round the plate. A laugh half a second late. Her phone checked eleven times when it hadn’t buzzed.

In bed, in the dark, he said it.

“Aurelia. Is there something you can’t tell me yet?”

The exact words. I cannot tell you this yet. Her own words. Clause three. In her own red ink.

She lay there and didn’t answer for a long time.

“Yes.”

“All right.”

He found her hand under the sheet and laced his fingers through.

“I’m good at waiting. You’ve complained about it. In red ink.” A pause. “But if it can hurt you, you tell me before it does. That’s not clause three.” His hand tightened. “That’s just me.”

He didn’t ask anything else. He put his arm round her and held on. She lay awake until four with her eyes open, watching her sister’s arm go up in the dark, over and over, with a white scarf in her fist.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday night she drove to the industrial district on her own. She texted first. She’d promised.

Aurelia: Going to see Serafina. Industrial district. Gun in bag. Back late.

Chen Si: Be careful.

Not Win. Be careful.

She read it twice before she put the phone away.

✦ ✦ ✦

He watched the dot.

He sat on the sofa in the dark. A coffee he’d made and wasn’t drinking. His phone on his knee. One small blue dot going east across the city. Past the Iron Docks. Into the grid of streets where the workshops were. Under the railway line. And stop.

Clause six. The Husband keeps the Wife’s location on his phone. The Wife knows.

She knew. She’d gone anyway. She’d texted anyway.

He could be there in twenty minutes. Zhendong could have someone there in ten. He thought about it the way he thought about everything, calmly and completely, from every side. He had a man in that district who could stand outside a garage all night and never be seen.

He didn’t call him.

He sat there. The coffee went cold. The dot didn’t move.

At one o’clock a train must have gone over, because the dot jumped, very slightly, and settled again. He found he’d stood up. He sat back down.

What was she doing in there for five hours? He didn’t know. He’d promised not to find out. Clause four. He would not at any time try to keep the Wife somewhere safe.

It was, without question, the hardest thing anyone had ever asked him to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

The garage was at the end of a dead street of shuttered workshops, right under the railway bridge. No sign. A steel shutter half up. Light underneath. Music, very loud. Petrol and hot metal and something frying.

She ducked under in a black coat and flat shoes.

Six cars. Four in bits. One on a lift with no wheels. A red one under a dust sheet in the corner with just its nose showing. And in the middle of the concrete under one hanging lamp, low and long and matte black, bonnet up, with a pair of legs sticking out from underneath on a creeper.

“Sera.”

The legs stopped moving.

The creeper rolled out. Serafina lay flat on it in overalls tied round her waist and a vest black with oil, spanner in one hand, a smear across her forehead. She looked up at her sister upside down.

“The gilded bird. In my garage.” She blinked. “Who died?”

“Nobody. Yet.”

Aurelia took the photograph out of her coat and held it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina looked at it from the creeper.

Then she sat up. She took it. She turned it over and read the back. She didn’t say anything. She got up and went to the bench against the wall and turned the music off.

In the sudden quiet a train came over the bridge. The whole building shook.

“When?”

“Yesterday.”

“Yesterday.” Serafina turned round. “And you’ve been walking round with it since yesterday. Not telling me.”

“I was deciding.”

“Deciding WHAT?”

Aurelia didn’t answer. How did you tell your sister she was the price?

Serafina’s face went cold and flat and furious. Exactly like their mother’s. Nobody was ever going to say so out loud.

“She wants something. From you. And I’m the price.” A laugh like a slap. “Of course I am. Of course! And you were deciding.” She threw the photograph down on the bench. “So what’s the rate, Aurelia? What am I worth these days? What’s she asking for your little sister?”

“A letter. From Chen Si. To the man who killed his father.” Aurelia’s voice cracked. “Asking him for a favour.”

Serafina went still.

“And a party. At Christmas. At the Peak. In gold.” She swallowed. “With a smile.”

The train was gone. Somewhere far off another one was coming.

“You haven’t told him.”

“No.”

“Why the hell not?”

“Because he’d write it!” It came out of her far too loud. It bounced off the concrete. “He’d write the letter. If it was what I wanted, he’d beg Fu Jianguo for something and sign it. For me.”

“Hey. Hey…”

“He’d do it tomorrow morning!” She was crying now. She hadn’t noticed it start. “And he’d never forgive himself. Never. And I’d never forgive me. And she knows that. That’s why she picked it. She knows he’d do it for me and she knows it’d kill him and she wants me to be the one who asks!”

Serafina stared at her.

“So you came here to ask me. If I’d rather go to prison.”

“No!” Aurelia wiped her face with the back of her wrist. Mascara everywhere. Wonderful. “I came to tell you what she’s done. Because you have the right to know. Because I was wrong not to come yesterday.” Chin up. Shaking. “And to tell you I’m not asking him. And I’m not letting her send you anywhere.”

“How?”

“I don’t know yet!”

✦ ✦ ✦

Another train. The garage shook. Serafina stood there and wiped her hands on a rag. One finger at a time. Slowly.

Then she went to the camping stove and picked up a dented moka pot.

“Coffee. You look like death.” Rough. “And I want to show you something.”

She made it. She drank hers standing up out of a mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST MECHANIC. She handed Aurelia the other one without comment. Then she went to a battered grey filing cabinet in the corner, yanked out a drawer that was clearly broken, pulled a folder out of it and slapped it down on the bench.

“Open it.”

Aurelia opened it.

Receipts.

Bank transfers. Invoices. Statements from a sponsorship account at a bank in Luxembourg. Every month. For three years. Tyres. Parts. Engines. The rent on this garage. Entry fees for the real races, the legal ones, at the circuit in the north. A gearbox from Germany. A transporter. Fuel. Hundreds of thousands. All of it from one account.

AS Holdings. Luxembourg.

Aurelia didn’t look up from the folder.

“I found out in August.” Serafina folded her arms. “I went to the bank. In person. They wouldn’t tell me who it was.”

“Of course they wouldn’t.”

“So I paid a man round the corner who used to work for a bank in Luxembourg.” Her voice was shaking. “AS, Aurelia. Aurelia Song. You’ve paid for everything. For three years. Since the night I walked out of that dinner and you stood at the top of the stairs and said nothing.”

Aurelia shut the folder.

“I didn’t want you to know.”

“Why?”

“Because you’d have stopped taking it.”

“Damn right I would!” Serafina’s eyes were wet and furious. “I don’t need your money! I don’t need anybody’s money! That’s why I left!”

“I know. That’s why I never told you.” Aurelia made herself look up. “You left. I didn’t. I stood at the top of the stairs and watched you go and said nothing, because Mamma was standing at the bottom. And I was scared.”

“Hey…”

“And afterwards I thought, I can’t go with her. I can’t be brave like that. But I can do this. I can make sure she never has to come back. Never has to need anything except a gearbox.” Her voice went completely. “It was the only brave thing I knew how to do.”

Serafina put her mug down on the bench so hard the coffee slopped over.

She crossed the garage in three strides. She grabbed her sister, oil and all. She hung on.

“You idiot.” Into Aurelia’s hair. “You absolute gilded idiot.”

“I know.”

“I named the car after you.” Muffled. “The black one. I didn’t know it was you paying. I just… I called it Gilded. Because it’s fast and beautiful and impossible to live with.” A wet laugh. “I was saving it. To tell you. As an insult.”

Aurelia laughed. The bark. The one from the balcony. Then it turned into something else, and the two of them stood in the middle of a garage under a railway bridge at midnight and held on while a train went over and shook the whole world.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning, with the coffee cold and the folder between them, Serafina tapped a fingernail on her front teeth.

“The legal races. At the circuit up north.”

Aurelia looked up.

“I’ve been entering under a fake name since March. If I used my own, Mamma would find out, and someone would get hurt.” She shrugged. “But I’m good. I’m really good. I came second in the provincial championship in September.” A face. “Second. I know. Don’t you dare say it.”

Aurelia didn’t say it.

“There’s a last race of the season. The twenty-first of December. If I win it, I get a licence. A real one. National.”

“And that helps how?”

She was talking faster now. “A licensed national driver with a team, a sponsor and her name in the papers is a lot harder to lock up for three years over a road in the industrial district. Li Zhenhua would just look like what he is. An old man with a grudge.”

“But.”

“But I’d have to race in my own name. And I’d need a real sponsor. Not a bank account in Luxembourg.” She looked at her sister. “A name. On the car.”

Aurelia did the sum. For once in her life, she liked the answer.

“AURELIA.”

“On the bonnet. In gold.” Serafina grinned. “Where Mamma can see it.”

“The twenty-first. That’s four days before the Christmas party.”

“I know. I checked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home at four with oil on her coat.

He was on the sofa in the dark. Harbour behind him. A cup of coffee on the table that he hadn’t touched. Waiting.

She stood in the doorway.

“You had my location.”

“Yes.”

“You watched me all night.”

“Five hours and ten minutes.” He didn’t look away from her. “I stood up four times.”

“Did you come?”

“No.” Something moved in his jaw. “I sat here.”

She went to him. She sat down beside him and took his hand. It was freezing.

“I can tell you now.”

And she did. All of it. The photograph. The bathroom floor and Enzo. Her mother on the phone. Li Zhenhua. The letter, the party, the smile. A folder of receipts. A black car called Gilded.

He let her get all the way to the end.

“You didn’t tell me because you knew I’d write the letter.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the harbour for a long time.

“You’re right.” Very low. “I’d have written it that night. Sent it in the morning. And never told you what it cost.”

“I know.”

He turned his head.

“Thank you. For not letting me.”

She put her head on his shoulder. Oily coat and all.

He lifted it again with two fingers under her chin, and turned her face to the light from the harbour. There was a black streak of engine oil along her cheekbone. He wiped it off with his thumb. Then he looked at his thumb.

“Last time it was pencil.”

“Last time you didn’t kiss me after.”

“Last time I was being strategic.”

He kissed her. Oil, coffee, tears, the lot. Then he undid her coat, button by button, and pulled it off her, because it was filthy, and wrapped the blanket from the end of the sofa round her instead. She tucked her frozen feet under his thigh. He let her.

“The twenty-first,” she mumbled into his neck. “Up north. Will you come?”

“Will you? You hate cars. You get sick in the back of taxis.”

“I’ll be in the stand. Front row.” Her eyes were closing. “In gold. Where she can see me.”

“Then I’ll bring a bucket.”

She kicked him under the blanket. He caught her foot and kept it.

chapters.title: The Racing Team She Pretends Not to Fund
chapters.desc: Aurelia sells Fu Kang a watch from Geneva and follows his money all the way to his father’s name. She also learns to change a wheel and rebuilds her sister’s sponsorship deck in one night.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t pretend to fund it any more.” “No. Now I pretend I’m not terrified.”
chapters.content:
“Mademoiselle Song. Your grandmother was the only customer my father was ever afraid of.”

“I’ve heard that.”

“In 1968 she argued with him for two hours about the finish on a balance cock.” A dry old laugh down the line from Geneva. “She won. He talked about it until he died. So.” A pause. “What do you need?”

She told him. Not all of it. Enough.

A young man in Macau who bought rare watches through a dealer with no other customers. A watch offered to that dealer. Quietly. As if by accident. A sale, paid the way the young man always paid.

Monsieur Aubert didn’t answer for a while. She could hear the bakery under his workshop. Somebody dropping a tray.

“You want me to sell a watch to a crook.”

“I want you to sell a watch to a crook so I can see where the crook keeps his money.”

She had her red pen in her hand. She was drawing boxes on the back of an invoice without looking.

“His money comes to an account in my name. It stays there. The same day, I send you the full price from my own. You get paid twice.”

“And at the end?”

“His father signs a bridge. And the ambulances get to a hospital eighteen minutes faster.”

Another silence.

“Your grandmother would have done exactly this.” He sighed. “I have one. Finished in September. A minute repeater, tourbillon, moon phase, white gold. The client who ordered it died in August.” Then, sharper: “It’s the best thing I’ve ever made. I will want it back, Mademoiselle.”

“You’ll have it back. I promise.”

That was the fourth of November. The first of three things. She did all three at once, for six weeks, and didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second thing was the team.

Four people. Serafina. Big Wu, the mechanic, forty and enormous, who’d been in prison twice for things he wouldn’t discuss. Mouse, nineteen, electronics and data, a ring through her nose, who spoke to nobody except Serafina. And Mr. Kwok, sixty-eight, forty years a taxi driver, who drove the transporter and made everyone’s lunch.

They looked at Aurelia the first day she came under the shutter. Cream suit. Heels. Exactly the way the men on the thirty-ninth floor had looked at her once.

“So this is the gilded bird.”

“This is my sister.” Serafina didn’t look up from the engine. “She’s paid your wages for three years, Wu.”

Big Wu looked at the heels.

“Can she change a wheel?”

“No.” Aurelia put her bag down on the bench beside the moka pot. “Can you read a sponsorship contract?”

Big Wu opened his mouth. Shut it.

He picked up a wheel brace and held it out.

She took it.

It took her fourteen minutes. In heels. She broke a nail on the first nut and swore in Milanese for the whole of the second. Big Wu stood over her with his arms folded and said nothing at all, which was worse than anything he could have said. When the last nut was tight she stood up with grease to the elbow and her hair falling down.

“Well?”

“Fourteen minutes.” He looked at his watch. “Car’s gone. Race is over. Everybody’s gone home.”

“Then I’ll come back tomorrow.”

She came back every day that week. By Friday she did it in four. Did Big Wu think any more of her? He did not.

“Paper sponsor,” she heard him say to Mr. Kwok on Friday night. “Rich girl. Nice for the photos.”

Mr. Kwok made her lunch anyway, the second week, with everyone else’s. By the third week he was putting extra chilli on hers. He’d noticed.

Mouse said one word to her on the twelfth day.

“Telemetry.”

Aurelia looked round. Mouse was holding out a laptop.

“Sorry?”

“Telemetry.” Very patient. Like Aurelia was slow. Mouse pointed at a graph. Then at the car. Then back at the graph.

Aurelia looked at it for a long moment.

“Oh! It’s a ledger.”

Mouse thought about that. Then she nodded. Once.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third thing was Fu Kang.

The watch went to the dealer in Macau on the twentieth, through a broker who’d worked with Monsieur Aubert for thirty years and asked nothing. The dealer rang Fu Kang that afternoon. Mr. Lu had a nephew who worked in the café across from the watch shop. The nephew reported that Fu Kang came the next morning by helicopter, spent forty minutes inside, and came out with the face of a man in love.

The money moved on the twenty-sixth.

She watched it go.

The workshop behind the boutique. Eleven at night. Chen Si on the little stool where women sat to try on rings, much too low for him, knees up round his ears. Qian at the bench with a laptop. Mr. Lu in his cardigan with a cup of tea he didn’t drink.

“There. It’s left the shop.”

“Where’s it going?”

“A company in Macau.” Qian typed. “Now a company in the British Virgin Islands.”

“And now?”

“Give it a minute, Mrs. Chen.”

A company in Singapore. A trust in Liechtenstein. Another company. And at the end of all of it, in the small hours, the account Aurelia had opened in Geneva in her own name.

Four hours, following it back.

At three in the morning Qian took his glasses off and rubbed his eyes.

“There.”

At the top of a chain of seven companies sat a trust. On a document nobody had ever expected anyone to read, there was a name for whose money it really was.

Fu Kang.

And underneath, the second one.

Fu Jianguo.

Nobody said anything.

Mr. Lu put his tea down on Enzo’s bench.

“Mrs. Chen. I’ve been a pawnbroker for thirty-one years.” His voice wobbled. “I’ve never seen anything so beautiful.”

Chen Si didn’t move.

He was looking at the second name. Just looking at it. His face had gone somewhere far away and very cold. Aurelia put her hand on his knee. His hand came down on hers and gripped so hard her rings bit.

“That’s not the son’s money,” he said, very low. “That’s his.”

“Yes.”

“His name. On paper. Nine years and I’ve never once found his name on anything.” He turned his head and looked at her. “You did it in three weeks. With a watch.”

“Mr. Lu did it. And Qian. And Monsieur Aubert. And a nephew in a café.” She turned her hand over under his. “I just sold a watch.”

“You have never just done anything.”

Only she heard it. Under the bench his foot found her ankle and stayed there.

“Clause five. His name on a document. That’s mine.” Still low. “I won’t use it yet.”

“I know.”

“You use the son. For your father. Keep the father’s name for me.” His thumb moved over her wrist. “In your safe. Under the Geneva pieces.”

“For the hall. At six in the morning.”

He nodded once.

Qian packed up. Mr. Lu buttoned his cardigan to the chin and bowed to both of them. The shop bell rang behind them in the dark.

Chen Si didn’t wait for it to stop ringing.

He came up off the little stool and took her face in both hands and kissed her against her own bench. Hard enough to knock a tray off the edge. A hundred tiny gold jump rings went everywhere, rattling across the floor like rain. She didn’t care. She had her hands inside his jacket before the last one stopped rolling.

“Nine years.” Against her mouth. “And you did it with a watch.”

She tried to say Mr. Lu’s name. He didn’t let her. He kissed her again, slower, until she couldn’t remember Mr. Lu or Liechtenstein or the name on the screen behind her. Then he stopped himself. Forehead on hers. Breathing all over the place.

“Tell me to take you home. Or tell me to stay.” Rough. “If I choose, it’s the bench.”

“Home.” She laughed into his neck. “Enzo counts the jump rings.”

So they picked them up first. Every one. On their knees on the workshop floor at four in the morning. He kissed her every time she found one. It took a very, very long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sponsorship deck happened on the first of December, because Big Wu said paper sponsor one time too many.

She sat on the garage floor at two in the morning under the one hanging lamp. Big Wu’s spare overalls, sleeves rolled up four times. Pencil behind her ear. Laptop balanced on a tyre. Serafina asleep in the back of Gilded with one boot hanging out of the window.

Every contract Serafina had ever signed. Every sponsor she’d ever spoken to. Every team in the national series and who paid them and how much.

Page eleven of the tyre contract stopped her dead.

She read clause fourteen three times. Then she said something in Milanese that would have got her slapped as a child.

At some point after four, she didn’t hear a thing, someone laid a camel coat over her shoulders. Someone set a paper cup down on the tyre beside the laptop. Hot soy milk. Under the cup, on a torn corner of cream paper, in a small exact hand:

Drink this. I didn’t. — C.S.

She drank it. She pulled the coat closed. How long had he been standing there? Long enough to bring soy milk. She didn’t look up. If she looked up she’d go after him, and she had nine pages left.

He’d stood by the shutter in the dark for a while first. Eleven minutes. He’d watched her chew the pencil. Watched her swear at a tyre contract in Milanese, under her breath, with a face like murder. Watched her push her hair back with a greasy wrist. He could have stood there till morning. He left before he woke her up by kissing her, which was the only other option.

At six she shook her sister awake.

“Sera. Sera. The tyre people.”

“Mmf. What about them.”

“Clause fourteen. You signed away your face. For tyres. Worldwide. For ever.”

Serafina sat up so fast she hit her head on the roof.

“I WHAT?”

“If you ever get famous, they own your face. For tyres.” Aurelia turned the laptop round. “I’ve fixed it. Well. I’ve worked out how to fix it. And I’ve done this.”

Forty pages. Logos. Numbers. A budget for a full national season. Eleven companies, every one of them a luxury house, every one of them somewhere Aurelia knew someone.

“They’re not buying a car.” She tapped the screen. “They’re buying a story. Two sisters from Milan. The one who left and the one who stayed. The gilded bird and the mechanic. And it’s true. That’s why they’ll pay for it.”

Serafina looked at the forty pages. Then at her sister, in Big Wu’s overalls, with a camel coat over the top and a pencil behind her ear and grease on her chin.

“You did this tonight? Why?”

“Because I’m good at it. I can read a contract and I can count tiles. Nonna said those were the only two things a woman needed.” She shrugged. “And because I’m not pretending I don’t fund you any more. I want everybody to know.”

“You don’t pretend to fund it any more.”

“No.” Aurelia laughed, a bit wildly. “Now I pretend I’m not terrified.”

Big Wu came in at seven. He read the deck standing up, with his coffee going cold, the whole forty pages. Nobody spoke. Mr. Kwok came in behind him and stopped dead in the doorway to watch.

Big Wu got to the end. He looked at Aurelia on the floor.

“Eleven companies.”

“Eleven.”

“Not four.”

“God, no.”

He grunted. It might have been approval. Then he went to the stove, made a fresh pot, filled the mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST MECHANIC, and put it into her hands himself.

Serafina’s jaw dropped. Nobody but Serafina drank out of that mug.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had lunch with Fu Kang at Da Gianni on the third of December.

Table by the window. Gold. The risotto.

He was handsome and lazy and wore a white gold minute repeater on his wrist. He flirted with her for twenty minutes, which told her he had no idea who she’d married. Which told her exactly how much his father told him.

Then she slid a folder across the cloth.

She watched him read. She watched him find his own name at the top of a chain of seven companies. Beside a watch shop in Macau with one customer. Beside fifteen per cent of eleven contracts. Beside a bridge.

She watched him go white.

“The vice-minister’s signature on Harbour Bridge Two. By the twentieth. No fifteen per cent. No company in Macau. No conditions.” She picked up her fork. “If it’s there, this stays in my safe. Nobody ever sees it.”

“And if…”

“If it isn’t, on the twenty-first it goes to the anti-corruption people. Three newspapers. And a man called Li Zhenhua, who I hear isn’t fond of your family.”

Fu Kang stared at her across the risotto.

“Who are you?”

She smiled at him.

“I’m the designer. I make jewellery.” She glanced at his wrist. “That’s a beautiful watch, by the way. Monsieur Aubert will want it back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The signature came on the nineteenth.

By fax, at four in the afternoon, to the Song Group. Her father rang a few minutes later and couldn’t speak at first. Just breathing. When he could, it came out in pieces.

“Tesoro… it’s signed. Fu signed. No conditions. Nothing.” A long breath. “Was it… was it you?”

“It was the bridge, Papà. It was always a good bridge.”

She heard him breathe out a long way off, at his desk.

“Your grandfather would have been very proud.”

She put the phone down and sat at her bench for a while.

That morning a plain brown envelope had come by courier from Macau. No note. She took the white gold minute repeater out of its tissue, wound it, and pressed the slide.

It chimed the time. Low notes for the hours. A double note for the quarter. Then the minutes, high and quick, clear as water on glass.

She wrapped it up and sent it back to Geneva, to a workshop above a bakery.

Thank you. It did exactly what it was made to do. — A.

chapters.title: Sisters at a Racetrack
chapters.desc: Serafina wins the last race of the season with AURELIA on her bonnet. Chen Si goes up to the VIP lounge to have a word with her mother.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t watch the car. Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
“You look like you came to buy the circuit.”

“I might. Later.”

Serafina laughed out loud. She was standing at the bottom of the grandstand at nine in the morning in her fireproof suit, top half tied round her waist, helmet under one arm, breath smoking in the cold. She looked up at her sister in the front row.

Every piece of gold Aurelia owned. All of it. A white coat with fur at the collar. Lipstick like a stop sign.

Beside her, in camel, her husband.

Serafina looked at him. He looked back. They’d met at the wedding. They’d said maybe forty words to each other since, and not one of them warm.

“Mr. Chen.”

“Miss Song.”

“If she throws up, hold her hair.”

“I will.”

“And don’t let her look away at the start. She’ll want to. Everybody does, the first time.” Serafina turned to her sister. Her voice changed. “Don’t watch the car, Lia. Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.”

Lia. Nobody had called her that since they were small. Since Milan. Since before everything.

Aurelia couldn’t answer. She nodded.

Serafina went back down to the pit lane, pulled on her helmet, and got into a black car with her sister’s name on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d never been to a motor race in her life.

Fashion shows. Auctions. The opera. Horses, once, at the old racecourse, where she’d been bored. A polo match in Argentina with her father, where she’d fallen asleep in a hat.

Nothing had told her about this.

Twenty-four engines started at once and the noise went straight through her body. It was like being hit. She grabbed the rail.

“That’s obscene!”

“Your sister’s is the loudest.”
