Chen Si didn’t flinch. Of course he didn’t. He took her hands off the rail, one and then the other, and pushed them into the pockets of his coat with his own. Inside, it was warm. His fingers laced through hers in the dark of the pocket and stayed.

She looked down at the grid. Twenty-four cars under a white sky. Red ones. Blue ones. Silver. Logos everywhere. And in the fourth row, low and long and matte black, a white number 7 on its side. Across the bonnet, in gold, in the same letters as the sign over 18 Harbour Road, one word.

AURELIA.

She’d seen it in the garage. She’d seen it on the transporter. She’d seen the proofs on her laptop at two in the morning. She hadn’t seen it here. On the grid. With eleven thousand people in the stands and cameras everywhere and her little sister sitting inside it.

Her eyes stung.

It was the cold. Obviously. It was very cold.

He took one hand out of the pocket and turned her coat collar up. One side. Then the other. Then he put his hand back.

She didn’t dare look at him. If she looked at him she’d go.

“Mrs. Chen!”

Mr. Kwok, at the bottom of the steps, waving a flask. Big Wu behind him like a wardrobe. Mouse behind Big Wu, hood up, earphones round her neck.

“Tea. With ginger. For the stomach.” Mr. Kwok pushed the flask up through the rail. “Sera says you get sick.”

“Sera talks too much.”

“Drink it anyway.”

Big Wu was looking at the sky, at the track, at anything except her.

“Fourth row,” he grunted. “Not good. Four.”

“Wu, she qualified fourth row…”

“I know. I’m not happy about it.”

Mouse came right up to the rail. She looked at Aurelia. At the gold. At her white knuckles. She reached up and tapped Aurelia’s hand once with one finger.

“Breathe.”

Then she was gone, back down the steps, before Aurelia could answer. Was that two words in six weeks? It was two words in six weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty laps.

The lights went out. The noise was the end of the world. Twenty-four cars went down the long straight towards the first corner like something poured out of a jug, and Aurelia did not look away.

She wanted to. God, she wanted to. Every part of her wanted to shut its eyes. They were too close together. The corner was too tight. Somewhere inside that river of colour was a black car with her name on it. Her sister was in it. What if anyone touched anyone? What if a tyre went? What if…

Don’t watch the car. Watch the gap.

She watched the gap.

She saw it open. First corner. On the inside, between a red car and the kerb. Less than a car wide. She saw it a whole second before anyone else in the stand because she was looking for it, and her body went cold all over.

No. Sera, no, it’s too small, it’s too…

The black car went into it.

Two wheels on the kerb. Two wheels on the paint. Through a gap that wasn’t a gap, and out the other side, and she came out third. The grandstand made a noise like an animal.

Aurelia found out she’d stopped breathing. She also found out she was crushing his hand inside his pocket so hard her rings were cutting into his knuckles.

He didn’t take his hand away.

She looked at him.

He wasn’t looking at her. He was watching the track with a face she’d seen exactly once. At her counter, the morning of the counter-offer. Total attention. Like he was learning something by heart and wouldn’t be told twice.

“She’s very good.”

“She’s insane!”

“Yes.” His eyes didn’t leave the black car. “That’s what very good means.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Third for eleven laps.

“Is that good? Third? Is third good?”

“Third is good.”

“It’s not first…”

“Wait.”

Second for six.

On lap eighteen, coming out of the tight corner at the far end they called the Needle, the car in first place went wide. A silver one, a Japanese name down the side. A metre. No more. And the black car with the gold name was already there, in the space it had left. Like it had known before the silver car did.

First.

“Si. Si! LOOK!”

“I’m looking.”

Aurelia didn’t hear anything after that. The stand was screaming and she didn’t hear it. She stood at the rail in the cold with every piece of gold she owned on and watched her sister drive the last two laps of the season alone in front. Nothing ahead of her but grey track and white sky.

She didn’t look away once.

The black car crossed the line.

The flag came down.

And Aurelia Chen, who did not cry in public, who’d walked out of her father’s party with her chin up and sat at the head of a criminal empire’s table and said no to her mother in front of three maids, stood in the front row of the grandstand and sobbed out loud. Both hands over her mouth. Ugly. Loud. Her whole face going.

Chen Si turned her into his chest.

One hand spread at the back of her head. The other round her back. Eleven thousand people. Every camera at the circuit pointing somewhere. He didn’t care about any of it. He held her face against his coat while she howled and the whole circuit shouted her sister’s name.

“She won.” Into the camel. Wet. “Si, she won…”

“I know.”

“I watched the gap!”

“I know. I saw you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the podium, in the cold, Serafina stood on the top step with a trophy in one hand and a magnum of champagne in the other. Her hair was standing up in sweaty spikes. She looked out at the crowd.

Then she found her sister in the front row. She pointed the bottle straight at her. She yelled something nobody could hear, and let go.

Most of it went over the photographers.

Some of it got the white coat with the fur collar.

Aurelia didn’t care. She stood there with champagne in her hair, laughing like an idiot, looking up at her sister on the top step. Somebody took that picture. It went on the front of the sports pages the next morning. And the business pages. And three weeks later, in Milan, on page one hundred and four of Italian Vogue.

SORELLE, said the headline. Sisters.

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw the mother first.

VIP lounge, above the pit lane, behind glass. In black. Alone at the window with a glass in her hand, looking down at the black car with the gold name on its bonnet.

Beside her, not quite next to her, a heavy grey-haired man in a dark suit. The face of somebody who’d been made a fool of and was trying to work out by whom.

“Li Zhenhua,” he said.

Aurelia followed his eyes. Her face changed.

“She brought him. To watch. So he’d see Sera. Her face. Her car.” Her voice went thin. “So when the photograph comes, he knows exactly who it is.”

“Wait here.”

“Si…”

“I’m not going to do anything.” Mild. “I’m going to say hello.”

He went up the stairs.

The lounge was warm and smelled of coffee and money. People moved out of his way without knowing why. He didn’t hurry. He took his gloves off as he walked, one finger at a time.

Li Zhenhua turned round. Saw him. Every bit of colour left his face at once. He’d heard the name, then. Good. That saved time.

“Mr. Li. Congratulations.”

“I… on what?”

“Your nephew. In the traffic division.” He folded his gloves together. “He’s been promoted. A post in the far west of the province. Very good post. A great deal of fresh air. It starts on the first of January.”

“I don’t…”

“You’ll want to see him off.” Pleasant. “He’ll be away a long time.”

Li Zhenhua put his glass down on the windowsill. He nodded twice. Quickly. A man who wanted a conversation to be over very badly. He went.

Then it was just the two of them at the glass.

Vittoria Song lifted her chin. Exactly the way her daughter did. It was almost funny.

“Mr. Chen.”

“Mrs. Song.” He looked down at the podium, where her younger daughter was spraying champagne at her elder one. “I read clause eight of my marriage contract in the car on the way here. To make sure I had it right.”

“And what is clause eight?”

“You’d recognise it.” He put his gloves in his pocket. “If you ever send a photograph of either of your daughters to anyone again, I’ll stop being polite.”

He left her at the window.

No need to look back. He’d seen her hand on the glass. The knuckles were white.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did you say?”

“To Li Zhenhua? Congratulations.” He opened the car door for her. “His nephew’s been promoted. Somewhere very far away.”

She stared at him.

“And to my mother?”

He waited till she was in.

“Something about clause eight. And that if she sent anyone a photograph of either of her daughters again, I’d stop being polite.”

She sat down in the car rather hard.

“Either.”

“Serafina. And you.” He got in beside her. “Your mother has two daughters. I married into both.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina caught them at the car park. Still in her fireproof suit. Still holding the trophy, which she clearly wasn’t ever putting down. Champagne in her hair. She leaned in at the window.

“Did you watch the gap?”

“I saw it before you went for it.” Aurelia’s voice was still wrecked. “First corner. I thought you were going to die.”

“So did I!” Cheerfully. “Big Wu says I’m not allowed to do that again till I’ve got a contract with a life insurance clause.” She looked past her sister at the man in the back seat. “Mr. Chen. You went to see my mother. What did you say?”

He looked at her for a moment.

“Something she didn’t want to hear.”

Serafina studied him. Then she stuck her hand in through the window, palm up. Like she wanted something put in it. Oil. Champagne. Bits of rubber.

He looked at the hand.

Then he took off his glove and laid his own hand flat on hers. His left. With the thin white line across the palm.

She looked down at the line. Then up at him.

“Zhao Zhendong has one of those. My sister told me what it means.”

“Yes.”

Serafina was quiet for once in her life.

“Then I don’t need to cut mine,” she said roughly, and closed her fingers round his once, hard. And let go. And went back to her car without looking round.

✦ ✦ ✦

The drive south was long and dark. Motorway lights went over them one after another.

Aurelia had her head on his shoulder.

“I didn’t throw up. I nearly did. At the first corner.”

“I know. I had my hand ready for your hair.” He kissed the top of her head. It smelled of champagne. “You didn’t shut your eyes once. I watched.”

He’d also, she found out that night, refused to let her put anything on his knuckles. Four little red crescents where her rings had gone in. She caught him looking at them twice before bed. The second time he saw her catch him and didn’t even pretend.

“Si.” A few miles later. “The Christmas party. In gold. With you. And a smile. That was her price.”

“The photograph’s gone. You don’t have to go.”

“I know.” She lifted her head. “I want to go.”

He looked at her.

“In gold. With you. And I want to smile.” She settled back on his shoulder. “Because I’ll be the only person in that house who knows she lost. And I want to watch her know it too.”

He laughed in the dark.

“My queen.”

“Don’t.”

“No?”

“Not yet. Save it.” She poked his chest. “For the party. I want you to say it there. Out loud. In front of everyone.”

He put two fingers under her chin and kissed her. Slow. Thorough. In the back of a car on the motorway with champagne drying in her hair, until she completely forgot she got sick in cars.

“Fine.” Against her mouth. “I’ll save that one.”

“Only that one?”

He kissed her again instead of answering.

chapters.title: My Queen Is Not a Title
chapters.desc: Aurelia wears a dress of gold to her mother’s Christmas party, and Chen Si calls her his queen in front of Fu Jianguo. Upstairs, in her old room, he makes her watch herself in the mirror.
chapters.epigraph: “She doesn’t need my name. She has her own.” — Chen Si
chapters.content:
“Hold still.”

“I am holding still.”

“You’re vibrating.”

“It weighs four kilos, Si. Everything I own is vibrating.”

The car had stopped at the bottom of the drive. Up the hill the house on the Peak was lit from top to bottom, every window gold, exactly like every Christmas she could remember. He turned her face to the light from the gate with two fingers. Then he ran his thumb along the edge of her bottom lip, once, slowly, and took away a smudge of red she hadn’t known about.

“There.”

“Is it straight?”

“It’s perfect.”

“You’d say that if it was on my forehead.”

“Yes.” He looked at his thumb. “But it’s straight.”

She grabbed his tie and yanked it. One side. Then the other. It had been fine before. Now it was hers.

“Better.”

“It was already…”

“Now it’s better.”

The driver opened the door. Two hundred people were inside that house. Her mother was inside that house. She put her hand on her husband’s arm and got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Christmas at the Peak never changed.

A tree in the hall, eight metres, flown in from Austria and done in white and silver by a man from Milan who came for a week every year and was never allowed to change a single bauble. Candles in every window. A string quartet in the music room. Franciacorta from her mother’s cousin’s vineyard. The same lobster. The same cake. The same faces.

The only new thing this year came through the front door at eight o’clock on her husband’s arm.

And every single person in the hall stopped talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d made the dress.

Not drawn it. Made it. Thousands of tiny links of yellow gold, each one smaller than a grain of rice, joined by hand into something so fine it moved like silk. Like the gold silk she’d worn on the balcony. Except this one weighed four kilos and caught every light in the room and threw it back at you.

Five weeks of nights after the garage shut. Nine hundred hours. Most of them Enzo’s, and two bench hands he’d summoned from Valenza who spoke no language she recognised. Every franc from the Geneva auction in November had gone into it. Including what Numero Uno had made.

In February, a man from Vogue would see one photograph of it and call it the most beautiful dress made in Asia this century.

Tonight, it was walking through her mother’s hall.

She didn’t look for her mother. No need. She could feel her somewhere in the house. Like a draught under a door.

✦ ✦ ✦

They found each other in the music room, by the fire.

Black, of course. Her mother was standing with an ambassador’s wife and the man who’d designed the opera house, who was sober this year, apparently. The room shifted when Aurelia came in. Her mother turned.

She looked at the dress.

She didn’t say anything.

Aurelia knew every single thing that face could do. Cold. Still. The Vogue smile. The little pause before the knife. She’d been learning it since before she could walk.

It didn’t do any of those.

For one second, by the fire in her own music room, Vittoria Conti looked at a dress her daughter had made with her own hands out of everything she’d ever sold. And her face just showed what she felt.

Anger? No. Aurelia had braced for anger. It looked like grief.

Then it was gone.

“Tesoro. You came.”

“You asked me to.” Aurelia smiled. “In gold. With a smile. Here I am.”

Her mother looked at her a moment longer. Then at the man beside her.

“Mr. Chen.”

“Mrs. Song.”

The ambassador’s wife, who knew nothing about anything, clapped her hands together.

“What a beautiful dress! Who made it?”

“I did.”

The ambassador’s wife laughed. Like it was a lovely little joke.

Her mother didn’t laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fu Jianguo was by the fire in the drawing room. He was always by the fire in the drawing room.

He came every year. A vice-minister. People went up to him one at a time. Like queuing for a priest. He was grey and thin and very ordinary. Rimless glasses. A cardigan under his suit jacket, like a retired schoolteacher. You’d pass him in the street and not look twice.

Chen Si saw him from the doorway.

Nine years. He’d been in rooms with this man perhaps thirty times in nine years. Galas. Openings. One funeral. He knew that Fu held his glass in his left hand so the right was free to shake. That he drank half of whatever he was given and no more. That he left every party just before eleven, by the side door, and that his driver smoked while he waited.

Four steps from here to the fire. He’d measured every room he’d ever shared with this man the same way. It was a habit. It meant nothing. It just happened.

Beside him, his wife’s hand on his arm tightened.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

He walked in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go to Fu.

He walked her straight into the room in four kilos of gold, and the room opened in front of them, the way rooms did. He walked past the fire. Past Fu Jianguo. Close enough that Fu had to step back half a pace to let them by.

He didn’t look at him. Not once.

Aurelia felt it. Nobody else could have. His face didn’t move. His arm under her hand didn’t change. He just went very still, all the way through, the way he did over the list with nineteen names on it. For about three steps he didn’t breathe.

Then they were at the far window, and her father was turning round.

He was with three men from the bank, the head of the port authority, and the man who owned the biggest television channel in the province. He saw them and his whole face lit up.

“Tesoro! Chen Si!” He grabbed his son-in-law’s hand in both of his. “I wanted to thank you. Both of you. The bridge…”

“Don’t thank me. I didn’t do anything.”

“But…”

“I didn’t write a letter.”

He said it mildly. Pleasantly. At exactly the volume that carried. To the men from the bank. To the port authority. To the television channel. And to the fire at the other end of the room, where a grey man in rimless glasses had gone very still with a glass in his left hand.

“I didn’t make a call. I didn’t speak to anyone at the ministry.” He turned and looked at his wife. “My wife did that. All of it. On her own.”

Five men turned to look at Aurelia.

“Your… wife, Mr. Chen?” The television man. Faintly.

“My wife.”

“In my house, and in my business, and in this city, when my wife speaks, she speaks for me.” Still mild. “She doesn’t need my name. She has her own.”

He lifted her hand. The one with the heavy ring made from her grandmother’s earrings. He kissed her knuckles. In front of all of them.

“She is my queen.”

It wasn’t for her. It was for the room. Nobody standing there took it for a pet name. It was a line drawn across the floor, and the far end of it was by the fire.

Nobody said anything.

Then her father, who’d said no to Fu Jianguo in March for a dead man with a suitcase, put his hand on his son-in-law’s shoulder and squeezed. Once. Hard.

“Thank you.”

“Papà, you’re crushing him.”

“Good.” Her father didn’t let go. “Good.”

At the other end of the room, by the fire, Fu Jianguo put his glass down on the mantelpiece. Half full.

And walked out. At nine. Nearly two hours early.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother found her at ten, on the landing.

The same landing. The same stairs. Where she’d stood three years ago, at twenty, and watched Serafina go out of the front door with one bag. Where she’d said nothing at all. Because their mother had been standing at the bottom.

Their mother was standing at the bottom now.

She looked up at her elder daughter in the dress of gold.

“You made it. Yourself. With your hands.”

“Yes.”

“From the auction.” Very low. “From Numero Uno.”

“Yes.”

Her mother was quiet for a moment.

“My mother wore her last gown at a show in Milan when I was six weeks old. I was there. On my nurse’s knee.”

Her hand was on the newel post. “She used to tell me about it. Valentino. She said it was the most beautiful thing anyone had ever seen.”

Aurelia didn’t move.

“It wasn’t as beautiful as that.”

“Mamma…”

“I wanted to be a designer. When I was your age.” She said it to the banister, not to Aurelia. Flat. Like reading out a receipt.

“You never…”

“My father said it was for shopgirls. A Conti didn’t make things. A Conti was seen in things.” She looked at the dress. “So I was seen. For twenty years. Every runway in Europe. I never made anything in my life.”

She turned round and walked away down the hall in black, towards the music room and the quartet.

She didn’t look back.

Aurelia stood on the landing in four kilos of gold and held on to the banister with both hands. Her legs had stopped working. They’d just stopped.

How long was she there? A minute? Ten?

When she looked up, Chen Si was at the top of the stairs behind her. He’d heard. Of course he’d heard. Every door in that house was glass.

He held out his hand.

“Show me your room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her room was at the end of the east corridor, and nobody had touched it since she was eighteen.

White. White furniture from Milan. White curtains. A white piano she hadn’t opened since Vienna. And the shelves. Floor to ceiling. Trophies, medals, certificates, rankings. Every one of them first. 1st. 1st. Winner. 1st Place. In gold frames, in rows, from age five to age seventeen.

There was a gap on the third shelf. The certificate from her last year of school said 2nd. Her mother had never framed it.

And opposite the bed, the mirror. Tall. Gilt frame. From her grandmother’s house in Milan. Every morning from fifteen to eighteen she’d stood in front of it before she went downstairs. Checking. Every hair. Every crease.

Chen Si shut the door.

He looked at the trophies one by one. The same way he’d once gone through her ledgers.

Then he looked at her, standing in the middle of the white room in front of the mirror.

“You checked yourself in that every morning.”

“Yes.”

“So there’d be nothing for her to find.”

“Yes.”

He came and stood behind her. In the glass she watched him. Slight. Dark. Very still. His hands came up and rested on her shoulders, on the gold.

“Clause nine,” he said.

She met his eyes in the mirror.

“Otherwise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Don’t look away.”

He found the clasp at the back of her neck. The whole dress hung from it, like the wedding dress had. When the clasp went, everything went.

He didn’t open it.

He put his mouth on the side of her neck, just above it, and kept his eyes on hers in the glass.

“You looked in this every morning to see if you were good enough.” Against her skin. “Tonight you’re going to look in it and watch what you do to me.”

She forgot how to breathe.

“Don’t shut your eyes. Not once. If you shut them, I stop.” His hand went down her arm, over the gold, link by tiny link. “I want you to see all of it. I want you to see your face when I…”

He told her. Low. In her ear. Exactly what he was going to do. Then he did it. Slowly. With his eyes on hers in the glass the whole time.

She didn’t shut her eyes.

She stood in the white room where she’d been perfect every morning for three years, in front of her grandmother’s mirror, in a dress made of everything she’d ever sold, and she watched. His hands on the gold. His mouth on her throat. Her own face, changing. Losing its chin. Losing its smile. Losing every single thing her mother had ever drilled into it, until the woman in the glass was flushed, wild, open-mouthed. Nowhere near perfect.

“Si…”

“Eyes.”

“I am…”

“Keep them on me.”

Her knees went. He caught her round the waist and held her up against him. No stopping. No hurry. She kept her eyes open out of pure spite. Mostly spite. He laughed into her neck. He knew.

When he finally opened the clasp, four kilos of gold slid off her shoulders and down her body and landed on her mother’s white carpet with a sound like rain.

“Look,” he said into her ear.

She looked.

“That’s what I see. Every day.” His arms came round her from behind. “That’s who I married. Not the one who checked the mirror.”

“She’s a mess.”

“Yes.” He kissed her shoulder. “Mine.”

She didn’t look away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards they lay on the narrow white bed she’d slept in at seventeen, under all those gold frames. Very faintly, from downstairs, came the quartet and two hundred voices.

1st. 1st. Winner. 1st Place.

“She never framed the second one.”

“I noticed.”

“I always thought it was because she was ashamed of it.”

“And now?”

She stared at the ceiling.

“Tonight I thought maybe she couldn’t stand to look at it. Because it was the only one that was mine. Not hers.” She shut her eyes. “She wanted to be a designer, Si. She never told me. Not once. My whole life.”

He didn’t say anything. His hand went up and down her back.

“I don’t forgive her.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I don’t. Not for Vienna. Not for the nine days. Not for the party. Not for Sera.” She opened her eyes. They were wet. “But I understand her now. A bit. And I hate that.”

“I know.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“You said it. Downstairs. In front of everyone. In front of him.”

“I wanted him to hear.” He touched her face. “A title’s something somebody gives you. They can take it back. They can come at six in the morning and walk it down the stairs.” His thumb wiped under one of her eyes. “Nobody gave you this. You took it. You sat in my chair.”

She put her head back down on his chest. On the floor by the mirror the dress lay in a heap of light.

Somebody knocked on the door.

They both froze.

“Signora Aurelia?” Signora Pina. Through the wood. Trying very hard to sound like a maid and not like someone who was laughing. “Signora Vittoria says the guests are asking where you are.”

Aurelia shut her eyes.

“Tell her I’m upstairs. With my husband.”

A pause.

“I already did, signora.”

chapters.title: A Snake in the Syndicate
chapters.desc: Someone parks a lorry across the coast road in front of Zhao’s car. Chen Si comes home with shaking hands, knowing Sun Wei sold his diary, and decides to go to Sun Wei’s New Year’s Eve dinner anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Zhendong doesn’t brake.” — Chen Si
chapters.content:
Zhendong always drove the coast road at night. He didn’t like tunnels.

Why not? “Two ends,” he’d said once, years ago, when Chen Si asked.

That was the whole explanation. It was the only road from the east into the city that didn’t go through one. So they took it. Cliff on the left. Sea on the right. A long blind bend above the old fishing harbour at Lantern Bay.

The meeting in the east had gone on too long. Chen Si was in the back with a file on his knee he wasn’t reading. It was two in the morning, the twenty-eighth of December. The car was doing eighty.

They came round the bend.

A lorry. Across both lanes. Sideways. No lights.

Zhendong saw it at forty metres. Chen Si saw his brother see it.

And Zhendong didn’t brake.

Anyone else would have braked. Braking was what the lorry was for. A car braking hard on a blind bend at eighty stops, or spins, and either way it ends up sitting in the road in the dark in front of a lorry. And whoever’s waiting behind the lorry has all the time in the world.

Zhendong dropped two gears and put his foot to the floor.

He turned the wheel hard left. At the cliff. At a gap between the front of the lorry and the rock that was maybe a car and a half wide. They went through it with the passenger side grinding along the cliff face. A long scream of metal. Sparks past the window like a firework going off sideways.

Out the other side. Still accelerating.

In the mirror, behind them, three flashes. Four. Tiny. Far away. Over almost before they’d started.

Nothing hit.

Chen Si sat back. He took out his phone and made one call. It lasted under a minute. Then he put the phone away and looked out at the black sea.

Four kilometres later Zhendong said:

“Hm.”

That was the only word either of them said until they got home.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was awake.

She was always awake when he came back late on the coast road. She sat on the long grey sofa with a book she wasn’t reading and a cup of tea she wasn’t drinking. Married seven months and she’d turned into him. Horrifying.

She heard the lift a little before three.

His key. His footsteps in the hall. She always heard them now. They stopped.

Then a second set. Heavier. Zhao’s voice, very low. Then nothing.

She put the book down and went to the hall.

Zhao was in the open doorway. Black coat. Not a hair out of place. Behind him, in the corridor, she could hear the lift going back down.

“He’s fine.”

“Are you fine?”

He looked at her. Four seconds. Maybe five.

“Hm.”

He shut the door himself, very gently, from the outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si was standing in the middle of the room.

Camel coat. Tie straight. Hair tidy. There wasn’t a mark on him anywhere.

His hands were shaking.

Fourteen months. A balcony, a counter, a chessboard, a bench, a registrar. She’d never once seen his hands shake. Not once.

“Si?”

He told her standing up. He couldn’t seem to sit down. The bend. The lorry. The cliff. The flashes in the mirror.

Then, in exactly the same voice, the rest.

“The lorry belongs to a haulage firm in the east. The owner reported it stolen at midnight.” Very calm. “By the morning his firm won’t have a contract anywhere in the province. Or a licence. Or a bank that answers the phone.”

“Si…”

“He’ll know why. Nobody will need to tell him.” His hands were still going. He didn’t seem to notice. “The man who parked it is at the Docks. On a plastic chair. With some of Zhendong’s people. They’re asking him one question.” A pause. “He can take as long as he likes to answer.”

She didn’t say anything.

She went to him. She took both his shaking hands in both of hers and held them. Hard. Pressed them flat between her palms. She stood there and held on until they stopped.

It took a long time.

When they had, she let go of one, reached into the pocket of her robe and took out the black jade queen. She’d been holding it all night on the sofa. She hadn’t even noticed she’d picked it up.

She put it in his palm and closed his fingers round it.

He looked down at his own fist.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Who knew you’d be on that road tonight?”

Her voice was level. It was costing her everything.

“The meeting was set up on Thursday. You didn’t tell me where it was until this morning. Zhendong always takes the coast road because he hates tunnels.” She looked at him. “Who knew all three?”

“Qian. Zhendong. You.” A beat. “And whoever was at the meeting on Thursday.”

“Who was at the meeting on Thursday?”

He didn’t answer.

He didn’t need to. She’d been there.

The thirty-ninth floor. The head of the long black table, in his chair, which was her chair now at every meeting, while he sat in an office chair at the corner. Five men along the window. The shaved head. The tinted glasses. The sunflower seeds. Mr. Lu in his cardigan.

And at the end, nearest the glass, with his warm, tired, fatherly smile, Sun Wei.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got him onto the sofa in the end. She had to push.

She poured him a whisky and put it into his hand. He looked at it. A man who never drank anything anyone gave him. Then he drank half of it in one go.

She’d never seen him do that. She sat down beside him very carefully.

“You knew.”

“Since the furniture. The basement in the old town.”

“That was more than a year ago.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve known he was stealing from you for a year. And you let him sit at the table every Thursday.” Her voice was dropping lower and lower. “You let him call you Si.”

“I wanted to know who he was stealing for.” He looked at the whisky. “I found out in October. I didn’t tell you.”

“Clause three.”

“I was going to. After Christmas. After the race and the party and your mother.” He shut his eyes. “I didn’t want to put it on you as well. That was wrong. I’m sorry.”

“Who?”

He opened his eyes.

“Fu Kang.”

She went cold all over. Fu Kang? The idiot with the watch?

“The furniture money went east. Then to a company. Then to another company. Then Macau.” Something that wasn’t really a smile. “The same seven companies you found with a watch. Two years of Sun Wei’s money. Paid to the son.”

“For what?”

“For a seat at the father’s table one day.” He turned the glass. “And what does an old man sell to get a seat like that? My diary. Where I’ll be. When.”

“The grey saloon.” It came out of her before she knew she was going to say it. “In September. Old. Nice manners. He called me son.”

“Sun Wei calls the waiters son.”

“He calls the waiters…” She put both hands over her face. “Dio.”

“And since you had lunch with him, Fu Kang has a very good reason to want me dead.”

She took her hands away.

“Me. He should want me dead. I’m the one who had lunch.”

“He doesn’t know that.” He put the empty glass on the floor. “He thinks you work for me. Everybody does. Except this room. And Zhendong. And your father.” He turned his head on the sofa to look at her. “I said it at the party. She speaks for me. He heard I sent her.”

A long pause.

“So he sent a lorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move.

She sat on the sofa in her silk pyjamas and looked at the harbour and made herself think. Like a machine. Like a ledger. Seven companies. A lorry on a bend. A kind old smile at the end of a long black table. Son.

“You’re not going to do anything.” Flat. “Are you.”

“Not yet.”

“Why not?”

“If I touch Sun Wei now, Fu Kang knows I know. He runs to his father. His father protects him.”

“So?”

“So I lose nine years of work over one lorry.” He looked at her. “And Sun Wei isn’t the only one. A man who’s sold my diary for two years has friends. On the thirty-ninth floor. In the routes. I don’t know all of them yet.”

“So you wait.”

“So I invite him to dinner.”

She turned and stared at him.

“There’s a dinner every year. New Year’s Eve. On a boat in the harbour. Everyone who matters.”

“I know about the boat.”

“Sun Wei has organised it for eleven years. He chooses the boat. The menu. The wine. This year I let him choose everything. And I watch who he talks to. And who he doesn’t.”

“And if he tries again? On the boat?”

“He won’t. Not in front of all the people who still believe in him.” A breath. “He’s a snake. Snakes are easy. Once you know which way they’re facing.”

She looked at him. At his calm face. At the queen still in his fist. At the empty glass on the floor.

“You were nearly killed tonight.”

“Zhendong doesn’t brake.”

“You were NEARLY KILLED, Chen Si!”

It came out of her as a scream. The whole flat rang with it.

He looked at her.

“Yes,” he said. “I was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

And that was it. That was the thing that did it.

She didn’t cry prettily. She’d never in her life cried prettily. Her face went and her whole body went with it and the noise that came out of her was the one she’d swallowed in Vienna at eleven and every day since. She doubled over on the sofa with her arms round her own ribs and howled.

He had her before she’d finished the first breath.

He pulled her into his lap and wrapped both arms round her and held on while she shook. She hit his chest. Once. Twice. He let her. She grabbed his coat in both fists and cried into it until it was soaked through.

“You were in a car…”

“I know.”

“On a cliff…”

“I know.”

“And I was sitting here with a book…”

He took her face in his hands. He kissed her eyelids. One. The other. They were swollen and wet and he kissed them anyway, very slowly, like he had nowhere else to be ever again.

“I’m here,” he said. “Aurelia. I’m here.”

She looked at him with her face wrecked and her mascara everywhere and her breath still jumping.

“Clause four.” Shaky. Furious. “You don’t keep me somewhere safe. So I’m coming to the dinner.”

“I know.”

“I’m sitting next to you. And I’m watching Sun Wei too. All night. Every word. Every glass. And if he so much as looks at you wrong I’ll…”

“I know you will.” He put his hands over hers. “That’s why I married you.”

She kissed him.

He was already reaching for her. Both hands. Hauling her in. Like he’d held himself together since the bend at Lantern Bay only so he could do exactly this.

It wasn’t how she usually kissed him. Not a move. Not a game. It was hard. Scared. Angry. Both her hands in his hair, her knees either side of him on the long grey sofa. He made a sound against her mouth she’d never heard out of him and pulled her down.

No clauses. No orders. No counting. No mirrors. Nobody set the terms. She dragged his coat off his shoulders, then his jacket, then pulled his shirt open so hard two buttons went flying and pinged off the window. He hauled her silk pyjamas over her head and threw them somewhere into the dark. They didn’t make it off the sofa. They didn’t try.

It was fast. Rough. Clumsy. Her elbow caught his jaw. He knocked the lamp over. Nobody stopped. She bit his shoulder, hard enough to leave teeth. He said her name into her throat like something tearing in half.

Two people who’d nearly lost each other on a road above the sea. Holding on with everything they had.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on top of him under his coat with her ear on his chest. His heart was still going much too fast.

“You were scared.”

He was quiet.

“Yes.”

“Of the lorry?”

“No.” His hand moved on her back. “Zhendong doesn’t brake. I wasn’t scared of the lorry.” A pause. “I was scared for the four kilometres after. When we were safe. I sat in the back and thought, if he’d braked, I wouldn’t have come home.”

She didn’t move.

“And you’d have sat on this sofa with your tea. Listening for the lift. And it wouldn’t have come.” His voice went very flat. “And nobody would have been here with you. Like my mother. In his chair. Watching the door.”

She lifted her head.

“I won’t be on my own. Not like that. Not ever.”

She put her hand flat on his chest, over that stupid racing heart.

“If anything ever happens to you, I won’t sit and watch the door. I’ll go and find whoever did it. And I’ll take everything they have. And then I’ll come back and sit in your chair.” Her chin came up. Swollen eyes and all. “And everyone will know whose chair it is.”

He looked at her for a long time.

“I believe you.” Something almost like a smile. “That’s not a comfort. That’s the most frightening thing anyone’s ever said to me.”

She put her head back down.

On the floor beside the sofa, his phone buzzed. Once.

He reached down for it. Looked at it. Then held it up so she could see.

Sun Wei: Si! Heard about the coast road. Terrible!! Thank God you’re safe. Don’t worry about a thing, I’ve booked the Pearl for New Year’s Eve, same as always. Best menu yet. You and your queen at the top table. Looking forward to it! W.

She read it twice.

“Your queen.”

“He heard it at the party. Everybody did.”

She looked at the text for a long moment. Then she handed the phone back.

“Reply. Say we’re looking forward to it.”

He looked at her.

She lifted her chin.

“And tell him I’ll choose the wine.”
